#5804. Aluminum–Air Generators for Data Centres Face a Metal Logistics Test

California startup Voya Energy announced a $35 million financing round in August 2026 for generators that use prepared scrap aluminum, air and water to produce electricity without combustion. Its immediate opportunity includes replacing diesel backup equipment at data centres, where exhaust, noise and permitting can be genuine obstacles. The company also describes a larger market for firm power at grid-constrained sites, including systems operating around the clock. The electrochemistry is established, but delivering competitive electricity requires a materials supply chain that the generator specifications do not describe.

An aluminum–air cell consumes aluminum. It does not accept electricity through a charging cable and return to its original chemical state. Aluminum reacts with oxygen and water, producing electrical energy and aluminum hydroxide, sometimes called aluminum trihydrate. The generator needs more metal when the fuel is spent, and the hydroxide has to be collected, transported and either sold into another market or processed further. The aluminum brought to a data centre already embodies substantial electricity used earlier to turn aluminum compounds into metal. That upstream energy belongs in the assessment.

I encountered the same supply-chain issues when I examined Wright Electric’s aluminum–air aircraft proposal in 2021. Prepared aluminum would have needed delivery to airports, followed by collection and processing of spent material. Data centres avoid the aircraft weight constraint, while retaining the need for deliveries of prepared fuel and industrial handling of reaction products.

The operating schedule determines the size of that problem. Voya’s August announcement emphasizes diesel replacement while also describing larger, continuously available power installations. To test the larger proposition, I calculated the materials needed for a hypothetical 100 MW data centre supplied continuously by aluminum–air generation. Using the company’s reported 57% conversion efficiency and aluminum’s theoretical electrochemical energy, the system consumes roughly 520 metric tons of metal each day and produces about 1,500 metric tons of aluminum hydroxide. That becomes approximately 190,000 tons of incoming metal and 550,000 tons of outgoing material each year. The additional byproduct mass comes from oxygen and water incorporated in the reaction. These are scenario quantities, not measured operations at a Voya site.

An intermittent backup generator could consume orders of magnitude less aluminum annually than the continuous 100 MW case, changing the economics of deliveries and residue handling. Voya’s interest in low-grade contaminated scrap deserves examination, since some metal streams are difficult to sort into high-quality recycled products. Yet scrap is not automatically valueless because it is contaminated. Recycling aluminum into new metallic products uses approximately 95% less energy than making primary metal, and improving scrap recovery is itself an important industrial decarbonization opportunity. Buying that scrap as expendable fuel can compete with other recovery routes as their technology and economics improve.

Voya initially expects to sell aluminum hydroxide and proposes metal regeneration as a longer-term option. Those are different uses for the spent material. A 2026 lifecycle assessment modeled electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency of 29–35% for aluminum–air storage pathways involving regeneration. That finding is not a test result for Voya’s equipment, but it indicates how much additional electricity and processing could be needed to close the material loop. A company selling the hydroxide cannot also assume it will recover that same material for fuel without buying it back.

Voya’s published metal-price target leaves limited room for other costs. In a 2025 California Energy Commission submission, the company listed targets below $0.30/kWh for delivered electricity and $0.50 per pound for the metal fuel. At 57% conversion efficiency, the latter implies about $0.24/kWh for aluminum alone, before fuel preparation, generator capital, transport, residue handling or financing. Saleable hydroxide could provide an offset where purity, processing costs and buyers support it. The generation target remains a target, rather than a demonstrated commercial tariff.

There may be worthwhile applications for compact, noncombustion backup power where diesel is hard to permit and suitable scrap is readily available. Continuous power for large AI facilities calls for a much larger comparison with grid connections, generation and rechargeable batteries. The chemistry works, but the economics must account for every load of metal delivered, every load of residue removed and the electricity consumed upstream.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment follows the aluminum through the generator, the possible recycling and regeneration routes, Voya’s cost targets and the very different material demands of backup and continuous generation.

#5803. Industry Voices—The other AI divide is already opening in healthcare

Industry Voices—The other AI divide is already opening in healthcare" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The debate over AI and inequality has largely focused on people—who will have access to the technology, who will benefit from it and who risks being left behind. But inside healthcare, another AI divide is already taking shape. This one is between the hospitals that have the money, talent and infrastructure to put AI to work and those that don't.

The numbers are striking. According to federal data on hospital AI adoption, 71% of U.S. hospitals used predictive AI integrated with their electronic health records in 2024. But adoption reached 96% among large hospitals compared with just 59% among small hospitals. Among hospitals belonging to multi-hospital systems, 86% used predictive AI. Among independent hospitals, it was only 37%.

That gap matters because AI is quickly becoming part of how hospitals survive, not simply an innovation project. The same federal data show some of the fastest-growing hospital AI applications are decidedly practical, including billing and scheduling. These are exactly the kinds of labor-intensive functions where financially stressed hospitals need to find efficiencies.

Yet those hospitals may be the least equipped to make the investment.

Hospitals remain extraordinarily dependent on people to operate. According to the American Hospital Association, workforce spending accounted for about 60% of hospital expenses in 2025, exceeding $1 trillion. Total hospital expenses grew 7.5% that year, more than twice the growth in hospital prices.

This creates a dangerous catch-22. The hospitals with the greatest need to use technology to redesign labor-intensive operations frequently have the least capacity to invest in doing so.

A large health system can afford an AI pilot that fails. It can hire an innovation team, absorb a lengthy implementation, build governance and compliance infrastructure, and try again if the economics don't work. A safety-net, community or independent hospital often has far less room for error. A multi-year software contract that might eventually produce savings still requires money today.

And buying the technology is only the beginning.

Successful AI deployment requires workflow redesign, change management, integration, measurement and governance. Even among hospitals already using predictive AI, the federal data show meaningful variation in how comprehensively models are evaluated for accuracy, bias and performance after implementation. Smaller, rural and independent hospitals also continue to lag their larger counterparts in adoption.

If we leave the market to work this out one hospital at a time, we should expect that divide to compound. Systems that successfully automate expensive workflows can reinvest those savings into their next technology investment. They build institutional knowledge. Their employees get better at implementation. They become more attractive partners to technology companies looking for sophisticated customers and proving grounds.

The hospitals that wait don't simply remain where they are. They lose ground. The answer cannot be telling every hospital to develop a better AI strategy. We need to change the ownership and financing model for healthcare AI.

Hospitals already know how to collaborate when acting collectively creates an advantage. Group purchasing organizations allow them to aggregate purchasing power rather than negotiate for every product independently. Clinical research networks allow institutions to pool patients, expertise and infrastructure to answer questions no single organization could address as effectively alone.

We should apply the same instinct to AI. Instead of requiring every health system to independently buy, implement and govern variations of the same technology, health systems should increasingly pool their purchasing power, operational expertise and capital to build common AI capabilities. And smaller, independent and safety-net organizations need a path into those collaborations rather than simply another vendor contract.

The venture community has a responsibility here as well. We need financing structures that acknowledge the economic reality of the organizations that really need to adopt technologies. That could mean performance-based models where payment is tied to verified savings rather than large upfront commitments. It could mean consortium models in which multiple health systems share implementation resources and governance.

And increasingly, it should mean giving health systems ownership in the companies and infrastructure they help create. Ownership matters because the economics of AI are changing quickly. As the technology itself becomes increasingly commoditized, enduring value will come from distribution, proprietary workflows, real-world implementation knowledge and access to the environments where healthcare actually happens. Health systems contribute enormously to each of those things. Under the traditional vendor model, however, they can provide the workflows, clinical expertise and proving ground and then pay someone else an annual fee for the resulting product.

That bargain deserves to be reconsidered. Collective ownership can help address the trust problem, too. AI adoption isn't only a technology decision. It requires decisions about validation, monitoring, clinical safety and who is accountable when something goes wrong. Federal researchers found that hospitals increasingly rely on multiple parties to evaluate AI, with 74% reporting more than one entity accountable for evaluation. Smaller hospitals should not each have to recreate that infrastructure from scratch.

Shared infrastructure could include common validation standards, clinical oversight, monitoring and implementation expertise. That would give more hospitals access not only to AI, but to the capabilities required to deploy it responsibly.

None of this means every hospital needs to own every AI company, or that traditional vendors disappear. It means we should stop assuming that the only scalable model for healthcare innovation is one technology company selling essentially the same capability to thousands of hospitals one contract at a time.

The AI divide between hospitals is already here. If adoption continues to depend primarily on the size of an organization's balance sheet, the institutions best positioned today will keep accumulating advantages while those with the least room for error fall further behind.

AI gives hospitals a real opportunity to break their dependence on increasingly expensive, labor-intensive ways of operating. But the organizations that need that opportunity most cannot be the last ones able to afford it. Preventing that outcome will require more than making AI cheaper. It will require giving more health systems the ability to build, govern and share in the technology's value, transforming them.

AI should become something hospitals build together, not another advantage reserved for those that could already afford to move first.

Amanda DeMano is SVP of venture creation at Abundant Venture Partners.

Editor's Note: Abundant Venture Partners is a strategic investor in the makers of certain AI technologies, including SpendRule and Playback Health.

#5802. Jeep Wrangler Scrambler SRT Concept Is Your Inner-Child's Dream Jeep With A Hemi V8, Reservable Jump Seats And Independent Front Suspension

Jeep has just done something with the Wrangler that has never been done before: given it independent front suspension, and somehow, that's not even the wildest part of its latest concept vehicle. The automaker just pulled the covers off the Wrangler Scrambler SRT Concept at the 2026 SEMA Show in Las Vegas, and right away you can tell this thing is no ordinary Jeep truck.

Right above that independent front suspension sits a naturally aspirated 6.4-liter HEMI V8 with 470 horsepower and 470 pound-feet of torque on tap. Out back, you'll find a Trophy Truck-style rear axle. The whole truck is finished in what Jeep calls Punk'n orange, and its bed is actually pretty functional while also serving as a nod to Jeep's own Scrambler history. It has reversible jump seats that let rear occupants face either forward or backward toward the rear of the truck — a layout built for desert chase trucks and spotters. Is it a gimmick? Yeah, but it's also sick as hell.

Equally sick as hell are the looks — especially up front where designers clearly took inspiration from the CJ-8 Scrambler of the early 1980s. However, it's a damn slight more aggressive than that car with its shark nose front end and massively flared fenders. The rear, while much shorter than your typical Jeep Gladiator, looks fairly similar. The body itself is far shorter as well, which isn't surprising when you consider it only has two doors. All in all, it doesn't look too dissimilar from the Jeep Sandstorm Concept we saw back in 2018, but they're certainly different vehicles.

Since the dawn of man, Wranglers have had solid front axles, but that changes for the Scrambler SRT. Developed with off-road racer Casey Currie, the new independent front suspension delivers 14 inches of travel up front and 15 inches out back. Jeep says the goal is better high-speed stability, more precise steering (impossible for it to be less precise) and better wheel control when blasting through the desert. This is a Jeep aimed at desert running, not the rock-crawling crowd that usually flocks to Wranglers.

As I mentioned earlier, the Trophy Truck-inspired rear suspension is its own feat of engineering. It's built to soak up high-speed impacts rather than slowly articulate over rocks. When paired with beefy 37-inch tires, it's clear that the Wrangler Scrambler SRT Concept is designed for off-road speed first and foremost. While I do love rockcrawling, there's nothing quite like prerunning to really get the heart pounding.

Of course, none of this is really, well, real. The Wrangler Scrambler SRT Concept is very much a concept, though I'll admit, I won't be too shocked if the Wrangler ends up getting independent front suspension at some point in the future. The Ford Bronco has it, and the Earth has yet to collapse in on itself despite that.

While this concept is still unmistakably a Jeep, Tim Kuniskis, head of American Brands, SRT Performance and Direct Connections at Stellantis North America, said the project was a dare to the brand's own playbook, which is probably where the use of an IFS comes in. Sure, it's going to tick some Jeep loyalists off, but some departures are good departures.

#5801. If The US Department Of Defense Gets Solar Power, Why Can’t We?

In the topsy-turvy world of today’s federal energy policy, solar power is a bad thing. Various members of the President’s cabinet have advised that solar is  “unreliable,” and that solar power plants routinely experience “catastrophic failure” with every sunset. So why does the US Department of Defense continue to pursue solar-enabled microgrids at its facilities? Asking for a friend…

Though some solar projects at military facilities are relatively small, they are stamped with the seal of approval from the Defense Department, and that can have an outsized influence on public perceptions about the reliability, security, and durability of photovoltaic systems.

The history-making White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico is a case in point. In February of 2025 the facility celebrated the launch of a new, 700-kilowatt solar array designed and built by the joint venture HSGS-Ameresco.

At 700 kW, the new array is peanuts compared to the megawatt scale common among modern solar power plants. However, a little can go a long way in some cases, particularly when solar is integrated with other energy resources in a microgrid that can operate independently, without interruption, if the local distribution grid goes down.

“The innovative microgrid system, which integrates a 700kW solar photovoltaic array, a 500kW natural gas generator, and a 500kW lithium-ion battery system, will provide backup power to four groundwater wells on the range,” Ameresco explained in a press statement last year, in which it described the White Sands project.

The four wells are the primary source of potable water to the main post at White Sands. The new microgrid meets a US Army requirement for up to 14 days of independent water and power delivery to the post in case of a grid outage.

“This self-sufficient energy system, designed to serve a specific geographic area, helps ensure that critical missions at WSMR can proceed without interruption,” Ameresco elaborates, adding that the microgrid underscores White Sands’s commitment to building more resilient energy systems into its future construction projects.

Ameresco also indicated that the now-familiar combineation of solar power and BESS (battery energy storage systems) will do most of the heavy lifting, with the gas generator playing a back-up role if necessary.

“The solar array captures energy from the sun during the day, while the natural gas generator provides a dependable backup power source. The lithium-ion battery system efficiently stores excess energy generated by the solar array and releases it when needed, helping to ensure an uninterrupted power supply,” Ameresco emphasized.

The role of a lithium-ion battery in the new microgrid may come as quite a shock to US Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who has somehow failed to get memo about energy storage systems for solar power. Energy storage is an actual thing that exists in the space-time continuum here on Earth, but apparently not in Burgum’s corner of the mulitverse.

“And of course, when the sun goes down, you have a catastrophic failure called sunset and there’s no solar energy produced, and yet we’re subsidizing these things that are intermittent, unreliable, and expensive,” Burgum told a Fox News audience in July of 2025.

Whether Burgum believes it or not, the HGSG-Ameresco project is living proof that solar power is just as reliable as any other energy resource, with a mature supply chain and knowledge base to back it up.

Take the Florida-based firm Cantsink, for example. A specialist in  piling specialist infrastructure, Cantskin installed the supports for  the solar racking system in the new microgrid.

“Cantsink delivered a foundation system engineered to withstand the demanding conditions of a military testing range,” the company reports in a recap of the project on its website.

“Given the site conditions, pull testing was performed to determine pile requirements, which confirmed that 17’6″ piles were needed to support the racking system,” Cantsink further explains.

Among other details, Cantsink notes that the racking system is supported by 193 8×10 piles measuring 17’6″ long. “Every bolt used had a torque requirement that was inspected by a vendor appointed third party,” Cantsink emphasizes.

Evidently the people in charge of energy systems at White Sands were satisfied with the results of their new microgrid, and the facility is on track to receive another solar-enabled microgrid. On November 3, the Kentucky-based global-facing engineering and infrastructure firm ABM described a new microgrid in the planning stages at White Sands, consisting of a carport-mounted solar power plant, BESS, and dispatchable on-site generators, presumably meaning gas generators for backup power.

The construction contract for the facility was assigned to ABM’s joint venture partner, AACON-RavenVolt. The AACON part of the venture is a general contractor based in Louisville, Kentucky. Ravenvolt is a subsidiary of ABM based in Georgia, having been acquired by the firm in 2022.

The relationship with RavenVolt is significant because ABM has positioned the partnership to zero in on microgrid opportunities throughout the federal government. “The partnership provides federal agencies with dependable, end-to-end energy resilience and infrastructure construction capabilities,” ABM notes.

Keep an eye on ABM and RavenVolt moving forward, as EV stakeholders in the US anticipate an uptick in sales following President Donald Trump’s decision to start a war against Iran last February. That will increase the demand for kilowatts, and RavenVolt is among those advocating for solar-enabled microgrids to avoid grid-related bottlenecks.

“It’s all about the easy integration of on-site renewables, whether that’s solar, battery or ensuring on-site resiliency and expansion capability,” explains RavenVolt co-founder and President of Sales Cody George. The company’s microgrid model is designed for ease of installation, combining whole-of-system standardization while tailoring the switchgear to customer-specific applications.

“We’re not beholden to one technology, so our customers aren’t locked into outdated infrastructure forcing them to completely retool,” George adds.

Circling back around to military applications, it’s not surprising to see solar power resurfacing as a resilient energy resource over at the Defense Department, regardless of last year’s sharp U-turn in federal energy policy. Resiliency was front and center in the early 2000’s, when the Defense Department began pushing the envelope on solar power while the civilian market was still spinning its wheels. Solar panels were still relatively expensive back then, and the civilian market was slow on the uptake. Energy storage systems were more expensive, too.

As one indication that the Defense Department is still carving out its own energy destiny, get a load of Defense Secretary Pete Hesgeth’s new “FORTRESS America” resiliency plan. The goal is to make major Defense Department facilities in the US energy independent for at least 90 days, alongside other emergency stockpiling measures.

Nuclear and fossil fuels are part of the plan, but keep an eye on the solar-plus-storage combo to be first out of the box on a speed-to-power basis.

Photo: White Sands Missile Range celebrated the launch of an on-site, solar-enabled microgrid last year, and the facility has already begun planning for another microgrid with solar power (cropped, courtesy of Cantsink).

#5800. Alignment Healthcare lowers 2026 outlook as it navigates cost headwinds

Alignment Healthcare lowers 2026 outlook as it navigates cost headwinds" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Alignment Healthcare is lowering its guidance for the year as it faces significant headwinds to finish out 2026.

The company said in an earnings report released late Thursday that it now expects to bring in $100 million in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or EBITDA, as well as $5.2 billion in revenue. Total membership is set to be at least 305,000, according to the report.

Alignment reported an $8 million loss in the third quarter, compared to a $3.8 million profit one year ago. Profits were $39.9 million through three quarters, up from $10.3 million across the first nine months of 2025.

Revenue in the third quarter was $1.4 billion, compared to $663.7 million in the prior-year quarter. Revenues through the first nine months of 2026 were $3.9 billion, up from $2.9 billion through three quarters in 2025.

CEO John Kao told investors on the company's earnings call Friday morning that some headwinds Alignment is facing include cost spikes in certain service lines, like catastrophic care and skilled nursing, as well as volatility in claims processing.

Last year, Alignment kicked off an effort to migrate to a comprehensive claims system with the goal of accelerating payment speed, growing automated adjudication rates and enhancing payment integrity. Through that process, once the dust settled on the shift, Alignment found "a notable increase in aggressive provider appeal and disputes in our paid claims data" that also drove up costs, Kao said.

Kao said that the insurer has spent the last several months building out its payment integrity capabilities, as well as deploying additional resources to support clinical best practices to mitigate the variation in outcomes for members.

He said that these investments have driven improvements, particularly in September and into October, but the company is still taking a cautious approach to the end of the year.

"Despite our progress, we are taking a prudent approach to the increased trend seen in Q3 and assume that higher costs in the third quarter will continue to weigh on our results for the remainder of the year," Kao said. "I want to emphasize that the guidance we have provided today is a guidance that we are confident in delivering."

Kao also addressed Alignment's performance in the latest round of star ratings scores. Based on federal data, 25% of its members are in plans with at least four stars in 2027, down from 100% in 2026. That four-star threshold is the key to securing quality bonus payments in Medicare Advantage.

He said that six of the company's seven contracts were above four stars, but a 3.5 score on the remaining plan, a core HMO offering in California, dragged down its overall performance.

Kao said that the team is "focused on really getting to the root issues in Stars." Alignment has also sued the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services over the 2027 calculations.

"That's something that we're going to be underscoring yet again," he said. "This is something that everybody in the company has to focus on ... and we'll get this fixed."

#5799. Overshoot Demands a New Era of Adaptation, Loss & Damage, and Climate Justice

As the world is on track to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius of global warming, climate action must double down but also go beyond emissions cuts to prioritize adaptation, respond to loss and damage, and confront growing inequality.

For decades, climate policy has been dominated by a central question: How do we avoid exceeding 1.5 degrees Celsius of global warming above preindustrial levels? An overshoot world—where warming exceeds 1.5 degrees Celsius before potentially declining—means more than higher temperatures; it means escalating risks to the communities, ecosystems, and species already bearing the brunt of climate change, with catastrophic consequences for many coastal regions and small island states.

The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) report on climate overshoot challenges us to confront a reality that many policymakers have been reluctant to fully acknowledge: The world will exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius. Decades of insufficient climate action have placed us in this predicament.

Aggressive emissions reductions can limit how far and for how long global warming exceeds that threshold. However, a future decline in global temperatures would not erase the losses experienced along the way. That reality should sharpen global climate ambition and broaden our understanding of what climate action requires. It is equally important to prepare for and respond to the escalating impacts that communities and ecosystems will experience in the decades between crossing 1.5 degrees Celsius and hopefully returning to a temperature below it.

One of the UNEP report’s central messages is that mitigation and adaptation are fundamentally intertwined, and both will be essential in navigating an overshoot world. The report also emphasizes the growing need for transformational adaptation: actions that go beyond incremental adjustments to fundamentally reshape systems, institutions, and development pathways in response to escalating climate risks.

Yet there is an alarming disconnect between the scale of adaptation that is needed and the reality on the ground. Many countries are still struggling to finance and implement basic adaptation measures. Adaptation finance remains grossly inadequate, national adaptation plans are underfunded, and frontline communities continue to lack the resources needed to prepare for worsening risks. The Adaptation Gap Report 2025 estimated adaptation finance needs in developing countries at up to US$365 billion per year by 2035, while international adaptation finance flows from developed countries reached just US$35 billion in 2024, only around 10 percent of what is needed.

There is reason for optimism. After decades of advocacy, adaptation is finally receiving greater recognition as a core pillar of climate action. Negotiations on the global goal on adaptation (GGA)—which aims to enhance adaptive capacity, strengthen resilience, and reduce vulnerability—have elevated adaptation within international climate discussions. Initiatives such as the Fostering Investable National Implementation (FINI) are also helping to mobilize public and private investments to scale adaptation efforts.

But overshoot forces us to think beyond closing today’s adaptation gaps.

What happens when livelihoods—particularly those connected to our food system—become untenable because of chronic drought, extreme heat, or repeated disasters? What happens when infrastructure designed for one climate must function in a dramatically different one; when transit and energy hubs become inoperable due to heat? What happens when fundamental changes in land use become unavoidable, and our forests and farmlands can’t keep up with those changes?

“The challenge is not deciding which type of climate action deserves support. We need all three: mitigation, adaptation, and responses to loss and damage.”

These are questions of transformation, requiring us to rethink how societies are organized, how development occurs, and how communities can thrive in a warmer world with greater climate impacts. The challenge is that we are asking societies to prepare for transformational adaptation before many governments have fully integrated adaptation into planning, investment, and governance.

Governments and funders—both public and private—must therefore treat adaptation as an investment in economic stability, public health, food security, water security, and human dignity, not as a secondary environmental issue. Support must be predictable, accessible, timely, and responsive to local priorities. Researchers, practitioners, governments, businesses, and communities must work together to envision, plan for, and implement systemic change, from rethinking infrastructure and land use to reshaping governance, livelihoods, and development pathways.

At COP31, progress on the GGA must be a priority. Countries must move beyond the stalled discussions to reach agreement on how adaptation progress will be measured and how implementation will be accelerated. Discussions on preparing for the next global stocktake must also grapple more explicitly with the implications of overshoot for adaptation and adaptation finance.

One of the most important implications of overshoot is that there are climate impacts that are unpreventable and irreversible. Some impacts exceed the capacity of households, institutions, and ecosystems to adjust, and others occur despite preparation. When communities lose lands to sea level rise, when repeated disasters force permanent displacement, when cultural heritage disappears, or when ecosystems collapse, we are no longer talking only about adaptation. We are talking about loss and damage.

Countries and communities need support for recovery and reconstruction, assistance with displacement and planned relocation, protection of livelihoods and cultural heritage, and solutions for slow-onset impacts such as sea level rise, desertification, and glacier loss. The scale of these needs is already staggering. Estimates find that loss and damage costs in developing countries could reach up to US$671 billion annually by 2030, and those figures only capture economic losses. They do not account for noneconomic losses, such as lives lost, cultural heritage erased, or permanent damage to ecosystems.

Yet climate policy discussions continue to focus primarily on the relationship between mitigation and adaptation. In an overshoot world, that is no longer enough. Responses to loss and damage must become a central component of climate action. The establishment of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) was an important step, but its success will ultimately depend on whether it mobilizes finance at the scale required and whether support reaches affected people quickly, directly, and equitably.

Loss and damage are also inseparable from questions of justice. The countries and communities contributing the least to climate change are those facing the greatest risks of irreversible harm. Small Island Developing States, Indigenous Peoples, women, low-income communities, and many countries across the Global South continue to bear disproportionate impacts despite contributing little to the problem.

Climate change has always raised questions about who bears the costs, who receives protection, and who gets left behind. Overshoot makes those questions even more urgent. If we are serious about navigating an overshoot world, loss and damage can no longer remain at the margins of climate policy. It must become a core pillar of climate action.

At COP31, loss and damage must be integrated across the full climate agenda rather than confined to a stand-alone negotiation track. Parties should move beyond procedural discussions and focus on delivering finance through the FRLD and other loss and damage funding arrangements at the scale required, with resources flowing quickly from pledges to actual disbursement. Access to support must become faster, more predictable, and responsive to the needs of affected communities. Discussions under the next global stocktake should also place loss and damage at the center of assessing collective progress, recognizing that overshoot will bring unavoidable and irreversible impacts that demand dedicated responses. Doing so will require rethinking current international approaches to climate finance and accountability, ensuring that support for loss and damage is treated as a core pillar of climate action alongside mitigation and adaptation.

One of the biggest barriers to addressing overshoot is the current approach to competing climate action. Too often, climate discussions become debates about mitigation versus adaptation and adaptation versus loss and damage. Overshoot makes it clear that this is the wrong conversation.

The challenge is not deciding which type of climate action deserves support. We need all three: mitigation, adaptation, and responses to loss and damage. These are mutually reinforcing responsibilities, not competitors. For climate finance, the problem is not only how we divide the pie; the problem is that the pie itself remains sorely inadequate for the challenges ahead of us. An overshoot world requires a dramatic expansion of overall climate finance that must be equitably distributed to mitigation, adaptation, and responses to loss and damage.

The findings from the UNEP report should serve as a blaring alarm—not only because overshoot is a reality, but because it forces us to confront whether our current systems, institutions, financing mechanisms, and political processes are capable of delivering the transformation required. An overshoot world is fundamentally about people: whether societies can adapt, how we respond to loss and damage, and whether the greatest burdens continue to fall on those who contributed the least to the problem.In an era of overshoot, our attention, ambition, and investment must finally match that reality.

By Dr. Adelle Thomas, Senior Director, Climate Adaptation, Environmental Health, NRDC

#5798. GTA VI Will Take Up To 212 GB On Your Console's Hard Drive

"Grand Theft Auto VI" is set to be the biggest video game of the decade, if not one of the biggest games ever made. That distinction isn't just figurative either because it's set to be absolutely huge in the literal, bits and bytes sense, too. Developer Rockstar Games announced Tuesday that the highly anticipated title will be available for digital pre-load starting November 10, and that the full game file will take up to 212 GB, "depending on your device," even telling gamers to "make sure you've got ample space to begin pre-loading as soon as possible."

To put that number into context, the standard PlayStation 5 comes with an advertised 1 TB or 825 GB of storage depending on whether you get the disc or digital version, and about 158 GB of that is taken up by the operating system. In other words, assuming the standard PS5 version of the game is indeed 212 GB and you've got a digital console without any external drives, just GTA VI will take up more than 25% of all your available space.

On the Xbox side, a Series X comes with either 1 TB or 2 TB while the entry-level Series S is offered in 1 TB or 512 GB drives, and of course, a good chunk of that is always reserved for the OS. Big thoughts and prayers for owners of the 512-gig Series S.

Given how much content this next Grand Theft Auto game is set to come with, a massive download isn't entirely surprising. The map is said to be double that of "GTA V," three times bigger than "Red Dead Redemption 2," and will apparently include "hundreds" of accessible building interiors. There are also hundreds of cars to account for, super detailed character models, and, y'know, the underlying logic and systems that make it all a playable game.

All that said, it's entirely possible that the quoted 212 GB size is only for the higher-fidelity PS5 Pro version of the game, and that console comes with 2 TB out of the box. However, the fact that Rockstar is quoting that number only as a blanket sort of thing leads us to believe that the standard version most people will download is indeed just as big, or not meaningfully far off.

Grand Theft Auto VI will release (or, for those who pre-load, become playable) on November 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S consoles. For the real keeners, pre-load starts on November 10 — midnight local time on PS5, midnight GMT for Xbox.

#5797. De-Escalated Treatment for HPV-Related Throat Cancer Gets Long-Term Supporting Data

— More than 90% of patients alive without evidence of disease at 5 years

Reduced-intensity treatment for human papillomavirus (HPV)-positive oropharyngeal cancer (OPC) led to durable cancer control in more than 90% of patients, long-term follow-up from a prospective study showed.

After a median follow-up of 5 years, 94% of patients had no evidence of disease and 90.6% were alive at last follow-up after de-escalated elective nodal irradiation (ENI) during definitive concurrent chemoradiation (CRT). Five-year locoregional control, distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS), and overall survival (OS) exceeded 90%. All but one patient with locoregional failure had recurrences in areas with known residual macroscopic disease. No treatment failures occurred in nodal basins that were omitted from treatment.

De-escalation came in the form of 30-Gy ENI instead of the usual 50-60 Gy dose and omission of low-risk nodal basins, reported Nancy Y. Lee, MD, of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City, and colleagues in JAMA Oncology.

"These outcomes were attained across the spectrum of T- and N-stage groups and smoking histories among patients predominantly treated with concurrent platinum-based chemoradiosensitization," the authors noted. "The systematic omission of uninvolved nodal levels IB/V did not result in failures in those areas and provides a simple class solution to reducing irradiated volume and toxic effects. The 30-Gy ENI dose remains the lowest among published approaches, is tailored to HPV-associated disease, and results in the lowest reported gastrostomy tube insertion rate."

"Although low-dose ENI without concurrent chemotherapy has been investigated, recent phase III randomized trials have demonstrated the superiority of concurrent platinum-based chemotherapy for achieving cure in HPV-associated OPC, underscoring the importance of de-escalating ENI within an optimally curative paradigm for HPV-associated OPC," they wrote.

The study showed that focusing on radiation dose is not the only strategy to de-escalate treatment for HPV-associated OPC, said David Sher, MD, of UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, who was not involved in the study.

"While we often focus on the total dose delivered to visible cancer, in actuality, ENI is responsible for a substantial amount of normal tissue irradiation and dose to critical normal structures, such as the salivary glands and swallowing structures," Sher, an expert for the American Society for Radiation Oncology, told MedPage Today. "There has been a progressive recognition that ENI dose can be a significant contributor to quality-of-life outcomes, and there are several studies, both prospective and retrospective, that have shown that the standard dose of 50 Gy can be substantially lowered."

"[The] degree of success is remarkable given the extent of dose reduction, and it is exciting to see such superb outcomes," he added. "Although we do not have quality-of-life data from this study, prior reports were also very favorable."

Providing additional context for the study results, Sher noted that all patients underwent PET-CT imaging and the vast majority had MRI as well. Such advanced imaging may play a key role in identifying smaller lymph nodes that might harbor cancer and require higher radiation doses. Additionally, all the patients received cisplatin-containing chemotherapy, and HPV-associated OPC is cisplatin sensitive. Also, the authors did not report how many "equivocal" lymph nodes were treated with a higher radiation dose.

Results of the current study add to those of a previous phase III trial that used a slightly higher nodal irradiation dose, he added.

"All of this work strongly suggests we are delivering ENI doses that are far too high, and we need to be more aggressive in reducing the acute and long-term side-effect burden of our treatments while preserving oncologic efficacy," said Sher. "For such a result to become a true standard of care, though, we do need a phase III randomized study to confirm non-inferiority in a multi-institutional setting, and hopefully such a trial can be available soon to patients and our community."

Lee and colleagues previously reported 2-year outcomes with the de-escalation strategy, showing good locoregional control and survival with "excellent" quality of life. The current report aimed to establish the durability of the strategy, as assessed after a median follow-up of 5 years.

The analysis involved 276 patients treated with intensity-modulated radiotherapy (n=256) or intensity-modulated proton therapy (n=20). Treated nodal and subclinical regions received 30 Gy in 15 fractions and a sequential boost of 40 Gy in 20 fractions.

The 5-year results showed that 260 patients had no evidence of disease at 5 years and 250 were alive at last follow-up. Five-year outcomes were:

A single elective nodal failure occurred 6 months after concurrent CRT in a contralateral indeterminate lymph node present at baseline and treated with 30 Gy, the authors reported. The last regional failure occurred 18 months post-treatment. Distant-only recurrences occurred in 23 patients. At last follow-up, 12 of the patients remained alive with no evidence of disease, and one remained alive with disease.

#5796. Sutter Health calls off flagship hospital build in SF's East Bay, citing regulatory issues

Sutter Health calls off flagship hospital build in SF's East Bay, citing regulatory issues" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Sutter Health scrapped plans to build a flagship campus on property it owns in Emeryville, California, and instead is shifting its focus to outpatient care in the area, according to a Sept. 30 statement.

The health system announced those plans in early 2025 (see that story below), with a medical center of up to 200 beds as the centerpiece of a $1 billion investment into San Francisco's East Bay. It attributed its decision to "the lack of a clear and predictable regulatory path" related to California environmental and land use law.

"Over two years, we pursued relief under the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA," the statement reads. "Those efforts did not secure the certainty needed to advance the hospital project, leaving it vulnerable to litigation that could delay construction and new hospital services for years."

Accompanying plans surrounding outpatient services "including primary and specialty care, diagnostic services and outpatient surgery" are now the priority for that community, though Sutter said it's still keeping an eye out for another potential location for a future hospital.

"Separating these projects keeps healthcare investment moving and allows us to advance additional outpatient services that can bring care to patients sooner. No alternative location has been selected, and we are assessing several options that can support comprehensive hospital, emergency and specialty care and the infrastructure needed for the future."

Sutter said that services will not be affected at Alta Bates, another hospital in the area it was planning to relieve with the new build, and that it plans to keep supporting that campus until another hospital can be finished. It added that hospitals across California have and continue to face "legal and regulatory challenges [tied to] significant seismic deadlines, while efforts to modernize or replace facilities can be exposed to lengthy regulatory reviews and litigation. A different location alone will not resolve these challenges."

Sutter Health will invest $1 billion to expand its services across Northern California's East Bay region, including a new flagship campus in Emeryville.

The health system announced Wednesday that the campus will feature a new medical center with up to 200 beds as well as a regional destination for ambulatory care. The plans also leave room for future expansion, according to the announcement.

The ambulatory services complex at the 12-acre campus will feature a wide array of specialties and will offer imaging and laboratory services. It expects to welcome its first patients as early as 2028, Sutter said.

The 335,000-square-foot medical center will include labor and delivery, surgical services, intensive care, emergency care and neonatal intensive care. The facility will be designed with the potential to add additional patient rooms in the future.

Sutter is targeting a 2032-33 opening date for the medical center, according to the announcement.

“Our Emeryville campus project represents one of the most significant investments we’re making across our system over the next decade and is part of our broader vision to meet the community’s growing demand for expanded access to our services across the East Bay footprint,” said Warner Thomas, president and CEO of Sutter Health, in the press release.

Sutter said it will put a focus on recruiting both primary care physicians and specialty care doctors, breaking down patient barriers to appointments and referrals and investing in initiatives to bolster the healthcare workforce. It expects to have 190 primary and specialty care clinicians staffing the new campus.

Beyond building the new campus, Sutter said it plans to grow the behavioral health services offered at its Herrick campus in Berkeley. The health system's Alta Bates campus will continue to operate as an acute care facility until the new medical center opens in Emeryville and then will be overhauled to provide ambulatory surgery services, urgent care and potentially skilled nursing services.

The health system is also renovating a medical office building in Berkley to serve as a primary care facility that will also offer OB-GYN care, according to the announcement.

Additional renovations are in the works as well, Sutter said.

“Too many people face challenges in accessing the care they need," Thomas said. "At Sutter, we’re committed to breaking down those barriers—expanding care facilities, enhancing imaging capabilities, improving online appointment scheduling and collaborating with the Sutter East Bay Medical Group and our community physician partners to attract more primary and specialty care physicians.

"These efforts will allow us to care for more patients while also investing in programs and partnerships that build the healthcare workforce of the future—ensuring more people get the right care when and where they need it," he said.

#5795. Stratos Data Center Will Emit Air Pollution That’s Linked to Premature Deaths and Health Economic Damages for Utah & States Downwind

A new report models emissions from different on-site methane generation power scenarios to show potential impacts on the people of Utah and residents of multiple downwind states.

Canadian businessman and television personality “Mr. Wonderful” (aka Kevin O’Leary) and his businesses have proposed the Stratos data center in Box Elder County, Utah, near Salt Lake City, that  will be one of the largest data centers in the world, requiring as much as 9 gigawatts (GW) of on-site power from burning methane gas. The Box Elder County Commission approved the project in May—under highly contentious circumstances and under a highly unusual arrangement within a project area created by Utah’s Military Installation Development Authority.

A new report prepared by EmPower Analytics Group for NRDC estimates that the air pollution, health harms, and economic damages from the proposed Stratos data center would be substantial: “[a]t the potential 9 GW full build-out, air pollution from Stratos’s methane-gas power generation is estimated to cause approximately 5–45 additional premature deaths and $75–$690 million in health-related economic damages every year.” The report also discusses additional health harms that extend beyond premature deaths and include new asthma cases, nonfatal heart attacks, hospital visits, and lost work and school days.

These ranges reflect scenarios that model the health harms and economic damage caused by air pollution from two possible methane-gas primary power generating technologies: modern combined-cycle combustion turbines and methane gas–fired reciprocating internal combustion engines (RICE). The primary harmful air pollution consists of tiny soot particles—particulate matter of 2.5 microns or less (PM2.5)—about 30 times smaller than the width of an average human hair.

The report further finds that over a 30-year period, at the potential 9 GW full build-out, the health and economic harms from this PM2.5 air pollution “could accumulate to approximately 856–1,350 premature deaths and $13.5–$20.7 billion under gas-fired RICE, compared with 145–253 premature deaths and $2.3–$3.8 billion under combined-cycle gas.”

Of the two methane-gas primary power generation technologies evaluated in the report, one uses a smaller number of large gas combustion turbines, while the RICE scenario reflected electricity generated by many individual engines operating in parallel. Indeed, the RICE scenario is patterned on a methane gas–powered data center with 69 RICE generators that the Utah Division of Air Quality permitted in Millard County in early 2026. RICE generators produce higher emissions than combined-cycle gas at the same generation capacity. Accordingly, the report finds that “[t]he technology used to power Stratos could make a five- to sixfold difference in its estimated health harms.”

Importantly, the modeled combined-cycle gas scenario does not estimate the emissions from the use of on-site diesel generators for backup power because those plans by Stratos remain unknown. (The report modeled diesel backup generators for the RICE scenario, scaled from the Millard County permit example.) Diesel generators are significantly dirtier than comparably sized methane gas generators, emitting 95 percent more smog-forming nitrogen oxides than an equivalent gas generator as well as 98 percent more non-methane hydrocarbons and 59 percent more carbon monoxide. Harmful PM2.5 emissions will be even higher from any data center employing diesel generators (the scale of that additional pollution would depend on whether they were truly used for “emergency conditions” versus being run more frequently; state permitting parameters for backup diesels is a critical issue for all data center developments).

The highest concentrations of harmful air pollution from the Stratos data center will occur near the facility in Box Elder County, neighboring areas of northern Utah (including Salt Lake City), and southern Idaho. But the health harms and economic damage from Stratos would extend well beyond these areas: The report finds that more than 80 percent of health harms and health-related economic damages occur outside the state, reaching downwind populations in Colorado, Wyoming, and as far away as Illinois. The report appendix identifies the full list of potentially impacted states.

The Stratos developers have maintained from the start that the massive data center will be powered by methane gas. “That’s never going to happen,” Utah Governor Spencer Cox told the Salt Lake Tribune in May. “The very first phase will be natural gas, but the other phases should not be. They should be nuclear, and they should be geothermal, and solar and other technology.” But the most recent filing by the Stratos developers with the state still show plans for the full build-out of the data center to be powered by methane gas. This filing shows that the developers now say that they plan a 7.5 GW data center using the dirtier and more harmful RICE generators that burn methane gas. None of these filings commit the developers to doing or not doing something different from what they are saying now, a reality that has characterized this data center project—and many other proposed data center projects nationally.

Data centers in Utah or anywhere else, of course, need not be powered by highly polluting, harmful fossil fuels like methane gas. Other data center developers have been doing better jobs showing how, in stark contrast to the Stratos proposal, it is possible to power these facilities with cleaner energy—such as a robust portfolio of wind, solar, geothermal, and batteries—and maxing out demand side resources.

NRDC commissioned this important EmPower Analytics report to raise awareness and concerns about the harmful health impacts and associated economic damages from dangerous air pollution caused by data centers like the proposed Stratos Project in Utah and by the proliferation of data centers across the United States. These harms arise especially from hyperscaler data centers powered by fossil fuels, like Stratos. While the dangers and costs of excessive water use by data centers are more well known, the deadly toll of air pollution—a silent killer—deserves greater attention and concern.

Harmful air pollution should be met with the best air pollution control technologies available. Data centers should be powered by new, additional, deliverable clean energy that does not release air pollution, along with batteries, storage, and other smart solutions. If someone nicknamed Mr. Wonderful wants to earn that name, he should live up to it, starting with the Stratos data center.

By John Walke, Director, Federal Clean Air & Senior Attorney, Environmental Health, NRDC

NRDC is the nation's most effective environmental action group, combining the grassroots power of 1.3 million members and online activists with the courtroom clout and expertise of more than 350 lawyers, scientists, and other professionals.

#5794. Dodge Rejoins NASCAR Cup Series After 14-Year Absence

The entire Big Three will be battling for stock car supremacy in 2027. Dodge announced Monday that it will return to the NASCAR Cup Series next season. Kaulig Racing's pair of Dodge Chargers will be the first to compete in stock car racing's marquee series since the manufacturer's departure after the 2012 season. Plenty of questions remain after the announcement, including who will drive the entries and what the Gen 7 Charger's bodywork will look like.

The team partnering with Dodge was never a question. Kaulig Racing first paired up with Ram for the brand's return to the NASCAR Craftsman Truck Series this season, fielding five Ram trucks. It's surprising how quickly Stellantis North America cobbled together a Cup program. NASCAR confirmed that Dodge completed its wind tunnel testing and will have its production body panels ready later this month. Tim Kuniskis, Stellantis' Head of American Brands, said:

"Everyone said it was impossible to get back in one year. We said, 'watch this,' Sure, we could spend three years planning, testing and perfecting ... or we could do all three in real time, on the track. It's going to be exponentially harder this way. But slow has never been part of Dodge DNA. LFG."

The biggest reason why a Dodge program for the Cup Series was organized in only a year is that the manufacturer will not be building its own engines. Dodge has yet to announce where it will source Kaulig's 2027 motors, but it is in talks with a third party. The Athletic reported that ECR Engines could potentially build engines for Dodge. The partnership has issues because ECR currently produces Chevrolet engines and is owned by Richard Childress, a Chevrolet team owner. NASCAR, Ford and Toyota would need to approve an exemption for ECR to build engines for both Chevy and Dodge.

Besides the powerplant, Kaulig expects to announce its 2027 Cup Series driver lineup this weekend ahead of the season finale at Homestead-Miami Speedway. It wouldn't be a shock if the team retained its current pairing of Ty Dillon and A.J. Allmendinger. However, the driver market has seen a major shakeup over the past month. Brad Keselowski is departing RFK Racing, a team he co-owns, after falling out with fellow co-owners Fenway Sports Group. He stated last weekend that he will be available to race elsewhere regardless of manufacturer. Keselowski won Dodge's most recent Cup Series title with Penske in 2012. The 42-year-old admitted that he hasn't discussed anything with Dodge or Kaulig, but he's open to the idea.

#5792. China Truck Sales Now Majority Electric. What’s Next?

EV heavy trucks hit 50.3% market share in China for September, with sales up 34% from a year ago. Long-haul big rig market share hit 64.5%. China is on track to have over 40% EV market share for the entire year, reaching their 2030 goal in a matter of months. This is not the first time China’s heavy truck market share topped 50%, but that previous blip in December last year was prior to subsidies ending, followed by a dip in January. Current sales rates are not bolstered by the subsidy and are now on a much more stable upward trajectory.

The speed of EV adoption for heavy trucks in China has recently grown much faster than for cars, having risen from just 13.6% in 2024. When I visited Guangzhou in November of last year and again in April of this year, I noticed a lot more green plates on trucks, indicating that they were electric. It seems that my perception is backed by sales data.

With the addition of LNG trucks, diesel’s share of heavy trucks has dropped to roughly 40%. While LNG sales have also declined with the rate of EV adoption, diesel trucks could soon make up less than 1/3 of sales and decline further from there. China could feasibly double its 2030 goal and hit 80% EV penetration, by which point many diesel models are likely to be discontinued.

With these levels of market penetration, in addition to retirements, China’s diesel demand is on track to fall by about 230,000 barrels per day this year, despite increased freight movement. Every additional electric truck that replaces a diesel truck then builds on that reduction. Due to their duty cycle, each electric truck sold has a much greater impact on fuel consumption than each car sold. And the price of fuel combined with the duty cycle has a much greater impact on overall truck economics.

To be clear, these improving results are not due to subsidies, as they appear in the year after subsidies were cut. They are also not due to mandates, as the 2030 goals were met before the ink was dry on their announcement. EV trucks are now more affordable to own and operate than diesel trucks in China. The increase in diesel prices has only increased the cost gap.

Last year, roughly 90% of all electric truck sales globally were in China. That percentage is set to expand this year, despite rising sales in some other countries. Those sales are simply not rising fast enough outside of China to keep pace with China. In comparison, the EU is looking at 2.5% EV market share this year. China is on pace to average roughly as many electric trucks sold per week as Europe sells per year. The US EV truck market looks like a rounding error in comparison at less than one percent.

In addition, China has rapidly been building out heavy truck charging infrastructure as part of the 28 million charging facilities planned to be in operation by the end of 2027, up from 21 million last March. This not only focuses on the major cities but also extends into more rural areas that have been slower to adopt electrification. In addition, several companies are building out battery swap stations. While we have yet to see if battery swap or MW+ charging wins in the truck market, expect the competition between the two approaches to be fierce.

Within Tier 1 cities, I could see a potential phase out of diesel trucks in the near future. Hainan province is already planning to end ICE passenger car sales by 2030, and I expect that to extend to diesel trucks as well. Although rural areas have been slower to adopt, they also tend to be less wealthy and thus more impacted by the changing economics. If diesel prices stay elevated while charging becomes convenient, many rural businesses will not be able to afford to buy new diesel trucks. With the end of diesel truck sales, strict emissions standards and a potential return of scrappage incentives could take remaining diesel vehicles off the road at an accelerated rate.

With fewer diesel trucks on the road in the largest market globally, diesel consumption is set to decline. In addition, the supply chain for diesel parts will also start to decline. As protectionism has targeted electric vehicles, rather than internal combustion  engine (ICE) vehicles, a decline in Chinese (ICE) parts has a potentially significant impact on global markets.

Of course, as EVs take over the majority of heavy truck sales in the fiercely competitive Chinese market, Chinese manufacturers will start looking outside of the country for growth.

The traditional thought would be to look at wealthy Western countries that have substantial buying power. However, many Chinese companies may be a bit reluctant to focus on those markets after the protectionist efforts against electric passenger vehicles. Many European markets, like Germany, also have very high electricity prices, which makes the financial proposition less attractive for commercial vehicles that are heavily motivated by costs. Chinese companies may start focusing elsewhere.

The Middle Corridor could become a focus. This essentially rebuilds the Silk Road land route from China, across the Caspian Sea, on to Turkey. Many of the countries along this route  once had prosperous trade, only to fall into decline when ocean trade routes were established. However, land transport is much easier to electrify than long ocean voyages. China is investing heavily with countries like Kazakhstan along the route with renewable electricity infrastructure. Electrified rail is expanding by 26-fold in Turkey. Electrified trucking is the next logical step, connecting the rail lines to more local production along the route.

Other Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) countries could also benefit. In countries like Ethiopia, which has expensive diesel but electricity prices to businesses of just $0.017/kWh, electric trucks could make perfect sense to transport between new factories and new ports. Trading partners like Vietnam and Thailand could also see an influx.

All this is not to say that local companies will not benefit. Unlike passenger cars, heavy equipment tends to be more modular. Due to the bulk and mass of the vehicles, final assembly is more likely to be localized, with greater use of local suppliers.

Overall, we could see much of the “Rest of the World” (ROW) leapfrog legacy economies in EV truck adoption. The purchase price is no longer prohibitive in China, and the operating costs are much lower. With infrastructure buildout and increasing renewable installed capacity, electric trucking is poised to take over rapidly.

That is not to say that the West will be completely left out. Countries with less prohibitive trade policies toward EVs will likely see increased adoption. While EVs have taken over passenger car sales in Norway, their trucking industry still has a way to go at just 14.4%. And the geographically most eastern country typically lumped in with the “West,” Australia, is likely to see EV truck sales follow a similar pattern to EV car sales. If Canada continues to open up, they could also benefit. Of course, as the majority of the economic benefit from electric trucks comes from their use, inflated trucking costs hurt every company that moves products by truck, and those inflated costs then lead to inflation throughout the economy. That impacts overall affordability. As such, there is a chance that protectionists do not put as much effort into undermining electric truck imports as they put into passenger EVs.

And the EV heavy truck global supply chain will become increasingly well established. This could mean more parts availability for brands outside of China to build competitive vehicles, if those companies have access to global supply chains. Competitive markets will also drive innovation, moving the technology forward at an accelerating rate. Meanwhile the supply chain for diesel trucks will shrink.

While the US still seems to be figuring out how to make a safe EV Semi, battery-powered heavy trucks are becoming increasingly mature products elsewhere. As electric trucks move from majority share to complete market dominance in the largest market, other markets will follow, and the transition will become inevitable. Hopefully, the largest oil producing country in the world will not be left too far behind.

#5790. Weekly Rundown: Doximity launches DoseCheck; AI recommends costlier care than doctors, study finds

Weekly Rundown: Doximity launches DoseCheck; AI recommends costlier care than doctors, study finds" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Stay up to date on the latest in health tech, digital health and health AI news with this weekly brief. Read below for news from the week of Oct. 26 to 30.

Doximity launched DoseCheck, a new safety feature within Doximity Ask designed to catch unsafe or incorrect medication dosing recommendations generated by artificial intelligence.

Doximity Ask is the company's clinical decision support tool.

Rather than relying on an LLM to double-check another LLM, DoseCheck adds a deterministic, rule-based verification layer, checking AI-generated dosing claims against structured information including FDA labeling and professional guidelines, the company said. By checking against FDA labeling and professional guidelines, DoseCheck increases accuracy to more than 99%, the company claims.

Doximity tested nine widely used AI models with over 8,000 dosing questions based on real physician queries. At least 2.3% of dosing claims made by these models were wrong, and 43.8% of detected errors were serious or potentially lethal.

According to the analysis, common sources of errors include dosing newer drugs, failing to account for patient-specific factors such as kidney function, age, weight and medical history, and mistakes involving units, decimal points or drugs with similar names.

"AI is probabilistic. Drug dosing can’t be," said Louis-Antoine Mullie, M.D., chief AI researcher at Doximity. "DoseCheck doesn’t ask a language model to grade its own homework. It checks dosing claims against a structured, authoritative database, so physicians get the same verified dosing answer every time."

DoseCheck is free and has been rolled out to all Doximity Ask users across mobile and desktop.

Health and wellness platform Hims & Hers plans to launch a peptides specialty after the federal government signaled it will allow compounding pharmacies to manufacture six peptides temporarily.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services will not take action against licensed pharmacists who dispense certain unapproved peptides, according to a new policy published this week in the Federal Register.

Stopping short of a formal declaration allowing their use, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has cleared the way for the compounding of six popular wellness peptides, Fierce Pharma reported. Under Kennedy’s "enforcement discretion policy" issued Wednesday, HHS will not take enforcement action against pharmacies, physicians and federal facilities compounding six specific peptides, assuming those parties meet certain specific qualifications.

The specific compounds included (PDF) in the list are BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, semax and TB-500, all of which were discussed in a meeting of the FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) in July, with the panel ultimately voting to recommend including the treatments onto the 503A Bulk Drug Substances list.

Through its new Peptides+ specialty, Hims & Hers plans to offer access to Sermorelin, Glutathione, B12, NAD+, and L-carnitine, with BPC-157 and TB-500 to follow when allowable. "If a customer is eligible, a personalized treatment plan will be prescribed and delivered by independent providers, treatments supplied by licensed pharmacies, with ongoing clinical support our customers can trust," CEO Andrew Dudum wrote in a blog post.

"We’re focused on entering this specialty the right way, not the fastest. Most of what we know about these compounds is still early—with limited published studies, we draw primarily from clinical experience from the last decade. We’ve consistently acknowledged that while these compounds hold promise, there is still information we do not yet know. Provider-supervised use is how we plan to build on this foundation and make sure that access and innovation can move at the same pace," Dudum said.

The tech giant launched Google AI for Healthcare Professionals Certificate, a new program designed to teach healthcare professionals responsible, practical ways to use AI in their day-to-day work. Clinicians at Google developed the virtual course, and the program is accredited for up to five American Medical Association (AMA) continuing education credits.

The NYU Grossman School of Medicine, the University of Alabama at Birmingham and Touro University are offering the program to their faculty, residents and medical students. Leading nursing institutions, including Purdue University School of Nursing, are offering the certificate as part of their healthcare professional training, according to Google.

"As I’ve traveled around the world this year, I’ve heard loud and clear from healthcare professionals how much need there is for a thoughtful but practical educational resource on AI, made specifically for healthcare," Michael Howell, M.D., Google’s chief health officer, wrote in a blog post.

Large language models recommend more up-front testing, referrals and treatment than the physicians who actually saw the patients and at more than three times the cost, according to a study published in NEJM AI.

Researchers from the Technion, Stanford University and collaborating institutions tested 20 general-purpose and four specialized medical AI systems on records from 200 real outpatient and emergency visits. Each received the clinical presentation without the physician’s assessment and plan. The team priced the recommended tests and referrals in both the AI and physicians’ plans using the same 2026 Medicare rates.

Across the 20 general-purpose systems, AI-suggested care cost a mean of $314 per visit, compared with $97 for care recommended by attending physicians. Suggested care was more costly in 180 of 200 cases. The average cost of care per AI system ranged from $209 to $599.

Diagnostic testing rose from $71 per visit in the physicians’ plans to $176 across the systems, about $105 more per visit. The referral rates for the physician’s plans were 0.15 per visit compared to 0.87 for the LLM’s plans, which, at the corresponding Medicare rates, is $111 more per visit, according to the study.

"The four specialized medical systems showed comparable excess (2.7× to 3.5×), so medical fine-tuning did not curb—and may reinforce—cost escalation," the study authors wrote.

The researchers used MTSamples, a publicly available collection of 4,999 real de-identified medical transcription sample reports contributed by practicing clinicians as reference material for medical transcriptionists. The notes are documentation from real patient visits, but they are a convenience sample assembled for transcription training rather than a representative draw from U.S. ambulatory practice, the study authors wrote.

"Under a single standard prompt, every AI system we evaluated, general purpose and medically specialized alike, suggested more diagnostic tests, medications and specialist referrals than the treating physician on the same cases," the study authors wrote.

LLMs appear optimized to be comprehensive and avoid missing diagnoses, and may show an analogous tendency toward exhaustive workup, the study authors noted.

The researchers argued that much of the excess can be reduced through better prompting, suggesting cost inflation is partly a deployment and design problem rather than an unavoidable feature of AI.

Researchers reevaluated 19 models using different instructions. A simple cost-aware prompt telling models to recommend only clinically necessary, cost-effective items reduced average recommended costs from 3.2 times physician costs to 2.5 times.

A stronger "parsimonious-but-safe" prompt told models to focus on the three most likely diagnoses, explicitly rule out dangerous "cannot-miss" conditions, and recommend only tests whose results would change management. That cut costs to just 1.4 times physician costs. But diagnostic agreement with physicians fell in 17 of the 19 systems, illustrating why cost reductions need to be evaluated alongside other changes in the recommendations, the study authors noted.

"Getting the diagnosis right matters, but so does the path you take to get there," said Prof. Dvir Aran of the Technion, the study’s corresponding author, in a statement. "Accuracy and safety have dominated how clinical AI is trained and evaluated. Efficiency needs the same attention: whether each test or referral is likely to help the patient."

Digital health company Eko Health launched a new stethoscope, the CORE 300, that integrates traditional and digital listening modes directly into a single chestpiece.

The AI-enabled stethoscope, which received FDA clearance, is also in line with premium traditional stethoscopes, making the digital technology more accessible to a broader group of healthcare professionals, the company said.

With a twist of the chestpiece, clinicians can switch between familiar traditional listening and Eko’s advanced digital listening technology, with up to 35x amplification, active noise cancellation and real-time heart rate displayed directly on the device. When connected to the Eko App and Eko's FDA-cleared AI for structural murmur detection, CORE 300 can also bring AI disease detection into the physical exam.

"Millions of healthcare professionals around the world use a stethoscope to examine patients every day," said Connor Landgraf, co-founder and CEO of Eko Health, in a statement. "Our goal is to bring the most ubiquitous clinical exam into the precise digital era. Once the physical exam becomes digital, we combine better listening with objective measurements and AI-powered clinical decision support right at the point of care."Clinical technologies are evolving quickly, but adoption depends on making new capabilities fit naturally into the way clinicians already practice, said Steven R. Steinhubl, M.D., chief medical officer of Eko Health and a board-certified cardiologist.

"CORE 300 bridges that gap. With Eko's digital stethoscope, clinicians can record, visualize and save heart, lung and body sounds and interpret the data with Eko’s FDA-cleared AI and software. According to the company, the device could expand screening capabilities in primary care offices, busy clinics and rural healthcare settings.

Eko Health launched its first Eko CORE digital stethoscope attachment in 2025, and to date, has delivered more than 750,000 digital stethoscopes and AI-enabled devices worldwide.

Healthcare engagement and payment solutions provider RevSpring debuted a conversational intelligent virtual agent that helps patients manage payment plans over the phone.

Let’s Talk expands on RevSpring’s voice platform and is integrated with its payment portal. It gives patients the ability to make payments, create payment plans, ask questions and respond to outbound voice reminders.

Initial results of the tool show a 36% increase in patient payment rates and a 27% decrease in transfer to live agents, the company says. Moreover, average call durations decreased 25% with Let’s Talk.

Enterprise healthcare operations software provider symplr launched Monday an integrated workforce management solution combining AI-driven scheduling and timekeeping.

The tool—dubbed symplr Time and Scheduling—combines symplr’s predictive nurse and staffing scheduling tool with its timekeeping solution. Nurse managers can identify and address staffing gaps "hundreds of days in advance," ultimately reducing time spent on staffing and timecard tasks by approximately 50%, executives say.
