Cleveland Clinic Cancer Institute launched an AI task force Monday in a bid to evaluate the technologies and streamline adoption in a "safe and deliberate manner."

The task force is dubbed the Cancer Institute Office of Technology and Digital Strategy. It is led by Paul Thambi, M.D., and Louis Williams, M.D. AI is currently being used by the institute to personalize radiation doses, reduce note-taking time and streamline patient referral processes, according to the Oct. 27 announcement.

#5789. Ford Settles Transit Trail Class Action Lawsuit By Paying Owners Less Than The Package Cost

The current trend of automakers "off-roadifying" their road cars has created a new breed of hiked up, black plastic-clad soft roaders that buyers can't seem to get enough of. Ford gave its Transit full-size van the treatment back in 2022 with the all-wheel-drive Transit Trail, but recalled all of them in early 2024 and replaced their 30.5-inch all-terrain tires that rubbed against the wheel wells with the same 28.5-inch tires on standard Transits, and owners were not pleased.

They were so displeased, in fact, that they filed a class action lawsuit that we first reported on last year. Ford finally reached a settlement with the plaintiffs last week, offering Transit Trail owners a $6,000 payout for the diminished off-road abilities of their vans. This is a pretty healthy payout from a class action lawsuit settlement, but it's still less than half of the original price of the Trail package that cost $12,500 when new.

According to classaction.org, "Eligible for the settlement are all individuals who, as the original owner or lessee, bought or leased a model year 2023 or 2024 Ford Transit Trail before June 1, 2024 for personal, family or household use and who have not already received any compensation from Ford, including any settlement payment or repurchase, related to a covered vehicle or to any alleged defect of, or economic loss relating to, the vehicle." More fine print about how to prove membership in the settlement class is available on the Class Action site.

The Ford Transit Trail was marketed by Ford as having an "adventure-ready chassis is re-tuned and tested to meet the same BUILT FORD TOUGH durability standards as the rest of the Transit lineup," complete with 6.7-inches of ground clearance, upgraded underbody protection, and the 30.5-inch Goodyear Wrangler Workhorse tires that led to the recall. The 28.5-inch tires that Ford replaced the Wranglers with reduced the ground clearance of Transit Trails down to 5.5-inches, or the same as the standard Transit. Nearly 2,000 vehicles were included in the recall, but it's not immediately clear how many owners are eligible for this class action lawsuit settlement.

#5788. Why Oscar Health is putting a focus on personalization for ACA exchange plans

Why Oscar Health is putting a focus on personalization for ACA exchange plans" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Another open enrollment period is set to begin on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges, and the team at Oscar Health is focusing on the unique ways it can innovate in the turbulent market.

Oscar is growing the number of counties in its geographic footprint by 24% in 2027, offering plans across 713 counties in 21 states. It is also investing in new specialized plans, such as its RetireEase offering, and in expanding coverage options designed for individuals with certain conditions.

Janet Liang, president of Oscar Insurance, told Fierce Healthcare that it's critical for plans to learn as much as they can about the individual consumer, so that they can shape benefits that effectively meet the needs of the people who are coming to the marketplaces for coverage.

"We are completely dialed in to the individual consumer," she said. "We know the people who are in the ACA, and it's a broad, broad range of people. It's not one size fits all, and what we do is we spend the time to understand who comes into the ACA and what are the services and needs that individuals have."

That includes putting a focus on collecting plenty of feedback from existing members, and what they're searching for as existing enrollees, as well as collecting data on broader consumer behaviors on the exchanges.

The RetireEase plan, for example, was born from this thinking, Liang said. The offering, which is launching in five states next year, aims to support members in the transition to Medicare coverage, targeted to people aged 55 to 64.

Benefits include set prices for key services in this age range, from preventive care to physical therapy to cardiology. Members that enroll in RetireEase can also access specific supports designed for the handoff to Medicare, for caregivers and transportation if needed.

Liang said this population tends to have unique concerns about affordability as employers shift their approaches in a way that is leading more people to retire early, leaving them on a fixed income. It's also an age range where people begin to develop challenging chronic conditions that will need to be managed in the future.

The team took that feedback and those particular needs it heart when building out RetireEase, Liang said.

Oscar's suite of specialized offerings includes some of its most popular plans, she said. In addition to the new launch, Oscar is expanding the reach of its existing specialized plans. HelloMeno, its plan designed for women navigating menopause, will grow to 15 states by 2027, for example.

Liang said that these plans have higher Net Promoter Scores than its traditional plans, and they also tend to have higher retention rates than the broader offerings.

"Based on the retention rate and the high NPS scores, we know that we're meeting an unmet need," she said.

And the Oscar team is already planning for the future around these specialized plans, and has determined where to go next for 2028. Expanding this slate is a central part of Oscar's broader strategy around the ACA, which also includes enhancements to bronze, silver and gold plans as well as a focus on individual coverage health reimbursement arrangements, or ICHRA.

ICHRA plans have rebranded as Custom Health Option and Individual Care Expense, or CHOICE. But in these models, an employer offers workers a stipend to purchase an exchange plan, rather than offering coverage directly.

Liang said Oscar believes this is an area that will continue to grow. She said that they're seeing higher numbers of employers requesting quotes for potential CHOICE arrangements, and Oscar has doubled its membership between 2025 and 2026.

She added that Oscar expects to triple its CHOICE market share by 2029.

"So there's an obvious interest by employers to reduce their costs," Liang said. "And we also look at markets where there's just a lot of interest by both small employers, regional employers, to just start off. What you see is new employers and new companies that are forming will go straight to CHOICE instead of starting on the traditional insurance path."

#5787. How Does Oahu Get to an Economically Resilient, 100% Clean Energy Future?

Oahu is a unique place. It’s the home of one of the largest clean tech incubators in the world, Elemental Impact, for a reason. Exorbitantly high electricity rates combined with ample natural resources make it an incredible laboratory to bring clean tech solutions to market. Rapid investment for WWII created a grid that was dependent on foreign oil. Path dependency (the idea that “what you know” becomes what you continue to do) hampered innovation and resulted in the creation of infrastructure (multiple power plants across multiple islands) that still, today, burns diesel fuel as large generators, to produce electricity for the island. Throw in a dependence on imported fuels that must come at least 3,000 miles to arrive, being the strategic hub for the entire Pacific theater of the U.S. military, one of the wildest weather years and hurricane seasons the island chain has ever seen AND the state’s economic dependency on tourism dollars, high cost of living, and low wages, and and wow – you’ve got yourself a puzzle and a half to solve in order to get the place to a sustainable future.

Analyst Mike Barnard loves a challenge, so he set forth to put together a roadmap to help Oahu get to 100% clean energy, which helps recirculate money in the state, lower costs, create jobs and foster economic resiliency.

Recently I gave a talk at Hawaii Tech Week in which I summarized this report, added in my own experience running an energy efficiency service that has now greened more than 20,000 homes and is saving Hawaii residents over $10 million a year on their utility bills, and then compiled the new and coming technologies that can help the island get off fossil fuels.

Mike’s report did something very important. The state’s own reporting and strategy looks at the big picture, a very difficult mountain to climb. Mike looked at that mountain and removed some of the false summits and unachievable viewpoints, resulting in a much more achievable and strategic pathway. What he did was eliminate the things we simply cannot fix right now – long distance flights, maritime bunkering, and military fuels – and tackled the problem of Oahu’s actual energy consumption for its residents. The result was that it was achievable, and there are technologies right now today that can be deployed in what he refers to as a “no regret stack” first and foremost.

I combined that with my approach, which was to showcase the economic resilience it creates. Case in point, an LED bulb saves so much money on Oahu that it pays for itself in 18 days. Every day after that, it is like change plinking in a piggy bank for the person who put it in. That builds economic resiliency for those who need it most. From LEDs to e-bikes to heat pump water heaters to balcony solar – it all adds up – fast payback periods, and financial independence.

Mike comes back to the things we simply can’t fix right now and argues that the tech will come – but for the duration of the 2020s and into the 2030s, we should be installing parking lot solar canopies, agrivoltaics, heat pump water heaters, and more.

Scott Cooney (LinkedIn) is a serial eco-entrepreneur focused on making the world a better place for all its residents. Scott is the founder of CleanTechnica and was just smart enough to hire someone smarter than him to run it. He then started Pono Home, a service that greens homes, which has performed efficiency retrofits on more than 20,000 homes and small businesses, reducing carbon pollution by more than 27 million pounds a year and saving customers more than $6.3 million a year on their utilities. Scott wanted to contribute to native ownership of the clean energy revolution, so he gifted Pono Home to a long tenured employee with native Hawaiian roots for just the liquidation value, turning down a mainland company interested in purchasing the company. In a previous life, Scott was an adjunct professor of Sustainability in the MBA program at the University of Hawai'i, a consultant at Saatchi & Saatchi S, where he worked with a team to educate and empower millions of employees to live healthier and more sustainably. He is the author of Build a Green Small Business: Profitable Ways to Become an Ecopreneur (McGraw-Hill) , and Green Living Ideas. Scott is an occasional investor, currently he has investments in Rivian (RIVN).

#5786. Mid-Air Helicopter Collision Near Everest Base Camp Kills Tourist, Injures 2 Others

Although an entire tourism industry has grown around climbing Mount Everest, summiting the world's tallest mountain remains a tremendously dangerous endeavor. Two helicopters collided in mid-air while attempting to land at the same spot below the Everest base camp. Helicopter company Fishtail Air stated that the crash killed an Indian tourist, and the chopper's captain and another passenger were injured. The other helicopter's pilot somehow escaped without injury. The second chopper was only carrying cargo.

The footage is harrowing, to say the least. A red helicopter is hovering, gradually descending and rotating to a landing spot at Pheriche. The Nepali village sits 13,780 feet above sea level. Then, a second helicopter comes into frame, seemingly appearing out of nowhere. Both pilots take evasive action far too late. The second chopper's main blades smash into the other rotorcraft, slicing off the tail boom. Both helicopters immediately plummet right into the snowy terrain as people waiting on the ground scramble away. Miraculously, none of the bystanders were struck by flying debris or injured. There's never a good outcome when two helicopters hit each other.

It's pretty baffling how two helicopters could collide in completely clear conditions. Maybe the pilots didn't realize they were trying to land in the same spot. Helicopter flights aren't rare in this part of the world, either. According to the BBC, helicopters are the only way to get trekkers and guides down from Everest when they are sick or exhausted in inhospitable conditions. It's also the tail end of the mountain's autumn climbing season.

The tourists who spend thousands of dollars to climb Everest do so with the understanding that it's inherently dangerous. Those dangers are typically low oxygen levels and freezing temperatures at absurdly high altitudes. Just getting to the mountain can be just as dangerous. Most journeys to Everest base camp begin at Tenzing-Hillary Airport, named after the first mountaineers to climb the mountain. The facility is often called the world's most dangerous airport because of its short 1,729-foot runway with a 12% gradient and the mountain wall at one end. Not to mention, the terrain doesn't allow pilots to go around despite the rapidly shifting weather conditions. Just flying in would be enough of an Everest adventure for me.

#5782. Who’s responsible when clinical AI goes wrong? AMA weighs in

Who’s responsible when clinical AI goes wrong? AMA weighs in" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Building on its recent guidance for organizations’ use and governance of clinical AI, the American Medical Association on Thursday gave a deeper breakdown of how it believes different parties should be responsible for decisions, actions and failures involving the technology.

The latest framework from AMA’s Center for Digital Health and AI addresses liability issues the group said are currently unanswered by existing liability frameworks. Those structures, it said, could leave physicians facing "liability for risks they cannot reasonably prevent, while patients may struggle to seek remedies when AI causes harm."

Other key issues with the status quo liability frameworks, AMA said, are ambiguity around when product liability applies to AI; how contract terms and disclaimers from developers can distance responsibility from risk control; and whether deploying healthcare organizations hold various responsibilities specific to AI, such as local testing or outcomes monitoring.

AMA said the clinical AI liability framework it’s advancing "recognizes that multiple parties may bear liability for the use of AI when something goes wrong," and then aligns that accountability based on a party’s ability to prevent harm. Responsibility is spread out in areas where control is shared, but it does not become interchangeable, and no party’s obligations disappear because another party also bears some,” AMA wrote in a brief outlining its thinking.

As for the physicians AMA represents, the liability framework calls for doctors to "be responsible for the clinical judgment they can meaningfully exercise, based on the system’s intended use, known limitations and the information available at the point of care."

The group also said that oversight from a physician "cannot substitute for adequate evidence, appropriate system design or the conditions necessary to make clinical review meaningful." Physicians should also retain the authority to decline an unproven AI system, or those "whose clinical validation, usefulness or place in the standard of care remains uncertain," without penalty from their organization, AMA said.

"Patients must have meaningful avenues for recourse when clinical AI causes harm, and physicians must be able to use these technologies with confidence that responsibility reflects what they can reasonably know and control," AMA President Willie Underwood III, M.D., president of the AMA, said in a release on the liability framework. "As AI assumes more clinical functions, developers, healthcare organizations and physicians each have important responsibilities. We need clear expectations that protect patients, support sound clinical judgment, and ensure accountability remains with those best positioned to prevent harm."

The liability framework breaks down in detail one aspect of a broader clinical AI governance framework unveiled by AMA and its Center earlier this month. Those principles and focus areas will guide how AMA works with providers and stakeholders as it tackles issues like licensure and regulation for the fast-moving technology.

"We cannot afford to wait for these questions to be answered through trial and error in patient care," AMA CEO John Whyte, M.D., told Fierce Healthcare of the efforts earlier this month. "The AMA's new framework sets out our ambitious agenda to address these questions. … It will guide our work with physicians, patients, technology developers and policymakers to ensure clinical authority is earned through evidence, how oversight must evolve with risk, and how accountability is maintained."

#5780. Oil Companies Will Love That The 2027 Chevrolet Silverado's New V8s Get Worse Gas Mileage Than The Old Ones

Due to a litany of misguided decisions on behalf of the Trump administration, gas is ridiculously expensive right now, corporate fuel economy requirements are worryingly low, and we're in an affordability crisis. In totally unrelated news, the oil and gas companies that spent millions to elect Trump are raking in record profits that are more than double what they were at this time last year. Those oil companies are doing fine, but they will still likely be stoked to learn that GM announced the fuel economy numbers for V8-powered examples of the freshly redesigned 2027 Chevrolet Silverado today, and they all get worse gas mileage than the outgoing Silverado's V8s. These numbers should all also apply to the 2027 GMC Sierra, too.

According to documents posted by GM Authority, the fuel economy of all Silverados equipped with either the new 5.7-liter V8 or the new 6.6-liter V8 has dropped between 1 and 2 mpg across city ratings, highway ratings, and combined ratings. While these drops aren't especially significant, it's rare to see redesigned versions of cars debut with worse efficiency than their predecessors, even when we're talking about big trucks.

2027 Silverados fitted with the 5.7-liter V8 are rated at 16 mpg city, 19 mpg highway, and 17 combined in two-wheel-drive form; opting for four-wheel drive drops both the highway and combined ratings by an additional mpg. Those city and combined figures are each down one mpg, and the highway rating is down two mpg compared to the 2026 Silverado.

Trucks with the 6.6-liter V8 are only shown in four-wheel-drive, and are rated at 14 mpg in the city, 18 mpg on the highway, and 15 mpg combined. If you go for the off-road-oriented Silverado ZR2, it drops the city and combined figures by 1 mpg and the highway figure by 3 mpg. (The same should go for the Sierra's AT4X equivalent.) All of those numbers are down by either 1 or 2 mpg when compared to their fuel economy ratings in 2026.

Even opting for the 3.0-liter inline-six turbodiesel powertrain option won't save as much fuel as it did last year. Most diesel-powered 2027 Silverados return between 1 and 2 mpg worse than last year, except for city mileage in some four-wheel-drive trims. City and highway mileage for the diesel ZR2 remains the same. Mileage ratings for the turbocharged 2.7-liter four-cylinder powertrain have not been published yet.

Considering that the Chevrolet Silverado almost always lands in the second-place spot on the list of best-selling vehicles in the U.S. behind the Ford F-Series, and the GMC Sierra isn't too far behind, the impact of small changes in efficiency get magnified. So far through the third quarter of 2026, GMC sold 252,639 Sierras and Chevrolet sold 413,383 Silverados, and production of the new-gen trucks only just started in October. Though not all of these trucks will be fitted with one of the new V8s, certainly a ton of them will, and decreasing even just V8 gas mileage by a single mpg will still result in a massive increase in collective fuel usage.

#5777. Post-midterms, hospitals still face a long road to policy relief, advisers warn

Post-midterms, hospitals still face a long road to policy relief, advisers warn" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Hospitals facing major policy headwinds won’t be able to sustain operations through cost cutting or revenue protections alone, and they shouldn’t bank on immediate political relief following this week’s midterm results, BRG policy and health system operations consultants warn.

Health systems across the country have been gearing up for the years-long rollout of Medicare and Medicaid policy changes from 2025’s H.R. 1, whose standout changes, such as Medicaid work requirements and state-directed payment restrictions, will begin in earnest on Jan. 1. The implementation is expected to reduce the number of patients with coverage and limit supplemental payments to providers, compounding challenges they’re already facing this year after expired Affordable Care Act subsidies pushed many patients off marketplace coverage.

“I’m generally an optimist as [my] personality, but the quote that comes to me is ‘It can never be so bad that it can’t get worse,” David Wildebrandt, a managing director in BRG’s healthcare practice, said during a Thursday media roundtable on federal policy takeaways for healthcare providers. “It’s really very troubling, the cumulative toll of everything that’s happening, because health systems have an incredibly difficult ecosystem in general in terms of capacity constraints, payer mix, softer volumes.”

Those headwinds will land amid a midterm election in which healthcare issues are top items for voters. Reversing or hobbling H.R. 1 has emerged as a priority for Democratic candidates and party leaders, promises that would have no small impact on hospitals hoping for a financial lifeline.

“I do think the biggest ticket item here for the next couple of years is how One Big Beautiful Bill Act implementation goes, how states respond and whether or not Congress tries to have a say by potentially trying to amend that bill in the first couple of years,” John Barkett, managing director in BRG’s Healthcare Transactions and Strategy practice, and formerly an advisor on the White House Domestic Policy Council, said. “It's not uncommon for big bills, including Obamacare or Medicare or any other big bill, to be amended within a couple of years of passage.”

In a scenario where Democrats take both the House (currently considered very likely by pollsters) and the Senate (more of a toss-up), BRG’s healthcare practice advisors said they anticipate a slew of new congressional oversight and investigations into health agencies and some of the organizations they’d cut deals with in recent years. And even if they can’t get a partisan health bill signed into law, there’s still room to write and pass bills that could become new policy in a future majority, as was the case with Medicaid work requirements pushed by Republicans during the end of the Biden administration but ultimately codified last year.

As for the OBBBA, the BRG consultants acknowledged that revisions to the sweeping Medicaid changes are possible, but pointed out the steep hill they’d need to climb.

“President Trump will still be president, and he will view a policy that amends the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in favor of hospitals as a concession to Democrats—and therefore, he’ll be looking for something in return,” Barkett said. “And so the question will be—how big is the ask for what the Trump administration would want in return for amending a signature law … and what he’s asking for would have to be palatable for Democrats. And that’s where I think there’s a lot of uncertainty right now.”

“Providers shouldn’t really plan on relief coming from Washington in that way,” Dave Brueggeman, another managing director in BRG’s healthcare practice, said of an OBBBA amendment and a potential swift return of marketplace subsidies.

Barkett noted that second-term, lame duck presidents tend to look at their legacy as lawmaking grinds to a halt. That could make Trump and his administration “even more emboldened to take action through [Centers for Medicare and Medicaid] rulemaking,” he said.

“The question I’m thinking about is—what signals is the president giving about what he wants his legacy to be on healthcare in the last couple of years,” he said. “I’m not sure that anyone who’s saying they know what that is necessarily has the mind of the president. I think it could go in several directions, and it’s particularly interesting given that the Supreme Court … has been constricting what an executive branch can do when they’re thinking creatively about how to interpret statutes.”

Should Republicans maintain control of The Hill, Barkett said the industry should expect a continuation of the policy agenda from the past two years—reduced coverage, lower spending and deference to regulatory agencies—with “maybe some bipartisan work going on,” such as pharmacy benefit manager reforms from earlier this year.

“The bottom line here is that revenue pressure from the OBBBA isn't a one-year problem,” said Brueggeman. “It builds over the next decade, and the systems that come out of it in best shape will be the ones that start adjusting the revenue and cost strategies now.”

The policy landscape is unprecedented ground for management teams that, likely for the first time in their careers, are facing a year in which overall health insurance coverage isn't increasing.

Wildebrandt's chief advice, based on best practices BRG is seeing among big names like HCA Healthcare and Tenet Healthcare, is to cut through the unknowns and develop a financial exposure plan with “very sophisticated predictions of what's going to happen with charity care, uncompensated care, the amount of uninsured, EBITDA forecasts."

“The one thing I would certainly want to impress upon everyone is [that] it is different for every hospital. You cannot use a blanket statement,” he said of the policy impacts going into effect. Such predictions “really create a true north for everyone to look at. […] Some of the systems that are doing that, it’s been very much an awakening event.”

The immediate next priority, Wildebrandt said, is for systems to model and protect enrollment among patients who will still be eligible for coverage after January’s work requirements implementation deadline, for instance by “standing up outreach centers to help with the documentation and the education of the work requirements.” Brueggeman similarly raised red flags over yet-to-be-shared state guidance on how the changes could impact Medicaid presumptive eligibility, and noted that many BRG hospital clients are reviewing their collections and self-pay and charity care policies amid an expectation of increased payment difficulties.

From there, health systems will need to begin ramping up their cost optimization and strategic realignment, likely to a greater extent than what they’ve already pursued over the past year.

“What we share with our clients and folks that are really getting ahead of this is another 5% to 7% of cost reduction on top of what they're already doing,” he said. “And that really gets you into deeper areas beyond labor, beyond supply chain. What we're working on mostly is a transformational roadmap.”

The chief opportunities here, he said, involve integrated care models and leaning into many of the skills systems developed under risk-based arrangements to direct patients to community providers or other lower-cost settings when possible.

“We’ll likely see an explosion of growth in partnerships with FQHCs and other community organizations to get folks into the right care setting and reduce unnecessary utilization,” he said. “And another important area, one we’ve honestly given some lip service to over time, is partnering to expand ambulatory access and, again, reduce preventable hospital use.”

Wildebrandt described these efforts as requiring “structural changes” addressing “fixed costs, and not just working into variable costs.” That means taking a hard look at what’s currently on offer.

“We see many organizations assessing their portfolio, looking at service rationalization—especially big systems that have integrated and have redundant OB units within the same perimeter,” he said. “You'll see more Centers of Excellence coming out of this, which will decrease access, but consolidating services, OB, pediatric intensive care units, and other non-core programs like post-acute rehab. … You’re seeing folks also spinning things off, spinning hospitals off, spinning service lines off. So definitely a lot of activity in this space.”

Leaders from major nonprofit health systems who were on the panel agreed. Matt Brown, president of CommonSpirit Health’s South Region, said it’s become more routine to hear of cost-conscious systems targeting stiffer benchmarks for their labor spending—salary, wages and benefits expenses below 45% of patient service revenue, “when 15 years ago under 60% was appropriate."

He and Gail Kosyla, chief financial officer at AtlantiCare, also acknowledged that nonprofits are already weighing options on service lines that are losing money for the system, noting that providers could mitigate the impact on patient access by partnering with another community provider already offering the same services.

“Those are difficult decisions, and they really go to patient need, community need, as well as that financial component,” Kosyla said during the roundtable.

With the scope of headwinds to come, panelists agreed that cost management alone won't close the gap without corresponding efforts to protect revenue.

Brueggeman said his team has been working “every day” on an “explosive growth” in termination planning, as providers negotiating new network agreements with payers are increasingly willing to play chicken in order to maximize revenue. Should those disputes come to a head, a hospital’s network exit could mean reduced access to care for local patients.

Brueggeman noted that the contentious negotiations have recently lost a natural common ground. Risk-based arrangements with shared upsides and downsides have become less appealing to providers due to a “lack of ability to specifically predict what those outcomes would look like,” with the policy changes, he said. “That creates a significant tension against what was, at one time, considered an outlet in these negotiations of creating a shared responsibility around risk. It's creating a little bit of a dam in that process.”

CommonSpirit’s Brown was up front about the need to go toe-to-toe, and the benefits for doing so.

“We’re doing everything we can with payers to understand how we maximize our reimbursement,” he said. “That means draconian things at times. We’ve had markets go out of network with Medicare Advantage providers. And we’ve gotten back in recently—specifically a community in Texas. We went out for a while and then came back in as a national player.”

“We have to do everything we can to leverage our scale in negotiations with payers—and with states to ensure that we don't get hit with provider fee problems in places like Kentucky, Colorado and California to the level that H.R. 1 projects,” he added.

How MRD is powering the next wave of precision oncology" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Cancer care is shifting beyond the detection of visible disease. A new generation of molecular residual disease, or MRD, testing can detect tiny traces of ctDNA that may remain during or after treatment, offering an additional way to identify disease when traditional approaches may not yet reveal it. Dr. Rick Baehner, Divisional Vice President, Chief Medical Officer, Precision Oncology, Abbott cancer diagnostics, explores why MRD represents the next chapter of precision oncology and how the next-generation Oncodetect® test could help move cancer care from reactive treatment toward more proactive monitoring.In this video interview with Kelly Hogan of Fierce Healthcare, Baehner explains how MRD testing can provide molecular insights into some of oncology's most pressing questions: Is treatment working? Is cancer truly gone? Has disease returned? He also explores why sensitivity is critical, particularly when tumor burden is low, including in low-shedding cancers and as ctDNA levels fall during and after treatment. Baehner explores the science behind whole-genome sequencing-based MRD tests and looks ahead to what broader adoption could mean for oncology workflows, clinical decision-making and patient outcomes. As MRD testing becomes more integrated into everyday care, he argues that cancer monitoring may become as individualized as cancer treatment itself. Watch the interview to learn why the next era of oncology may be defined not only by how we treat cancer, but by how quickly and intelligently we anticipate its return.

#5774. At $18,000, Could This 1997 Bentley Brooklands Let You See How The Other Half Lives?

Based on today's Nice Price or No Dice Bentley's price, you don't have to be a one-percent-er to live life large. Let's see if this stately and imposing saloon makes us want to live it up.

On their third album, "Learning to Crawl," Chrissie Hynde and The Pretenders warned us of "Time the Avenger." A song about bad decisions, regret, and the inability to turn back the clock, it fit the album's tone perfectly, following the untimely deaths of two band members.

The fact is, time keeps marching forward, and we can never slow its pace or fully reverse its effects. That makes looking at cars like the 2001 Audi A4 Quattro Avant we considered yesterday such a scary proposition. While the seller promised that many of the car's wear-and-tear items had been addressed, with any old Audi, there's always some new surprise to darken a day and lighten a wallet. That expectation of future failures on this 25-year-old Audi gave pause, calling into question its $7,450 asking price. In the end, that was just too much to risk, and we saw an overwhelming 73% 'No Dice' loss as a result.

Okay, if you all had a hard time justifying the potential future costs of an old mid-level Audi, let's see how you do with today's far fancier-pantsed 1997 Bentley Brooklands saloon. Bentley offered the Brooklands for a short five years, from 1993 to 1998, though the model was merely an evolution of the earlier Mulsanne, introduced all the way back in 1980. That makes the model a grand dame of British luxury comportment.

Following the marque's fancy of naming its models after race tracks or sections thereof, the Brooklands takes its name from the Brooklands circuit outside of Surrey, England. It was the world's first banked oval raceway, inspiring the Indianapolis Motor Speedway when it opened in 1907 and hosting its last race in 1939. In the years in between, Bentleys raced on the track, reinforcing the model's legacy. In another unique connection, the British aircraft manufacturer Vickers located a factory at the Brooklands Aerodrome, right next to the track, and later, when this Brooklands was built, that company was the majority owner of Rolls-Royce and Bentley.

With that bit of history out of the way, let's get to just what this car is. When it was built, Bentley and Rolls-Royce were kissing cousins (I know, eww, that phrase), with both marques sharing production in Crewe on the same platform. That means that, save for its rounded grille, some suspension tuning, and a whole herd of Flying B badges, this model is essentially the same as the contemporary Rolls-Royce Silver Spirit. That means it also shares the Rolls-Royce 6.75-liter OHV V8 engine.

When it debuted in 1993, the Brooklands was meant to be a less expensive (but still very expensive) model slotted under the Turbo R. As such, it was initially available only with a naturally aspirated version of that Rolls engine. That changed in 1996, when the Brooklands got a light-pressure turbo edition, producing 300 horsepower and an impressive 442 pound-feet of torque. That's a good thing, considering this luxury barge is fitted with every comfort and convenience feature the late '90s could offer, bringing the car's weight to over 5,300 pounds. That means reasonable performance and jaw-dropping thirst for premium fuel.

This Brooklands, which the ad claims to be painted in Black Emerald Mica over a parchment Connolly leather interior with spruce trim on the dash and doors, looks to be in fabulous condition. The paint, which appears dark green in the pictures, is accented by elegant but not overwhelming chrome trim and a handsome set of factory alloy wheels.

One notable feature of the Brooklands' cabin is the placement of the four-speed automatic shifter. It sits on the center console, a first for the model line, which traditionally used a column shifter.

The interior, swathed in two-tone leather and elegant wood, cossets passengers like they're in an English drawing room. The only thing missing is the sound of a fire crackling in a hearth. In fact, the ad says nothing is missing from this car, stating categorically that it "needs nothing." In addition to being mechanically and visually sound, the seller notes that the 67,402-mile car comes with a clean title, a passing smog test grade, and a Carfax report offering the kind of dull reading you want on any used car.

Of course, this is a Bentley. And it's a Bentley of a certain age (even older than yesterday's Audi), which means this Brooklands will likely need something in the future. That's to be feared, not eagerly awaited, because parts for these cars are incredibly expensive, and certain maintenance and repair work often requires special tools. Do you possess those? I certainly don't.

That's why anyone interested in a car like this needs to choose the best one they can find and afford. The thing is, these cars are getting very affordable to buy, even in good shape, for a variety of reasons. This one asks $18,000, which I think we can all admit seems like a lot of car for the money. But will it cost far more in the long run? Magic 8-Ball is inconclusive.

What's your take on this Bentley at an $18,000 asking price? Is that a safe bet to slip into the lap of luxury, at least until something major breaks and sullies the experience? Or is even that amount too much to fall into this Brooklands' honey trap?

Los Angeles, California, Craigslist, or go here if the ad disappears.

#5773. The Confidence Trap: What a New Survey Reveals About AI and Health Decisions

The Confidence Trap: What a New Survey Reveals About AI and Health Decisions" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Healthcare remains difficult to navigate. People often must piece together information from providers, benefits, pharmacy, digital tools and care teams while trying to understand costs and what to do next.

Increasingly, they’re turning to consumer AI chatbots for answers. The appeal is understandable: they’re available anytime, respond instantly and can make complex information more digestible.

But healthcare decisions require more than quick answers. The quality of guidance depends on context. General-purpose AI tools typically don't have access to a person's medical history, benefits, costs, care team or broader health circumstances, and they aren't designed to provide clinically governed guidance.

According to a new survey commissioned by MD Live, 37%  of people surveyed turn to AI chatbots for health questions because they're available any time; 31% because they're faster than seeing a doctor; and 30% because AI is reassuring when people are worried about a health concern.

Most people don’t realize how much what they say, or don’t say, impacts the answer they get. The survey findings reveal just how often people reframe questions to elicit a preferred  response, or how much influence these tools have on site-of-care decisions.

Fifty-three percent of respondents admit to rewording questions until an AI tool gives them the answer they were hoping for. Nearly three-quarters leave out relevant medical history when they ask, and this gap can go unnoticed: 22% believe AI factors in their personal medical history even if they’ve never shared it.

The same trust carries over to their children, too, with 71% comfortable relying solely on AI to determine what kind of care their child needs, and 68% to decide whether their child needs care at all.

The behavior is understandable. People often seek reassurance when they're uncertain or worried about a health concern. But in healthcare, reassurance alone isn't always what's needed. Decisions are strongest when they are informed by relevant context, clinical expertise and an understanding of what happens next.

What we’re seeing is a growing number of people making site-of-care decisions with tools that may lack important clinical context. When guidance is generated without a complete understanding of the individual, recommendations may feel personalized while remaining fundamentally generic.

The issue isn't whether AI has a role in healthcare. It does. In fact, AI's capabilities are advancing quickly. The more important question isn’t whether AI can generate an answer. It’s whether that answer reflects the individual’s unique health situation, care needs, benefits, costs, and available care options. Without that context, even sophisticated tools can produce guidance that doesn't reflect a person's real circumstances.

As a result, healthcare organizations may increasingly face a challenge where generic guidance drives highly personal healthcare decisions, with downstream implications for utilization, costs, and patient outcomes.

AI models can prioritize agreeableness in ways that complicate health decisions. A Stanford study published in Science in March 2026 found that large language models endorsed a person's position 49% more often than a human would and affirmed harmful or clearly wrong choices 47% of the time.

That mechanism explains why rewording works so well: the models adjust to please their users. People have learned to reword their questions because the system is built to reward persistence with reassurance, whether that reassurance is warranted.

The impact of this behavior is not theoretical. The survey found that 59% of respondents say they've received AI health information that they later realized didn't fully apply to their personal situation, and 49% acted on it anyway before finding out.

This is also backed by independent research: Oxford researchers, publishing in Nature Medicine in February 2026, ran the largest user study to date on LLMs assisting the public with medical decisions and found that people using AI made no better choices in real triage scenarios than those relying on a search engine or their own judgment.

A separate BMJ Open study from April 2026 audited five popular chatbots across common health topics and rated nearly half of all responses as problematic, while also finding that the tools consistently responded with confidence and certainty.

Studies show that AI’s clinical capabilities are advancing quickly. But healthcare is different from many other consumer use cases. The quality of the response depends not only on the technology itself, but on how well it understands the person behind the question. In healthcare, broadly correct information is not always the same as clinically appropriate guidance. Not to mention, this isn't a fringe behavior. Pew Research found that a quarter of Americans now use AI chatbots to self-diagnose symptoms, and KFF's tracking poll puts overall AI use for health information at 32%, on par with social media.

The consumer need for fast answers and on-demand access is real and isn't going away. The question is how healthcare leaders meet consumers where they are while helping them make informed care decisions.

At MD Live, we believe the future of healthcare AI isn't simply about delivering answers. It's about helping people make informed decisions with appropriate clinical support and a clear path to care when the situation calls for it. People are already using AI to determine where to go for care. The opportunity now is to ensure those decisions are supported by experiences that combine technology with clinical expertise, helping people move from information to informed action.

#5772. FDA Panel Largely Pans Trial Data for Myopia Eye Drops

— Atropine slowed progression but clinical meaningfulness, robustness of data questioned

The regulatory status of a low-dose atropine eye drop formulation for myopia remained unresolved following a day-long FDA advisory committee meeting, but closing comments did not bode well for SYD-101.

The Dermatologic and Ophthalmic Drugs Advisory Committee (DODAC) did not vote to recommend for or against approval of the eye drops, but panelists' responses to key questions posed by the FDA suggested the evidence from a phase III trial of SYD-101 did not meet standards for approval.

"Basically, the summary is that, although the clinical trial is positive, it's not a robust outcome that would meet the standard presented to us as the reason for approval by the FDA," said DODAC Acting Chair Michael X. Repka, MD, of the Johns Hopkins Wilmer Eye Institute in Baltimore. "The issue of missing data remains sort of difficult for this committee to manage."

Primary support for the approval application came from the SYD-101-001 randomized trial (also known as the STAR trial) comparing two doses of atropine sulfate ophthalmic solution versus vehicle to slow myopia progression in 852 pediatric patients 3 years or older. The primary endpoint was the proportion of patients with myopia progression exceeding 0.75 diopters at 36 months.

The primary analysis showed that 39.5% of patients randomized to the 0.01% solution met the primary endpoint as compared with 49.3% of patients randomized to the control group (P=0.0452). The 0.03% treatment arm did not achieve statistical significance versus the control group.

The difference between the 0.01% arm and vehicle translated into progression slowing of 0.079 diopters per year or a cumulative difference of 0.21 diopters versus control. In a briefing document prepared for the meeting, FDA staff said the difference, though statistically significant, was not clinically meaningful and that the magnitude of benefit decreased over time.

Additionally, primary endpoint data were missing for 26% of patients in the 0.01% treatment arm and 23% of the control group. Sensitivity analyses showed the outcome data were influenced by different assumptions about the statistical impact of missing data.

The staff report also noted that the trial failed to show a significant reduction in axial length, which raised questions about the treatment's potential to alter myopia-related structural changes. Half of the participating centers did not measure axial length, and measurement was not uniform at the centers that did. Additionally, "external evidence from other randomized controlled trials conducted in non-Asian Western populations has generally been unsupportive of the efficacy of 0.01% atropine."

Summarizing the panel's comments regarding the clinical meaningfulness of the differences observed in the trial, Repka said, "The [committee] basically considered the clinical meaningfulness of the observed efficacy profile uncertain, both because of the magnitude, the question of just a shift or delay in myopia progression by the 6-month or 1-year cycle, and also the lack of corroboration on axial length in those centers that were able to perform it. [The committee] would recommend to manufacturers in the future to consider including axial length as a primary or key outcome measure."

The panel also appeared to agree with FDA staff that the published literature did not provide confirmatory evidence, beyond the SYD-101-001 trial, that would rise to the standards necessary for approval.

"When I look at the other studies, they were not as well performed or designed as the [SYD-101-001] study we're discussing," said panelist Timothy G. Murray, MD, of the University of Miami Bascom Palmer Eye Institute. "The size, stratification, and randomization that was done was a plus. The way that the data was looked at is a plus. The other studies fall far below that standard, and therefore, I wouldn't consider that substantial evidence or a standard for approval."

In a separate report for DODAC, representatives of Sydnexis noted that the SYD-101-001 trial was designed with input from the FDA. They emphasized that the trial met the prespecified primary endpoint and that the levels of statistical significance increased in a multiple-adjusted analysis (P=0.0226). Data for the key secondary endpoint also achieved statistical significance for the 0.01% solution versus vehicle (P=0.0002).

Though acknowledging missing data, Sydnexis stated that "missing efficacy data and discontinuations were not meaningfully imbalanced across groups. All prespecified missing-data sensitivity estimates favored SYD-101 0.01%, with treatment estimates generally consistent with the primary result."

DODAC panelists did not dispute the statistical significance of the primary endpoint but rather questioned the robustness and clinical meaningfulness of the results. Murray said the lack of robustness "calls into question our ability to interpret the data further."

Alex Kaizer, PhD, a biostatistician at the University of Colorado Anschutz in Aurora, noted that confidence intervals for efficacy data approached 0%, making the results susceptible to small changes.

"I think what this means to me, with the discussion around the potential clinical significance and the heterogeneity of the patient population, is that it feels like more data is truly needed to understand, especially in younger ages and fast progressors, what the benefit would be," he said.

Acknowledging that the treatment seems promising and is approved elsewhere in the world, Kaizer added, "These borderline results do make it challenging, because if just a few people change their outcome, it could change the result suddenly to a very different discussion than the one we're having today."

Throughout the meeting, several speakers noted that dozens of studies have demonstrated atropine eye drops' efficacy in myopia and that low-dose formulations are available in many nations, but not the U.S. Clinicians in the U.S. can and do prescribe low-dose atropine eye drops, but the medication is available only through compounding pharmacies.

The DODAC meeting had its genesis in a complete response letter the FDA sent to Sydnexis in October 2025.

"The FDA acknowledged in the complete response letter that this primary endpoint was met but stated its view that the data do not support the effectiveness of low-dose atropine in children with myopia," company officials stated in a press release. "No deficiencies were noted related to safety or product quality."

In response, Sydnexis submitted a formal dispute resolution request to the FDA, which subsequently scheduled the DODAC meeting to consider the evidence in separate presentations by FDA staff and speakers representing Sydnexis, including several pediatric ophthalmologists.

The next step is up to the FDA, and no timetable for a decision was announced at the conclusion of the DODAC meeting.

#5771. From Transparency to Defensibility: The Standard Mid–Revenue Cycle AI Requires

From Transparency to Defensibility: The Standard Mid–Revenue Cycle AI Requires" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Written by: Hani Judeh, MD, CMO and CMIO, Accuity Healthcare and Stephanie Smith, MD, Vice President, Clinical Intelligence, Accuity

Healthcare AI is moving from enthusiasm to accountability.

The Health AI Partnership's AI Vendor Disclosure Framework, described in NEJM AI, gives health systems a structured way to evaluate AI vendors across intended use, system performance and compliance, data stewardship, integration, and lifecycle management. That transparency matters — it gives buyers a better way to ask what an AI system actually does before it's purchased and implemented.

For mid–revenue cycle vendors, though, disclosure is only the starting point. The more important question is whether the recommendation can be defended.

That distinction matters because mid–revenue cycle AI doesn't operate at a distance from consequence. It sits inside decisions that affect documentation integrity, coding pathways, reimbursement, denials, payer scrutiny, reviewer burden, and provider trust. A single recommendation may influence whether an opportunity is surfaced, escalated, deprioritized, or acted upon — and hospitals and physicians remain accountable for the decisions they make using vendor AI outputs.

At Accuity, we believe that responsibility requires a higher standard: clinical and coding integrity.

Clinical and coding integrity means an AI-supported recommendation should be clinically meaningful, documentation-supported, coding-relevant, and defensible under review. It should be clear why the recommendation was made, what evidence supports it, what uncertainty remains, and whether the case is appropriate for automation or expert review. That is the difference between AI that can be described and AI that can be defended.

Health systems are operating on thin margins, which means they need automation that stays reliable after launch — not automation that creates new volatility. Missed clinically valid findings become revenue leakage. Unsupported recommendations create rework, denials exposure, and payer clawback risk. Prioritization pathways without monitoring can make work disappear from view while risk quietly accumulates.

Stable automation doesn't happen by accident. It requires evidence standards, decision boundaries, monitoring, change control, and rollback criteria. Governance isn't administrative drag. It's how automation stays reliable as documentation patterns, payer behavior, coding guidance, and client workflows shift over time. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework identifies these same measures as core functions of trustworthy AI systems.¹

This is why mid–revenue cycle automation can't be judged by throughput alone. A clinically plausible finding isn't automatically a coding-supported opportunity. A documentation phrase isn't automatically evidence of an active, reportable, reimbursable condition. The work requires careful translation across medicine, documentation, coding guidance, payer scrutiny, and operational workflow — and that translation cannot be left to automation alone.

Accuity's approach combines physician-led clinical logic development, physician-coder adjudication, governance controls, and downstream appeals management for the cases we touch. Physicians and coders bring different but complementary expertise: physicians contribute clinical context, disease understanding, plausibility assessment, and judgment under uncertainty, while coders bring documentation standards, coding guidance, reimbursement logic, and defensibility discipline. Together, they determine whether an AI-supported opportunity is valid and appropriate for action — giving automation both structure and restraint.

Physician-authored logic defines the clinical intent of the technology. Expert judgment determines when evidence is strong enough to act, when uncertainty should stop automation, and when human review is required. That is the Accuity value proposition: not automation for throughput only, but automation governed by the people who understand the clinical and coding consequences of being wrong.

Lineage is where defensibility becomes real

A vendor AI output doesn't remove accountability. The hospital still has to act and respond to scrutiny. The physician still has to stand behind the clinical record. The coding and revenue cycle teams still have to defend the resulting claim.

That's why evidence lineage matters. A recommendation should be traceable from the output back to the record evidence, diagnosis or procedure, coding rationale, and logic or model version that produced it. Mid–revenue cycle decisions don't rest on isolated words — they depend on source, timing, attribution, clinical context, documentation sufficiency, and coding relevance. Lineage allows reviewers and governance teams to understand where the evidence came from, why it mattered, and whether it was strong enough to support action. It also creates the path for error review, drift detection, recurrence tracking, and logic correction.

Accuity extends that defensibility downstream. For the cases we touch, appeals management connects the original recommendation to the evidence, clinical rationale, coding rationale, and payer-facing defense. That matters because defensibility isn't proven when an AI output is generated — it's proven when the recommendation can withstand denial and audit scrutiny. Without lineage, an AI output is an assertion. With lineage and downstream defense, it becomes part of an operating model that can stand behind the work.

The HAIP framework is an important step toward more disciplined AI evaluation and procurement in healthcare. But in the mid–revenue cycle, transparency is the floor. Clinical and coding integrity is the standard.

Defensible automation means AI-supported work shaped by physician-authored logic, physician-coder judgment, evidence lineage, lifecycle governance, and appeals support for the cases we touch. That's how automation can reduce burden without hiding risk, support efficiency without sacrificing defensibility, and help protect financial stability in an environment where margins are thin and volatility is costly.

The future of mid–revenue cycle AI won't belong to the largest model or the loudest automation claim. It will belong to systems that can be trusted at the point of use. More defensible AI. Not just more confident AI.

#5769. Midstream Health nabs $20M series A to help hospitals recover lost margin

Midstream Health nabs $20M series A to help hospitals recover lost margin" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Health systems are losing margins they’ve already earned, according to Sumit Kadakia, CEO and co-founder of Midstream Health. The startup bets that artificial intelligence can improve hospital margins by finding money that is already embedded in contracts and transactions.

Midstream Health, an autonomous financial operations platform for health systems, picked up $20 million in series A funding to expand its AI financial platform. The company is expanding across a customer network representing more than $100 billion in annual operating expenses and over 250 hospitals nationwide.

Valtruis led the financing round with continued participation from Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), Foundry and CommonSpirit Ventures, bringing Midstream’s total funding to $29.2 million. Fairview Health Services and Keck Medicine of USC are among the newest health systems to join the platform, alongside CommonSpirit Health, Mount Sinai Health System and Houston Methodist.

Midstream says its AI financial platform helps health systems find and recover margin across revenue and cost, strengthening the financial capacity needed to keep investing in care and serving their communities.

"We bring all of a health system’s data together, across pharmacy, supply chain, managed care, revenue and cost, into a single source of truth, and then put AI agents on top of it to find and recover money the system is owed. We call it the 'second financial brain' for a health system," Kadakia said in an interview.

He added, "That’s a lot of technical talk for a pretty shocking problem: hospitals are multibillion-dollar enterprises, and most of them don’t have any form of managerial finance."

With that data foundation in place, Midstream Health's domain-trained agents proactively flag and prioritize cost-saving and margin opportunities such as missed rebates, pricing errors, payer underpayments and policy-driven denials.

Kadakia describes the platform as "an army of agents that runs alongside a health system’s finance and supply chain teams, never sleeps, and is constantly finding and recovering margin."

The company plans to use the fresh funding to expand its product and engineering capabilities, particularly as it moves into new verticals. It also plans to continue formalizing its sales and marketing functions and building a dedicated research function that owns its underlying data connections, Kadakia said.

Health systems are facing a financial sustainability crisis, fighting to protect razor-thin margins. More than 110 rural hospitals have closed over the past 20 years, and another 720—representing roughly a third of all rural hospitals—are at risk of closure. Much of what’s slipping away is money health systems have already earned, buried in their own contracts and spend.

According to Kadakia, one system can have thousands of contracts across supply chain, pharmacy and managed care, each with its own pricing tiers, rebate triggers and amendments. "Nobody has time to check every one against what the system actually buys and pays, so a six-figure rebate can disappear because one form was missed. Meanwhile, most healthcare AI money has gone into the claims fight between hospitals and insurers. Every dollar one side wins, the other side loses, and the total cost of care goes up. Deflationary AI will make care cheaper to deliver, and the most direct way to do that is making sure [that] health systems collect what their contracts already say they’re owed. Margin that stays buried in a contract never reaches patients," he said.

Kadakia says he has a personal perspective on the issue—his father practiced at two rural West Virginia hospitals that have since closed.

"In today's challenging healthcare environment, we have to be thoughtful about how we manage our resources and continually look for opportunities to operate more efficiently," said James Hereford, CEO of Fairview Health Services, in a statement. "By leveraging AI-driven financial operations, we can improve financial performance, allowing us to focus more resources on delivering care to our patients and communities."

CommonSpirit Health, one of the largest nonprofit health systems in the U.S., was an initial investor in Midstream and became one of the first healthcare partners chosen to implement and validate the platform through integration with supply chain operations. After implementation, Midstream's AI agents provided "measurable gains within days, surfacing opportunities like missed rebates and underpayments," according to Daniel Barchi, CommonSpirit Health's chief information officer.

"It is a closed-loop AI system that transforms financial intelligence into real-time action, delivering a data foundation, visibility and execution capability," Barchi said in a statement.

Across its customer base, Midstream claims it has identified more than 1,500 financial recovery opportunities this year, from six-figure rebates buried by a single missed form to systemic payer underpayments. Early Midstream partners are projecting more than 5x ROI this year. The platform is on pace to reach $100 million in client savings by the end of 2026, the company claims.

In the near term, Midstream is on pace to reach $100 million in client savings by the end of 2026.

"The longer-term piece is what I’m most excited about, because I think this enables a renaissance in value-based care. Value-based care was built on an unstable foundation. To take on risk, a hospital needs a clear view of what care is actually costing it and why, and the systems to give hospitals that view were never built. If we give them that foundation, they can take on more risk, and that’s how you start to deflate the arms race between payers and providers," Kadakia said.

In the current financial environment, health systems need solutions that can improve their financial position quickly, noted Mike Spadafore, managing director of Valtruis. "We’re backing Midstream because it’s built first-of-its-kind infrastructure to turn complex financial data into action. Where enterprise healthcare technology can take years to demonstrate value, Midstream delivers within the quarter," he said.

AI is intensifying an ongoing financial battle between health systems and insurers, and data shows that this AI "arms race" is driving up short-term healthcare costs. The Blue Cross Blue Shield Association estimates hospitals’ AI coding tools added nearly $1 billion in costs over two years, and insurers are answering with AI of their own.

"Patients, employers and taxpayers pay for that arms race. The next decade should be judged by a simpler test: does the technology bring total cost down? That’s the standard we hold ourselves to," Kadakia said.

#5768. Upfront TAVR May Be the Way Forward in Moderate Aortic Stenosis, Trial Suggests

— First randomized study to evaluate TAVR versus clinical surveillance in moderate AS

Upfront transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) was more protective against death and heart failure events compared with clinical surveillance among patients with moderate aortic stenosis (AS) with at least one at-risk feature, the randomized PROGRESS trial showed.

At 2 years, a composite endpoint of death from any cause or a heart failure event occurred in 16.7% of patients in the upfront TAVR group versus 23.9% of those in the clinical surveillance group (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48-0.93, P=0.02 for superiority), reported Philippe Généreux, MD, of the Gagnon Cardiovascular Institute at Morristown Medical Center in New Jersey, during the Transcatheter Cardiovascular Therapeutics annual conference, hosted by the Cardiovascular Research Foundation.

In addition, TAVR with the balloon-expandable Sapien 3 platform had a safety event rate of 5.9% at 30 days, which was well under the prespecified 13.7% performance goal, and the bulk of events were hospitalizations for device- or procedure-related complications (5.6%).

The study was simultaneously published in the New England Journal of Medicine.

"Moderate AS is not benign, and these patients would benefit from earlier referral to a valve clinic for comprehensive evaluation to establish the optimal management strategy," Généreux concluded. "Rather than waiting for progression to severe AS, PROGRESS supports TAVR for patients with moderate AS and at-risk features."

Importantly, the trial has follow-up planned for 10 years. In the meantime, Généreux said that the PROGRESS trial has already identified the "optimal time" for intervention in AS considering the balance of safety and efficacy.

Among the clinical surveillance patients who started out with moderate AS, 57.4% eventually underwent a delayed aortic valve replacement (AVR) by 24 months. Of these patients, over 80% had progressed to severe AS.

Meanwhile, the TAVR arm showed the "best hemodynamics that we ever saw" with the Sapien valve, Généreux reported, citing the effective orifice areas, mean gradients, and minimal paravalvular leaks achieved. "The future will tell, but I strongly believe based on the data today ... [that] this is the optimal timing of intervention to ensure optimal treatment for a patient given that we can treat a second time."

"This disease progressed faster than [we] expected," he stressed. "You need to follow these patients. You cannot abandon them."

During a press conference, panelist Pinak Shah, MD, of Mass General Brigham in Boston, called the trial a "truly practice-changing study" that "really underscores the importance of close follow-up and the fact that AS is not a benign disease."

The results also suggest a drastic widening of the pool of TAVR candidates.

A large registry study, also by Généreux and colleagues, recently showed that patients with moderate AS outnumber those with severe AS by nearly 2:1, and over a quarter of those with moderate AS in this study progressed to severe AS by 2 years.

Ultimately, Généreux argued for doing away with the dichotomy of moderate versus severe AS altogether and moving towards intervention on "clinically significant" AS instead.

For their trial, the investigators sought participants who were at least 65 years old with moderate AS plus at least one at-risk feature. The majority were recruited from the U.S. (87.1%), with a minority coming from sites in Japan, Australia, the Netherlands, Canada, and Switzerland.

Out of 1,294 patients screened, 744 were randomized 1:1 to transfemoral TAVR or once-yearly clinical surveillance from October 2021 to January 2024. Mean age was 78 years, and 39% were women. The Society of Thoracic Surgery risk score was about 3.0%, and fewer than half of patients were deemed low risk per the heart team. New York Heart Association class III/IV symptoms were observed in about 35% at baseline. The Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) score was about 64 on average.

The top at-risk features that qualified people for the study were valve-related symptoms (96.4%) and diastolic dysfunction (43.8%).

Généreux reported that 91% of enrolled patients had moderate AS in terms of both moderate aortic valve area (AVA) criteria and peak velocity/mean gradients. The mean AVA was 1.2 cm2, the mean gradient was just over 25 mm Hg, and the peak velocity was 3.3 m/s. About one in four people had an elevated aortic valve calcium score.

The effectiveness endpoint was a composite of death (8.4% vs 7.3%, HR 1.14, 95% CI 0.67-1.93) and heart failure events (10.8% vs 19.0%, HR 0.55, 95% CI 0.37-0.81). Of note, a heart failure event had to meet all three criteria: new or worsening heart failure symptoms, two or more objective indications of new or worsening heart failure (physical, laboratory, imaging, and/or invasive findings), and escalation of heart failure treatment.

Altogether, the number needed to treat for benefit at 2 years was 14 in the trial.

Separately, as a standalone endpoint, heart failure hospitalizations were fewer in the TAVR arm (7.4% vs 14.9%, HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.30-0.77). However, the composite of death, stroke, or heart failure hospitalization did not statistically give TAVR an edge (17.7% vs 23.3%, P=0.07).

As for health status improvement, the mean KCCQ score was 79.6 points in the TAVR arm at 30 days. The proportion of patients alive with an improvement of 10+ points in KCCQ score at 1 and 2 years favored TAVR (39.0% vs 23.2%, P<0.001).

Généreux noted that when it came to delayed AVR in the control arm of the study, KCCQ scores generally dipped before the delayed procedure, followed by a substantial improvement 30 days later.

The incidence rate of new permanent pacemakers was 13.0% with upfront TAVR versus 10.4% with clinical surveillance.

Of note, limiting wider generalizability, PROGRESS had notable exclusion criteria that barred people with unsuitable anatomy for transfemoral TAVR, significant clinical comorbidities, very low ejection fractions, or prior aortic valve replacement or valvuloplasty, among others.

"Certainly, we have to be very careful with patient selection," commented Shah. "For most, the lifetime management is going to be important ... A lot of these patients are probably going to come back for repeat procedures."

#5766. Washington state resident dies from bird flu following exposure to infected cattle

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

NEW YORK — A person in Washington state has died from complications of the bird flu, the first such U.S. death in a year.

The Yakima County resident, who had previous health conditions, was exposed to avian influenza at a dairy with infected cattle and had been hospitalized. The person died Sunday, county health officials said.

Two other U.S. deaths have been tied to bird flu since it became a national public health concern in 2024. The first, announced in January 2025, was an elderly person in Louisiana who had a version of bird flu known as H5N1. The other, in Washington state, died in November 2025 from a rarer version called H5N5.

Yakima County officials did not release any additional details about the person who recently died. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said the person was infected with H5N1.

County officials have reported that 33 dairy herds recently have tested positive for H5N1.

They say three human infections have been linked to exposure at a dairy, and that the Yakima Health District is working with the state health department to find people who were in close contact with those people and monitor them for symptoms.

The H5N1 bird flu has been spreading widely among wild birds, poultry, cows and other animals for several years. Health concerns escalated in early 2024 when infections spread among U.S. livestock. Its presence in the environment increases the chances that people will be exposed, and potentially catch it, officials have said.

More than 70 human infections have been reported in the U.S. since the beginning of 2024, according to the CDC. But there is no known person-to-person spread and the risk to the general public is low, the agency says.

The agency analyzed the genetic sequence of the virus from the person who died in Washington and found no changes that would make the virus spread more easily or cause more severe illness, a CDC spokesperson said Monday.

Officials continue to urge people who have contact with sick or dead birds to take precautions, including wearing respiratory and eye protection and gloves when handling poultry. People who work on farms are considered to be at higher risk.
