#5765. Athenahealth launches tool to bring patient health records into Anthropic's Claude

Athenahealth launches tool to bring patient health records into Anthropic's Claude" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Electronic health record company athenahealth is opening up patient health records to outside AI assistants, starting with Anthropic’s Claude, through a new connection designed to give patients personalized answers based on their clinical data.

The new server solution, athenaPatient MCP, uses the Model Context Protocol to connect Claude directly with the athenaOne platform. Patients authenticate using their athenahealth patient portal credentials and decide what information Claude can access, according to the EHR company. Credentials are not shared with Claude.

Paul Brient, athenahealth's chief product and operations officer, said that information is encrypted in transit, patients control what information is shared, and they can revoke access at any time. "Once the connection is established and patients approve what types of data they would like to share, the rest is between Claude and the patient," he told Fierce Healthcare in an interview.

Brient noted that AI can meaningfully reduce complexity and help patients play a more active role in their care. "At its core, this is about helping patients get value from their own healthcare data," he noted.

Athenahealth is committed to responsible AI integration, company executives said.

Patients are turning to generative AI, like Claude and OpenAI's ChatGPT, to interpret lab results, medication instructions and other medical information. More than a third of U.S. adults (34%) have used AI assistants for health-related purposes, including looking up symptoms to understanding a diagnosis, according to an August Pew Research Center survey. This trend reflects a growing expectation for immediate, conversational health guidance, but also introduces new governance challenges, athenahealth executives noted.

"Claude is the first connection we’ve enabled for athenaPatient MCP, but it's not intended to be the only one," Brient said. "Anthropic has been a strong launch collaborator because of its approach to responsible AI development. But our strategy isn't built around a specific AI model. The AI landscape is moving incredibly quickly, with new models and tools coming to market seemingly every week. We designed athenaPatient MCP with that reality in mind and built it on a Model Context Protocol (MCP) that has become an industry norm for AI interoperability."

Claude Pro and Max users in the U.S. can add the athenaPatient MCP connector within their Claude settings. Patients can then ask Claude questions about their health information using natural language. With a patient’s permission, Claude can reference information such as lab results, medications, vitals, health conditions, diagnostic reports, immunizations, visit history, allergies, procedures and care plans to generate personalized answers based on their clinical data, instead of generic or incomplete information, athenahealth executives said.

"Patients often have questions about their health records between visits, from what a lab result means to what to ask at their next appointment," Syed Mohiuddin, head of healthcare at Anthropic, said in a statement. "athenahealth is giving patients a way to bring their own records into Claude when they choose to, so they can explore those questions and feel more confident and prepared in conversations with their care team."

Athenahealth's EHR is a cloud-based, open platform, Brient noted, and the company's objective is to "create a secure way for patients to use their health information with the AI assistants they choose," he said.

The company plans to expand access to other models, but Brient did not provide any details about additional integrations.

The company built athenaPatient MCP to connect to general-purpose AI assistants rather than build those generative AI capabilities entirely within athenaPatient.

"It's not our job to decide which AI assistant patients should use. Patients are increasingly using AI tools in their daily lives, and I expect that trend to continue. If we've learned anything over the last few years, it's that people will gravitate toward the experiences that work best for them. Healthcare shouldn't be isolated from that reality," Brient said.

"At its core, this is about giving patients access to their health information in the places where they want them—safely, of course. Our patient-facing connector is consistent with our broader interoperability capabilities. Consumers increasingly expect their personal data to integrate into the digital tools they use. Healthcare shouldn't be an exception," he said.

Some providers have raised concerns that as patients increasingly use AI chatbots to interpret health records and lab results, it will drive an uptick in follow-up messages to physicians. Brient noted that giving patients an easier way to connect their health records to AI tools helps patients better understand the information their providers have given them and have more informed questions.

"One of the realities of healthcare is that patients often leave an appointment with more information than they can reasonably absorb in the moment. Lab results often arrive after the patient has seen their doctor. Questions come up after the visit. Medication instructions get forgotten. That's not a criticism of patients or clinicians. It's just reality," he said.

"When patients have a stronger understanding of their healthcare situation, conversations with their care teams tend to be more productive. From the clinician perspective, we were equally focused on what this should not do. We did not want to create additional work for clinicians. A recurring theme across our product strategy is reducing work while improving outcomes. The best healthcare technology helps patients become more engaged without creating more administrative burden for clinicians," Brient noted.

Athenahealth provides EHR software, revenue cycle management and patient engagement solutions to small and independent provider practices. A year ago, the company unveiled new AI features for ambulatory providers as part of a larger upgrade to an "AI-native" athenaOne platform. This summer, the company rolled out more than 80 new AI features for RCM operations on its AI-native athenaOne platform.

Athenahealth executives describe the launch of athenaPatient MCP and the connection to Claude as just the first step, suggesting a broader strategy of allowing patients to use AI tools with their health records.

"The immediate focus is helping patients securely access and understand their health information through the AI assistants they choose to use. Looking further ahead, I think it's reasonable to expect both the number of AI assistants and the capabilities available through them to expand. One of the reasons we're excited about MCP is that it creates a standardized way to provide context to AI systems. Context is what makes AI particularly useful. Without context, AI can provide general information. With context, it can provide a more detailed, personalized set of information and is less likely to lead you astray," Brient said.

Major EHR companies are moving forward with AI integrations to connect patient data with AI tools OpenAI's ChatGPT for Healthcare now integrates with Epic's EHR to enable authorized clinicians to access and summarize patient information from medical records within ChatGPT or directly in supported Epic workflows. That integration can now pull together clinical notes, lab results, medications and specialist documentation, the company said in a blog post.

Oracle’s AI-powered patient portal allows patients to chat directly with their electronic health record using a conversational interface built on OpenAI frontier models.

In healthcare, MCP creates a common framework for connecting AI agents to clinical systems and data.

"I think it's still early, but this is an important trend to watch," Brient said. "One of the challenges with AI is that intelligence without context isn't particularly useful. In healthcare, context must be accurate, permissioned, secure, and current. That's a much harder problem than simply connecting a chat to a data source."

What makes MCP interesting, he noted, is that it provides a framework for connecting AI systems with the context they need while preserving appropriate controls and governance.

"Whether MCP ultimately becomes the interoperability layer for AI in healthcare remains to be seen, but I think the demand for this type of interoperability is only going to increase. Patients and providers are already using AI. The question is whether healthcare data can participate in those experiences safely and effectively," he said, adding, "I feel good about where the industry is headed, and I believe standards like MCP can play an important role in getting us there. But we're still in the early innings, and much work remains. Our goal is straightforward: reduce friction, maintain trust, and help patients and providers benefit from advances in AI without compromising security or control."

#5764. Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

In the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

When writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

In the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

Social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

To encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

An effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt users to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

#5763. ‘Three-parent IVF’ was supposed to prevent mitochondrial disease. Studies are raising doubts

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Megan covers the intersection of science and society. How is biomedical research funded? Who benefits? And how do new technologies reflect and shape our values? You can reach Megan on Signal at mmolteni.13.

The news out of the U.K. last year that eight healthy children had been born to mothers carrying disease-causing mutations in their mitochondria showed the promise of a pioneering reproductive technique known as “three-parent IVF.” The long-anticipated results seemingly showed the procedure, formally called mitochondrial replacement techniques, or MRT, could reduce the risk of babies inheriting sometimes fatal diseases, and raised hopes that other countries, such as the U.S. where MRT is banned, might soon permit it.

But even as regulators and researchers in Australia, the second country to explicitly legalize the specialized technique, prepare to launch their own national experiment with MRT, some scientists and ethicists are rethinking the potential risks and benefits of the technology, which combines genes from a mother and father with mutation-free DNA in the mitochondria of a donor egg. Emerging data from the U.K. as well as several small pilot studies from fertility clinics in other parts of the world are raising questions about whether trying to prevent mitochondrial disease is really the best first use of MRT.

“The general public may have the idea that it is very safe and low risk and that’s just not the case,” said Bert Smeets, a professor in clinical genomics who studies mitochondrial diseases at Maastricht University in the Netherlands.

Until now, pushback against MRT has mainly focused on its expanding use as a treatment for infertility. A STAT investigation published on Monday showed that IVF clinics globally are pitching it to older women desperate to have biologically related children despite scant evidence that it works for them. But some scientists are now saying that carefully run studies addressing severe forms of infertility may present the most ethical way to develop MRT safely.

Smeets serves on the oversight committee that reviews and approves applications for patients to receive MRT at Newcastle University, the only clinic that currently has a license in the U.K. to perform it. Newcastle is where one of the main methods of MRT, known as pronuclear transfer, was first developed in the early 2000s. It involves creating embryos from both the biological mother and the egg donor and then swapping out the nuclear DNA in one for the other.

Data published in 2010 by Newcastle scientists showed that in lab experiments, only a tiny amount of the mother’s mutation-bearing mitochondria — less than 2% — showed up in the reconstructed embryos. The technique looked safe and showed promise in preventing mitochondrial disease, they reported, though not very efficiently (meaning a lot of embryos didn’t survive the process).

Shortly after U.K. regulators began accepting applications from clinics to offer MRT, this picture grew more complicated. Shoukhrat Mitalipov, a developmental biologist at Oregon Health & Science University, had been developing his own method for MRT, called maternal spindle transfer. It involved putting a mother’s genetic material into a donor egg with healthy mitochondria prior to fertilization, when the egg’s chromosomes are lined up in a structure called the spindle.

In 2009, Mitalipov’s lab had reported the births of the world’s first monkeys following maternal spindle transfer. The animals had appeared healthy with no traces of mitochondrial DNA left over from the original eggs. But when his group tried the technique in the lab with human eggs, they noticed something odd.

Despite refining the spindle transfer to the point where his lab could swap up to 99% of defective mitochondria with healthy replacements, analyses run by one of his postdocs showed that the few problematic ones that had managed to cling to the spindle began to take over as the fertilized egg continued to divide. With each subsequent generation of cells, they saw fewer and fewer of the healthy mitochondria — the power plants of cells — and more and more of the mutated ones.

Before Mitalipov’s team fully understood why or how that happened, they rushed out a paper describing this problem, which they dubbed “reversion.” Their data, published in November 2016, suggested that in roughly 15% of cases, reversion could cause MRT to fail, allowing fatal defects to resurface or new health issues to arise. The revelation caused a stir but ultimately did not prevent the U.K. from moving forward with the Newcastle group’s plan to use pronuclear transfer. The group won a license for the work in 2017.

Mitalipov, stymied from pursuing his own clinical trial of spindle transfer in the U.S. by a 2015 congressional ban, began evaluating the technology as a potential fertility treatment. He and his collaborator Nuno Costa-Borges of the Spanish company Embryotools wanted to test the idea that young mitochondria might be able to help overcome poor egg quality — one of the reasons IVF fails. They recruited 25 women under 40 years old who’d had multiple IVF failures to a small study conducted in Greece. The results, published in 2023, showed that spindle transfer could produce pregnancies. But it also showed that reversion wasn’t just theoretical; it happened in the IVF clinic too. Two of the seven children born carried a mix of mitochondria from the biological mother — as high as 51% in one child and 35% in another — and the donor.

Two groups have now found that reversion can happen with pronuclear transfer, too.

When the Newcastle University team published papers last year about the births of the eight babies, the researchers noted that although the children showed no signs of disease, they found low levels of reversion, between 5% and 16%, in three of the infants.

A Ukrainian group from the Nadiya Clinic, led by its director Valery Zukin and embryologist Pavlo Mazur, has also found evidence of reversion. Out of six children whose parents allowed testing, two were found to have reversion — one with maternal mitochondrial levels up to 12% and the other with levels as high as 72% — according to unpublished data shared with STAT.

In the case of the Nadiya Clinic, pronuclear transfer was being tested as a fertility treatment, and the mothers’ mitochondria carried no apparent disease-causing mutations, so the finding of reversion is less of a concern, at least in terms of known risks, said Jacques Cohen, a New York-based embryologist who has reviewed the Ukrainian group’s data. But it adds to the growing evidence that even a tiny amount of maternal mitochondria carryover could compromise the efficacy of MRT, which would be a much bigger deal for people trying to avoid passing down mitochondrial diseases to any future children.

“To do it in a family affected by mitochondrial disease is to take a very big risk,” Cohen said. “The field is showing that it’s a bad idea.”

Cohen, who would like to see a moratorium on the use of MRT for preventing mitochondrial disease, is at one extreme of an ethical debate about what to do with this emerging information. He and others think that it’s most prudent to pause studies involving current iterations of the technology until scientists can figure out how to minimize the risks of reversion. That would allow scientists in the U.K. to continue to follow up on the children already born to see if the amount of faulty mitochondria continues to increase over time and to monitor for any resulting health complications.

Guido Pennings, a bioethicist at Ghent University in Belgium, has argued that because of the residual risk of serious disease to the offspring of carriers of mitochondrial mutations, MRT should be developed in carefully controlled trials only for infertile couples. That would enable researchers to sort out the mystery of reversion — insights that could lead to more refined methods of MRT — without exposing unborn children to known risks.

It would also allow scientists to study the unknown risks posed by the mismatch between the donor’s mitochondrial DNA and the mother’s nuclear DNA. (Mitochondrial DNA is typically inherited from the mother.) Some research in mice suggests this phenomenon could lead to immune issues or other unintended health complications. There have also been reports that mice carrying a mix of mitochondrial DNA from two animals had behavioral, cognitive, and other abnormalities.

Most ethicists and scientists who spoke to STAT wouldn’t go as far as Pennings. But there is an increasing recognition that prohibitions of trials of MRT in the context of infertility should be revisited.

In 2024, Esther Braun, of the Institute for Medical Ethics and History of Medicine at Ruhr University in Germany, laid out a case for changing the laws in the U.K. and Australia to allow for clinical trials for treating infertility, highlighting that previous ethical assessments may have underestimated both the risks of MRT for preventing mitochondrial disease and the suffering caused by involuntary childlessness. That shouldn’t be taken as an ethical green light for a burgeoning global MRT tourism industry, she emphasized.

“It seems evident that the routine clinical use of a novel medical procedure is impermissible until clinical trials have established that the procedure is effective,” Braun wrote. “However, this does not imply that conducting such clinical trials is itself impermissible.”

A spokesperson for the U.K.’s fertility regulator — the Human Fertilization and Embryology Authority — told STAT in an email that its scientific committee has considered research exploring the use of MRT for infertility, but that for now, only people who are at very high risk of passing a serious mitochondrial disease onto their children are eligible for this treatment.

Over the past year, a few research teams from around the world have made policy recommendations for how such clinical trials might responsibly proceed. In March, a group led by Smeets in the Netherlands proposed a staged approach to first identify and define types of infertility that MRT might plausibly address, then study its impact in the lab before moving on to small pilots to test its effectiveness only in patients exhibiting those specific infertility conditions. That would allow for the field to more critically evaluate which conditions MRT could safely tackle. The urgency has increased, Smeets said, as MRT is increasingly being adopted by commercial clinics as an all-purpose add-on, despite a lack of clear evidence.

“As a biologist, I always want to know that the intervention I’m doing targets the cause of something you want to solve,” Smeets said. “So this might be relevant to do this for certain subgroups of infertility where changing the mitochondria and the maternal factors in the oocyte is really allowing the embryo to develop. But that’s not the age-related cases.”

An example of what Smeets’ group has proposed is already underway in neighboring Belgium, at Ghent University. For the past few years, Dominic Stoop, a fertility specialist, and Björn Heindryckx, a reproductive geneticist, have been tracking down the molecular culprits behind the most difficult-to-treat infertility cases. They’ve helped define clinical criteria for diagnosing those kinds of cases, commonly grouped together under the term OZEMA — for oocyte/zygote/embryo maturation arrest. In a not-yet-published study spanning tens of thousands of IVF cycles at the Ghent University Hospital’s fertility clinic and a collaborating clinic in the U.S., Boston IVF, they found that OZEMA seems to occur across all ages more or less equally.

Stoop’s team has asked Belgian regulators for approval to study the effect of nuclear transfer technologies in three different patient populations — individuals with a history of mitochondrial disease, OZEMA patients, and women of advanced maternal age. The plan, he told STAT, is to treat seven patients in each group to start. So far, the government has given the green light for the first two, which Stoop hopes to be recruiting for this fall, with the first results out next year.

His team is still generating preclinical data to justify doing it for the advanced maternal age group.

“The patient population where the ethical committee finds the least problems is, in my opinion, the most risky group,” Stoop said, referring to the families with mitochondrial disease. “For the advanced maternal age and the OZEMA patients, it’s different. There may be a risk we don’t know. But if there’s a risk there, it will also be in the mitochondrial disease patients on top of the risk of these abnormal mitochondria. So these patients need very good counseling before doing it.”

Mary Herbert — a former leader of the Newcastle group who relocated to Monash University in Melbourne several years ago — said communicating both known and unknown risks to parents, and monitoring the long-term health of any resulting children, are essential for ethical use of MRT. “We have known for a decade that MRT may not work in all cases,” she told STAT.

Her own preclinical research, in addition to data from the Mitalipov group, suggested that MRT could reduce the risk of mitochondrial disease but could not guarantee prevention. That’s how it should be described to potential patients, not “as a means of preventing” mitochondrial disease, she said.

So far, clinical data from the Newcastle program have shown that MRT resulted in a 75% to 100% reduction in transmission of disease-causing mitochondrial mutations, she said. Even in the cases where reversion was observed, mutated mitochondrial levels were below the 50% threshold where disease symptoms are expected to arise. Herbert’s group at Monash has been training embryologists on MRT and is preparing to ask the Australian government for permission to begin a clinical trial in women carrying mitochondrial mutations. It would include follow-up studies of any carried-over mutated mitochondrial DNA “to ensure that levels remain stable over time and across different organ systems,” Herbert said.

STAT’s coverage of bioethics is supported by a grant from the Greenwall Foundation and the Boston Foundation. Our financial supporters are not involved in any decisions about our journalism.

Megan covers the intersection of science and society. How is biomedical research funded? Who benefits? And how do new technologies reflect and shape our values? You can reach Megan on Signal at mmolteni.13.

#5762. Brigham and Women's nurses set Nov. 12 date for open-ended strike

Brigham and Women's nurses set Nov. 12 date for open-ended strike" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Union nurses at Brigham and Women's Hospital are set to strike in the coming weeks after failed contract negotiations, in what could be the largest open-ended nurse strike in Massachusetts history.

Brigham and Women's Hospital said in a statement it received notice from the Massachusetts Nurses Association (MNA) on Nov. 1 about an open-ended strike beginning Thursday, Nov. 12 at 7 a.m.

"While we had hoped to avoid another strike, we are prepared to continue providing safe, high-quality care throughout any work stoppage, building on our experience and extensive contingency planning," the statement read. "We deeply value and respect our Brigham nurses and remain committed to reaching a fair and responsible agreement. Our latest offer provides market-leading compensation and competitive benefits while recognizing our responsibility to our patients, our entire workforce and the long-term financial sustainability of Brigham and Women’s Hospital."

Negotiations with MNA are set to resume Nov. 9, the hospital said.

MNA said in a statement negotiations will focus on "securing a fair contract that meets the needs of the nurses, their patients and the community members they serve." Nurses are seeking the following terms as part of a fair contract, per the union:

"We are ready to strike but are equally prepared to negotiate a fair contract that protects patient care, respects nurses, and averts the strike," said Kelly Morgan, chair of the union's bargaining committee for the hospital. “Brigham nurses are resolved to fight for as long as it takes for patient safety and the professional respect we deserve.”

Union nurses at Brigham and Women's Hospital voted to reject management's "last, best and final offer" on updated contracts, potentially steering the dispute back toward what could be the largest open-ended nurse strike in Massachusetts history.

The Massachusetts Nurses Association had previously scheduled the strike for Oct. 14, but postponed to give its members a chance to vote on the proposal from Mass General Brigham, the hospital's parent system. The union said it has requested to resume contract negotiations this week, with the hospital responding in its own public statement this it "is prepared to maintain uninterrupted care and respond to any steps the union may take."

MGB's rejected offer would have retained the hospital's existing nursing wage progression system of annual 5% step increases until 20 years tenure, with the addition of two additional 2.5% increases at the top of the prior structure. The union has said it is seeking limits on the use of temporary nurses, more affordable health insurance benefits and “a meaningful cost-of-living wage increase” that includes a differential for nurses floating between units.

“This vote shows the resolve of Brigham nurses, who are fighting for patient safety and for the professional respect we deserve," Kelly Morgan, chair of the union's bargaining committee for the hospital, said in a weekend release. "It’s [time for] MGB to return to the table ready to negotiate in good faith to reach a fair agreement that recognizes the value of Brigham nurses and the expertise they offer for the care of some of the region’s most complex patients every day.”

Brigham and Women's Hospital said it was "disappointed" by the rejection, and that its proposal "reflected the hospital’s commitment to investing in our nurses while supporting long-term sustainability, including meaningful compensation and benefit enhancements that kept Brigham nursing pay among the highest in the market."

Notably, the announcement of the member vote's outcome coincided with news that MGB has begun a new round of layoffs affecting both clinical and operational programs. The unspecified number of cuts reflect a financial need to further adjust operating MGB's structure even after roughly 1,500 people were laid off in 2024, the system said.

Nurses at Brigham and Women’s Hospital have lifted their notice of an Oct. 14 strike after their union and Mass General Brigham management made progress toward a potential contract deal late Saturday night, the sides said in statements.

The 4,000-member open-ended strike would be the largest in state history if launched, and follows months of contract negotiations between the health system and the Massachusetts Nurses Association (see that coverage below).

A formal deal has yet to be struck, though the union said it agreed to call off its 10-day strike notice "given the complexity of the agreement and the impact of a potential strike on our nurses and the community." The proposal is being presented to members for a vote, which might yield a new 10-day notice if rejected.

Brigham and Women's Hospital, in a Sunday statement, said its "last, best and final offer ... reflects significant movement on several of the union's priorities while maintaining a responsible approach to supporting nurses, patients and the long-term strength of the hospital."

It added that the offer retains the hospital's existing nursing wage progression system of annual 5% step increases until 20 years tenure, with the addition of two additional 2.5% increases at the top of the prior structure. The withdrawn notice also saved the hospital from having to implement its contingency staffing plan of hiring temporary nurses.

"We are thankful the MNA has pulled its indefinite strike notice and will allow its members to vote on the hospital's final offer," the hospital said. The union's statement did not specify the timing of that vote.

Editor's note: On Oct. 2, the Massachusetts Nurses Association announced an Oct. 14, 7:00 a.m. start time for their strike if no deal is reached.

Nurses at Brigham and Women’s Hospital have voted to authorize an open-ended, 4,000-member strike that could become the largest nurses’ strike in Massachusetts history.

The Massachusetts Nurses Association announced the 93% in favor vote that was held Thursday evening. No date has been set yet by the union, which is legally required to give employer Mass General Brigham (MGB) 10 days' notice.

“Brigham nurses have made clear that we are prepared to stay on strike for as long as it takes to win a contract that protects our patients and respects the nurses who care for them,” Kelly Morgan, a labor and delivery nurse and chair of the Brigham and Women’s Hospital MNA Bargaining Committee, said in the union’s announcement. “An open-ended strike is a serious step that will undoubtedly create a healthcare crisis in Massachusetts. MGB can prevent the strike by returning to the table and negotiating the contract our nurses need to keep providing world-class care.”

Contract negotiations between the sides have been ongoing since last November, with the prior agreement expiring on March 31. In July, the nurses (plus an additional 450 home care clinicians) conducted a one-day awareness strike that was also a record breaker for the state and the first at Brigham and Women’s, a flagship hospital and founding member of the nonprofit system.

Demonstrations have continued in the weeks since, including a rally held earlier this week outside of an MGB-hosted World Medical Innovation Forum, where bargaining members painted a contrast between executives’ conversations with investors on AI and the demands of their clinical workforce.

The hospital, in statements given to press, said “we remain committed to bargaining in good faith and have put forward a fair and responsible proposal that maintains Brigham nurses’ market-leading compensation, preserves meaningful wage growth and competitive benefits, and balances those investments with the long-term financial sustainability of our system,” the hospital said in a statement given to press.

The hospital has previously said it has found agreements with the union on several issues. However, the union has previously said that talks stalled in mid-August and reiterated Thursday that it still is seeking limits on the use of temporary nurses, more affordable health insurance benefits and “a meaningful cost-of-living wage increase” that includes a differential for nurses floating between units.

MGB is the largest private employer in Massachusetts with roughly 85,000 workers and $22.8 billion in annual revenue, making it among the country’s largest nonprofit health systems. Financial results released last month outlined a $15 million operating income (0.1% operating margin) across nine months of its ongoing fiscal year, up from a $44 million operating loss (-0.3% operating margin), though its nine-month bottom line including nonoperating gains like investment returns was $1.9 billion. Early last year saw the organization undertake the largest layoffs in its history, when it cut about 1,500 workers.

The union has pointed to MGB’s bottom line (nearly $2.4 billion across fiscal 2025), substantial total assets ($35.8 billion) and the compensation of executives (almost $9.2 million for CEO Anne Klibanski, M.D.) in its calls for stronger contracts.

#5761. Opinion: How meditation helped me become a better doctor overnight

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Kinast is an ophthalmologist at Legacy Devers Eye Institute, a clinical scientist at Legacy Research Institute, and a clinical professor at OHSU Casey Eye Institute.

Last fall I attended a meditation retreat in the Santa Cruz Mountains. I had hoped for a respite from a busy ophthalmology practice in Portland, Ore. Instead, I returned to the most difficult challenges I have faced in practice.

One night, we were asked to remain awake in meditation through dawn. The teachers explained that this “all-nighter” would be quite different from those in our past, such as late nights studying in college or socializing with friends.

For me, however, the term “all-nighter” did not evoke memories from a library or party. Instead, I recollected the most devastating injuries I have ever witnessed as an ophthalmologist: a patient who survived an execution-style gunshot and required brain surgery and an enucleation; a serene woman waiting in her car near a street festival, struck by stray gang violence; and eyes ruptured by knives, fireworks, bungee cords, windshields, beer bottles, sticks, rocks, and fish hooks. Many of them “just minding my own business.” Each story life-changing and traumatizing.

Ophthalmologists are called in — often in the middle of the night — to help these individuals. With limited hope for preserving sight, we try to reconstruct their ruptured globes. An all-nighter in this context requires moving efficiently, precise care, and endurance. We must provide the best surgical care possible to help these wounded souls while leading an equally exhausted operating-room team, everyone aware of the day’s work still ahead.

Staying up all night in the meditation hall, I realized that I had never fully digested the trauma of these devastating injuries. I had never taken the time and space to sit with the losses — the eyes, the lives, the damage.

As dawn approached, an anticipatory excitement filled the hall and most joined in a rejoiceful meditative chant. I sat in the back of the hall and grieved.

Mourning into the morning led to a tremendous gratitude and respect for physicians who treat trauma, including my fellow ophthalmologists and myself. Patients may think of ophthalmologists as doctors who perform friendly examinations with “Star Trek”-like equipment and brief surgeries to help with sight, and that is true. We also perform vital work alongside emergency physicians and trauma surgeons, managing injuries so severe they can be difficult to even witness. In these worst moments, times of dire need, we come in and help. Sometimes, we stay up all night.

These “all-nighters” are a service of the heart that benefit our fellow human beings, even when our lionhearts are too closed to grieve in the moment. Across medicine, physicians need support to carry the profound emotional burdens of helping patients and families through tragedy. What feels like a weight of helplessness and sorrow on our shoulders may, with enough space, also reflect our remarkable capacities for strength, steadfastness, and compassion.

That night taught me how the inner work of meditation and self-inquiry can support the outer work of patient care. The stoic rigidity that held back my tears and helped me appear strong had also kept patients, and their distress, at a distance. Within that rigidity lay a fear of becoming overwhelmed by patients’ suffering and then unsettled just before operating. With a tonic of awareness, space, and time, the physical tension and fear released. In its place emerged a true strength: to be open to another’s suffering, present with their experience. Without a rigid barrier, I can better attune to my patients whether they are facing trauma, the loss of a loved one, or simply a bad day.

Since the retreat, I have tried to be more present with my patients in clinic. Each time I enter an examination room and sit on my swivel chair, I ritualistically sense my feet on the ground as a reminder to be mindful. Meditation is often described as a returning to the present moment after each successive drift. The returning itself is the practice. Each patient now offers an opportunity for both clinical and meditative practice. Forget my feet and then remember them; become overwhelmed by long wait times, then ground myself; slip into autopilot, then return. Clinic itself becomes a meditation. Returning again and again helps keep the heart open.

Trauma call remains my least favorite part of medicine and often the most meaningful. I see traumatic eye injuries only a few times each year; many physicians in other fields treat this type of suffering daily. Thank you to the trauma physicians and surgeons who care for unimaginable injuries, each a devastating story. May we mourn with open hearts the tragedies that find their way into our hands.

Robert M. Kinast, M.D., is an ophthalmologist at Legacy Devers Eye Institute, a clinical scientist at Legacy Research Institute, and a clinical professor at OHSU Casey Eye Institute in Portland, Oregon. He invented the GentleDrop eye drop guide and the CleverDrop eye drop monitor.

#5760. UnitedHealthcare eliminates prior authorization requirements on 2K pediatric services

UnitedHealthcare eliminates prior authorization requirements on 2K pediatric services" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

UnitedHealthcare will eliminate the need for prior authorization on more than 2,000 codes for pediatric services beginning on Dec. 1, the company announced Monday.

Earlier this year, the insurance giant said it would ease prior auth requirements on an array of pediatric care, and now it's detailing the codes that will fall under that initiative. Services range from diagnostic imaging to cancer treatment to orthopedic care and more.

Examples include sleep studies, MRI scans, joint procedures, ear and tonsil procedures and some chemotherapy services, UHC said in an announcement.

The company said that it "chose to fast-track services that are widely considered in the medical community to be safe and effective," per the release. The changes will reduce prior authorization volume in pediatrics by nearly two-thirds, and apply across commercial, individual market and community plans where eligible under state law.

The changes aren't limited to services provided at pediatric facilities, UnitedHealthcare said.

“Every child deserves a health care experience centered on their needs,” said Tim Noel, CEO of UnitedHealthcare, in the announcement. “These changes will help make that experience simpler for children, their families and the physicians who care for them.”

UnitedHealthcare is among the insurers nationwide that signed on to a pledge in the summer of 2025 to ease the administrative burdens associated with prior authorization and embrace electronic submissions and decisions. Since then, the insurer has taken multiple steps to reduce the requirements on prior auth.

On Oct. 1, the company eliminated prior authorization on 1,700 services across its insurance lines. In May, UHC said it was aiming to eliminate 30% of prior auth requirements by the end of the year.

UnitedHealthcare is set to eliminate close to two-thirds of pediatric prior authorization requirements by the end of the year.

The insurance giant announced Friday morning that it will nix prior auth on an array of diagnostic tests, routine surgeries and specialty services, including cardiology, neurology, pulmonology and orthopedics.

UnitedHealth also said it will offer authorization waivers for certain procedures when they're performed at leading pediatric hospitals as a reflection of their "consistent use of well-established care practices." The insurer said that the facilities in this program represent a broad national network across medical and surgical specialties.

“Parents should be able to spend less time having to navigate the health system and more time focusing on their children as they get the care they need,” said Tim Noel, CEO of UnitedHealthcare, in the announcement.

“These changes are part of our broader efforts to simplify healthcare and allow families—and their doctors and nurses—to pursue routine care with far fewer administrative steps, while higher-risk procedures continue to undergo reviews," Noel added.

The company is undertaking a broad review of all pediatric prior authorizations to determine which can be rolled back while maintaining safety and quality. It said it plans to eliminate pre-approvals for some diagnostic imaging, sleep studies, routine outpatient tests and some surgical services and therapies that are approved consistently.

UnitedHealthcare said prior authorization will remain in place for services with high clinical complexity or variability, such as experimental treatments, or where it is required by regulations.

The company said the changes will take effect across its commercial and Medicaid plans.

The move is the latest from the company as it aims to reduce prior authorization requirements. For example, last month, UnitedHealth said it would exempt rural providers from most prior auth requirements.

The company has also made a push to reduce a wide swath of reauthorizations at its pharmacy benefit manager, Optum Rx.

#5759. Opinion: What the 2024 electoral map reveals about America’s mortality divide

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

By Brandon Yan, Maddie Feldmeier, and Renee Y. Hsia

Yan is a physician and public health researcher affiliated with the University of California San Francisco Philip R. Lee Institute for Health Policy Studies. Feldmeier is a medical student at the UCSF School of Medicine. Hsia is professor and vice chair of health services research of the UCSF Department of Emergency Medicine.

In this 2026 midterm election season, health care ranks third on voters’ minds. That’s no surprise: U.S. life expectancy persistently lags those in comparable countries despite substantially greater spending on health care. As health and health care become increasingly political, we asked whether the leading drivers of mortality looked different by political geography in the United States.

In 2024, the mortality rate, adjusted for differences in age composition, was 19.2% higher in states that voted for Donald Trump than in states that voted for Kamala Harris. As the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) agenda continues to shape U.S. health policy, the causes for these differences deserve close attention.

The political mortality divide in the U.S. is a relatively new phenomenon. In 2001, mortality rates adjusted for age were just 2% higher in counties where the plurality voted for a Republican presidential candidate versus a Democratic candidate.

By 2019, that relative difference had widened to 16.1%. The widening gap followed slower declines in mortality rates in Republican versus Democratic plurality counties (-11.1% versus -21.9% from 2001 to 2019, respectively).

To better understand this divergence and its more recent evolution, we compared publicly available mortality rates (measured in deaths per 100,000 people in the population and adjusted for age) between states that by plurality voted for Trump and those that voted for Harris in the 2024 presidential election over the period 2016 to 2024.

Stark differences in mortality rates between states that went for Trump and those that went for Harris have persisted and widened. When Trump won his first presidential election in 2016, mortality from all causes was 17% higher (776 versus 664 per 100,000) in the states that eventually went for him in 2024 compared with those that went for Harris. By 2024, that difference had widened to 19.2% (774 versus 649 deaths per 100,000).

This reality in 2024 reflects modest improvement from when the gap was even wider in 2021, largely because of. Covid-19. Covid-19 mortality peaked in 2020 at 86 per 100,000 people for states that went for Harris, while Covid-19 mortality in states that went for Trump continued climbing to 122 per 100,000 in 2021.

Yet Covid-19 played just one part in a more widespread phenomenon. We also examined deaths from the leading causes in the U.S.: heart disease and cancer. Whereas heart disease mortality decreased 9.1% in states that went for Harris from 2016 to 2024, it decreased only 2.9% in states that went for Trump.

Similarly, cancer mortality decreased 12.9% in states that went for Harris but only 9.1% in states that went for Trump. The persistence of these differences beyond the pandemic points to chronic disease, not Covid-19 alone, as a key component of the political mortality divide.

Drug overdose mortality tells a different story. In 2016, drug overdose mortality was 18% (or 3.4 per 100,000) higher in states that went for Trump; in 2024, it was estimated to be 2% (0.4 per 100,000) higher in states that went for Harris. Beginning in 2023, estimated drug overdose mortality rates in states that went for Trump fell below those in states that went for Harris, following an earlier peak in 2021 for Trump states (35 per 100,000) compared with 2022 for Harris states (32.5 per 100,000).

In the nine years leading up to the second Trump administration, trends in mortality portray two increasingly disparate mortal Americas — one with persistently higher mortality from heart disease and cancer independent of higher Covid-19 mortality burden and another with a widening lead in overall mortality but slower to bend the curve in drug overdose deaths.

Politics play an influential role in health policy and access to health care likely play a part. Medicaid expansion under the Affordable Care Act has been associated with lower mortality, yet 10 states have not adopted expansion. All 10 of these states went for Trump in 2024.

Coverage losses have also been greater in non-expansion states during Medicaid unwinding, and policy changes related to Medicaid work requirements and reverification could further affect continuity of coverage.

Beyond insurance coverage, access to care is increasingly challenging in rural communities, which have historically voted Republican, with disproportionate hospital closures as just one example.

Policy responses to health events can shape mortality. Differences in political priorities could explain some of the higher Covid-19 mortality rates in states that went for Trump, recognizing that policies meant to save lives also bring collateral effects.

With the drug overdose epidemic, mortality rates from drug overdose between states that went for Trump over Harris have converged. An epidemic once thought to predominantly affect distressed rural and de-industrializing communities has spread to and persisted in coastal and urban communities, where political debates continue regarding harm reduction policies versus enforcement.

Beyond health care policy, social factors shape the environment in which health is determined. Education — a predictor of health risk factors including smoking, obesity, cardiovascular risk, and preventive screening rates — has become increasingly aligned with political geography. Differences in economic opportunity, access to necessities such as healthy food and internet access, and exposure to media and popular culture can also shape health behaviors, with downstream effects on mortality.

Finally, differences in mortality from Covid-19 raise concern about an increasingly troubling phenomenon: the stark polarization of trust in health care and public health institutions across political lines. Marked differences in vaccination rates between states that went for Trump and those that went for Harris serve as a salient marker of its health effects.

“Making America healthy again” requires confronting the realities of disproportionate chronic disease-related mortality in states that went for Trump, an evolving opioid epidemic with shifting burden toward states that went for Harris, and communities vulnerable to novel infectious disease along with growing mistrust in science.

Addressing these challenges will entail sustained investment in the conditions that shape health, such as expanding access to affordable health care, closing educational gaps, strengthening rural and behavioral health infrastructure, and rebuilding trust in public health.

Policymakers ought not treat “red” and “blue” states as fixed categories of health risk but instead tackle the drivers of preventable deaths across these diverse communities. Doing so involves communities and their elected leaders bringing lived and technical expertise together to find solutions rooted in truth, evidence, and a shared conviction that while death may be more certain than taxes, disparities in when and why Americans die are not.

Brandon Yan, M.D., M.P.H., is a physician and public health researcher affiliated with the University of California San Francisco Philip R. Lee Institute for Health Policy Studies. Maddie Feldmeier, B.S., is a medical student at the UCSF School of Medicine. Renee Y. Hsia, M.D., M.Sc., is professor and vice chair of health services research of the UCSF Department of Emergency Medicine. She is also a core faculty member of the Philip R. Lee Institute for Health Policy Studies.

#5758. Zocdoc opens infrastructure to AI agents, launches partnership with Instinct

Zocdoc opens infrastructure to AI agents, launches partnership with Instinct" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

As more patients turn to artificial intelligence agents to manage their healthcare, Zocdoc is opening its healthcare access infrastructure to streamline the process.

Beginning Oct. 28, agents can connect patients to care through a variety of channels—including MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers, deep links and more.

Zocdoc Chief Strategy Officer Alex Doyne told Fierce Healthcare that AI agents are “becoming a new starting point for patients seeking healthcare.”

Doyne said traffic from AI agents on the platform has “at least doubled roughly every three weeks since July.”

“AI agents can help patients navigate their healthcare options and take action on their behalf, but they're only as reliable as the information and systems they can access,” Doyne said. “By connecting agents to Zocdoc's infrastructure, we can ensure they are booking the right appointments for patients.”

Zocdoc has over 175 scheduling integrations, with more than 10,000 insurance plans and 200,000 verified providers in its network, according to Doyne.

“Opening that infrastructure to agents means they now have access to a reliable booking experience,” Doyne said.

Doyne added that healthcare is “particularly challenging,” for AI agents since “so much of the information available online is fragmented, outdated, or inaccurate,” which can have “real consequences for patients who may already be struggling to access care.”

“That's why it's critical that agents have access to reliable provider and insurance information, accurate availability and infrastructure that ensures the booking is integrated with a provider’s calendar and will hold on the day,” Doyne said.

“We've established a two-way promise that sets clear expectations for Zocdoc and the agents connecting to our infrastructure,” Doyne said. “Zocdoc commits to welcoming agents that register and identify themselves, while agents are expected to obtain explicit patient consent before booking appointments and protect patient and provider data.”

The company also announced a partnership with AI personal assistant Instinct to let agents use Zocdoc’s healthcare access infrastructure to find vetted providers, verify insurance benefits and book appointments.

“Instinct is built to genuinely improve your life and handle important everyday tasks,” said Ben Schwerin, Instinct chief business officer, in a statement. “Since healthcare is more complicated than ordering groceries or booking travel, the stakes are higher. By partnering with Zocdoc, Instinct can navigate that complexity—so getting an appointment can be as simple as sending a text.”

Instinct will join Zocdoc’s growing Care Access Network, which also includes Google Gemini, Amazon Health AI, Yelp, Healthgrades and more.

Last month, Zocdoc acquired Sohar Health in its push to evolve beyond an appointment-booking marketplace into broader healthcare access infrastructure.

Sohar Health helps healthcare organizations simplify insurance workflows, and its APIs automate insurance discovery, eligibility and benefits verification, network status checks and cost estimates.

It marked the company's first acquisition in its nearly 20-year history, executives said.

The injectable drug, lenacapavir, offers virtually complete protection against the virus with one administration every six months. More than a year after approving the brand name version, sold by Gilead Sciences, the agency gave tentative approval to Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories to make a generic version.

The move comes two years after Gilead reached licensing deals with six generic drugmakers, including Dr. Reddy’s, to produce and distribute a lower-cost version to 120 mostly low- and middle-income countries. #5756. Your blood could reveal inflammatory bowel disease 10 years before diagnosis

Scientists have identified hidden changes in the immune system that can appear up to 10 years before a person is diagnosed with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The findings, presented at UEG Week 2026, suggest that certain antibody patterns in the blood could eventually help doctors identify people at risk of developing the condition and even predict how severe their disease might become.

Inflammatory bowel disease refers to a group of long-term disorders, including Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), that cause persistent inflammation in the digestive tract. These conditions develop when the immune system responds abnormally, contributing to inflammation and damage in the intestines.

Scientists increasingly believe that IBD begins developing years before it is officially diagnosed. However, the immune system changes that take place during this early, largely hidden period have remained poorly understood.

Tracking Immune Changes a Decade Before Diagnosis

To investigate what happens before IBD is diagnosed, researchers examined 2,000 blood serum samples collected from 500 people. The participants included 200 who eventually developed Crohn's disease, 200 who developed ulcerative colitis, and 100 healthy individuals of comparable age and sex.

Blood samples were available from the time of diagnosis and from approximately two, four, and 10 years earlier. This allowed the researchers to look backward through a decade of immune activity and identify changes that emerged before the diseases were recognized.

The team analyzed antibody reactions to approximately 357,000 antigens associated with bacteria, viruses, food, and the immune system itself. Antigens are substances that the immune system can recognize and respond to, while antibodies are proteins produced by the immune system that help identify specific targets.

Across all 2,000 samples, the researchers detected 123,980 unique antibodies.

A striking pattern emerged. People who later developed Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis had significantly less antibody diversity than healthy participants, meaning their immune systems showed a narrower range of antibody responses. Distinctive changes could be detected in both diseases as far back as 10 years before diagnosis.

Different Blood Signals Reveal Crohn's Disease and Ulcerative Colitis

The researchers also found that Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis were associated with different immune signatures.

Among people who later developed Crohn's disease, antibody responses to herpesviruses and bacterial flagellin were elevated. Flagellin is a protein that forms part of the tail-like structures some bacteria use to move.

These elevated responses were especially noticeable in individuals who eventually developed complicated Crohn's disease or disease affecting the ileum, the final section of the small intestine.

At the same time, antibody responses to encapsulated bacteria gradually decreased as diagnosis approached. These bacteria are surrounded by protective outer coatings that can help them evade immune defenses.

People who later developed ulcerative colitis showed a somewhat different pattern. Their antibody responses to herpesviruses and autoantigens increased, while responses to encapsulated pathogens declined. Autoantigens are components of the body's own tissues that can mistakenly become targets of an immune response.

Together, these findings suggest that the immune system undergoes measurable changes many years before inflammatory bowel disease is diagnosed.

AI Identifies Hidden Disease Risk Years in Advance

The researchers then used machine learning, a form of artificial intelligence that identifies patterns in complex data, to determine whether these antibody signatures could distinguish people who would eventually develop IBD from healthy individuals.

Using blood antibody patterns from up to 10 years before diagnosis, the models distinguished future Crohn's disease cases from healthy controls with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.90. For ulcerative colitis, the corresponding value was 0.84.

AUC is a measure of how well a model distinguishes between two groups. A score of 0.5 indicates performance equivalent to chance, while 1.0 represents perfect discrimination.

The researchers also discovered that antibody patterns could help distinguish people who would develop complicated Crohn's disease from those whose disease would remain less complicated. This distinction was possible approximately 10 years before diagnosis, with an AUC of 0.85.

These findings raise the possibility that blood antibody testing could eventually help identify not only who is at increased risk of IBD, but also which patients may need more intensive treatment.

Commenting on the findings, lead author Dr. Arno Bourgonje said: "It is fascinating to see that complicated CD at diagnosis is associated with a distinct antibody profile years before the first clinical symptoms and is not simply the consequence of disease progression after diagnosis. Finding these patterns so early points to the potential of antibody profiling to support earlier risk detection, distinguish between disease subtypes and help identify patients who may benefit from more intensive therapy as early as possible."

Could a Blood Test Detect Gut Disease 10 Years Early?

Although the results offer compelling evidence that IBD has a detectable early immune signature, the researchers emphasize that the findings are not yet ready for use in routine medical screening.

The study establishes an important proof of principle, but additional research is necessary to determine whether these antibody patterns can reliably predict disease in broader populations.

Researchers must also establish whether antibody testing provides meaningful benefits beyond existing genetic information, clinical assessments, and other blood-based measurements. Any potential screening test would need to be accurate, affordable, reproducible, and ultimately shown to improve patient outcomes.

"The next priority is to validate these signatures in independent, more diverse and prospectively followed populations," concluded Dr. Bourgonje. "We also need to determine their added value alongside genetic, clinical and other blood-based markers, translate the findings into a reproducible and affordable targeted assay and, ultimately, demonstrate that using such a test actually leads to better clinical outcomes."

If future studies confirm these results, blood-based immune profiling could offer doctors a new way to recognize inflammatory bowel disease risk years before diagnosis, distinguish between disease subtypes, and identify patients who might benefit from earlier intervention.

#5755. Miami Cash4Keys Execs Accused of Stealing Vulnerable Senior’s Home in Brazen Scheme

A Florida man's $300,000 home was allegedly stolen in a real estate scheme dubbed “Operation Dirty Deed,” which investigators say involved fraudulent documents and the exploitation of the homeowner's dementia.

The case took a disturbing turn when the 71-year-old man, identified in court records as Thomas P. Hegarty, was allegedly kidnapped from his longtime Hollywood home and discarded at a "dilapidated rooming house" several miles away, according to the Broward County Property Appraiser's Office.

Now, two executives for Cash4Keys, a South Florida real estate investment company, each face six criminal charges in connection with the alleged plot. A notary and real estate agent also face charges in connection with the alleged scheme.

“His home was taken from him,” Hollywood Police Department Detective Theo Defreze said at a news conference last week. “He lost all of his possessions―belongings, cars. I mean, he lost everything."

Investigators allege that Brandon Lee Miguel and Jordy Luis Perez obtained Hegarty's signature on a power of attorney document and a warranty deed, which were then used to transfer ownership of the property to their company, Cash4Keys.

Monica Elizabeth Castelli, 56, a real estate agent with United Realty Group, is accused of kidnapping Hegarty, while Derek Enrique, 43, allegedly notarized the documents used in the transfer.

Hegarty’s property on Mayo Street was valued at approximately $300,000 but was allegedly transferred to the company for just $191,000.

Broward County property appraiser Marty Kiar said at the news conference that there is no evidence Hegarty received any of the money and that the suspects used the man's severe case of dementia to take advantage of him and take over his home.

The investigation was launched after Hegarty's family raised concerns about his declining health and became suspicious about the recent transfer of his home.

His sister-in-law, Peggy Hegarty, who was contacted by the rooming house where he had allegedly been taken, told CBS News that he believed he was signing paperwork to refinance his home, not sell it.

“It's shocking. Absolutely shocking," she said.

When she traveled from her home in Georgia to Florida after learning what had happened, she found Hegarty depressed, in shock, and not eating, according to the report. He is now living in an assisted-living facility in Jacksonville.

“Investigators allege that due to documented dementia and significant cognitive impairment, the victim was incapable of understanding the documents he was signing and appreciating their consequences,” the Broward County Property Appraiser's Office said in the news release.

After the alleged transfer, Miguel and Perez arranged for Castelli, of Margate, to remove Hegarty from his home, authorities said.

Castelli allegedly drove Hegarty to a “dilapidated rooming house” in Miami Gardens and left him there, according to investigators. Hegarty was distraught and crying, which then led to Castelli driving him to Memorial Regional Hospital in Hollywood.

Once Hegarty was gone from his house, Miguel and Perez allegedly went inside and removed his personal belongings, including three vehicles, according to the property appraiser's office.

Miguel and Perez each face six charges, including organized scheme to defraud $50,000 or more, grand theft exceeding $100,000, unlawful filing of false documents affecting real property, mortgage fraud, exploitation of an elderly person, and money laundering.

Castelli faces charges of kidnapping with intent to facilitate the commission of a felony and exploitation of an elderly person. Enrique faces one count of false or fraudulent acknowledgments.

Kiar said Cash4Keys still controls the property, but added that Hegarty's family has hired an attorney in an effort to get the home back.

Investigators believe the scheme could extend beyond Hegarty’s home, suspecting there may be additional victims and properties involved.

Realtor.com reached out to Cash4Keys South Florida for comment but did not receive an immediate response.

The case has also prompted warnings from local officials about the vulnerability of older homeowners to real estate fraud.

Kiar urged South Florida residents with elderly relatives to monitor their family members' finances and consider enrolling in the free Owner Alert program, which notifies property owners when a deed transaction occurs.

“It’s very upsetting, very sad, and what really bothers me is the person they picked on was about as vulnerable as they come and that really is what makes this case a case that’s very sad,” Kiar said. “I’m very glad that people have been arrested, and they will have their day in court.”

#5754. Child dies of measles in New York’s first such death in 30 years

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

LOWVILLE, N.Y. — A child in rural northern New York has died after contracting measles, marking the state’s first death from the disease in 30 years, state officials announced Monday.

The child died in Lewis County, about 93 miles (150 kilometers) north of Syracuse, Gov. Kathy Hochul said.

The U.S. stopped the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks of the viral disease.

Hochul, a Democrat, said the child’s death is “a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses.”

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed three measles-associated deaths in the U.S. this year, but state health departments have reported higher numbers. Pennsylvania health officials have reported five deaths this year and are investigating a possible sixth.

Hochul declared a disaster emergency in early October because of measles cases in neighboring states and in rural areas of New York. The executive order extended the pool of people who can administer measles vaccines to include paramedics, midwives and others, and it allowed nurses to join doctors in ordering testing.

#5753. FTC issues warning letters over deceptive marketing as ACA enrollment opens

FTC issues warning letters over deceptive marketing as ACA enrollment opens" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Open enrollment season is getting underway, and the Federal Trade Commission sent warning letters to 25 companies that conduct marketing or generate sales leads for insurers.

The commission said in an announcement that the letters aim to put these companies on notice about deceptive or unfair marketing tactics that are likely unlawful. Activities in question include misrepresenting the benefits or limitations of a plan, or portraying a plan as comprehensive when it isn't.

In addition, FTC also warned against misrepresenting any costs associated with a plan or falsely telling consumers that a plan offers free rewards, cash offers or other incentives.

"Making healthcare more transparent and affordable is a top priority for the FTC," said Christopher Mufarrige, Director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, in the announcement.

"Americans experiencing rising healthcare costs should not also have to worry about whether a healthcare plan or program is what it claims to be," Mufarrige continued. "The FTC will remain focused on monitoring this market and will not hesitate to hold accountable companies that unlawfully market or advertise healthcare plans to consumers."

The FTC letters were largely sent to firms that market plans on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges, where open enrollment opened on Sunday, Nov. 1. Medicare is also in its annual enrollment period, which continues through Dec. 7, and late fall is when most employers begin plan selections for workers.

The agency does not allege wrongdoing in the warning letters, but instead suggests that the companies "conduct a thorough review of their advertisements to ensure they are complying with applicable laws and rules."

The letters include examples of previous enforcement actions against marketers in the ACA space, such as Innovative Partners and Top Healthcare Options Insurance Agency.

In the letters, the agency emphasizes that its staff will be closely watching for potential violations.

"FTC staff will continue to actively monitor this market for potentially deceptive or unfair acts or practices and will take enforcement action as warranted," the FTC wrote in the letter (PDF).
