#5731. Measles update: New York reports first measles-associated death; US nears 5,000 confirmed cases

Measles update: New York reports first measles-associated death; US nears 5,000 confirmed cases" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The New York State Department of Health on Monday afternoon reported its first measles-associated death in 30 years.

The state has counted 210 total cases this year as of Nov. 3. The reported death was a child in the northern Lewis County, according to the department. No information was given about the child's specific illness or the role measles infection may have played in their death.

Sixteen confirmed cases of measles have been reported in Lewis County as of Tuesday, the department said. Many of New York's cases are located among upstate counties, and just eight are in New York City, according to the department.

In a statement, New York Governor Kathy Hochul—who on Oct. 5 declared a Disaster Emergency in response to rising measles case rates—expressed her sympathies to the child's family and told residents that "vaccination remains our best protection against this dangerous disease."

"This is New York’s first measles-related death in 30 years, a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses," the statement reads, echoing criticisms of federal health leadership voiced by Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro regarding measles-associated deaths in his own state.

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone said they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a new standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles."

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, in a statement to Fierce Healthcare, said it had deployed its epidemiologists and other experts to New York after receiving a formal request for support. The support is currently scheduled to run through Nov. 13, and includes on-the-ground "surveillance, data analysis, strategic planning and other outbreak response support," they said.

Of the roughly $100 million of additional measles and vaccine-preventable diseases funding the department said it has provided via the CDC since August, nearly $2.4 million has gone directly to New York State and $2.1 million to New York City, they said.

"Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles," they added.

The U.S. is in the midst of its worst measles outbreak in decades, with more than 4,000 cases reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as of early October and a sixth measles-associated death disclosed by local Pennsylvania officials on Monday.

The vaccine-preventable disease was declared eliminated in the U.S. back in 2000—meaning that there was no endemic spread of the disease—but has resurfaced in force during recent years as declining childhood vaccination rates have pushed most states below the 95% coverage bar for school-age herd immunity.

The CDC had counted 2,289 cases across the entirety of 2025, which had been the country’s highest total since 1990, and several public health officials have warned for months that number would likely be surpassed based on the scale and frequency of early-year cases.

Measles-associated deaths have also accompanied the higher case counts, though just how many is a subject of dispute. While three deaths were confirmed in all of 2025, this year logged its first in late August with Pennsylvania, which hosts more than a quarter of the total cases, now reporting six measles-associated deaths as of Oct. 13. The CDC, however, lists two deaths alongside a note that its count is subject to change, and has promised more broadly to develop a new, standardized case definition to be used across all reporting states.

That discrepancy is an example of friction between federal health leadership and the broader public health community that experts say has contributed to this year’s outbreaks.

Pennsylvania’s initial death announcements in August were contested by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who accused Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro of withholding sufficient information for the CDC to confirm the deaths and using his press conference announcing them as “gaslighting the public” for political purposes.

During an ensuing social media feud, the governor and the secretary described a heated phone call in which Shapiro (at the time) rejected federal assistance and accused Kennedy of fueling the outbreaks with only lukewarm endorsement of the MMR vaccine and a broader concurrent campaign to scale back other routine childhood vaccinations.

Numerous state public health officials and experts have lobbed similar criticisms of Kennedy, who is affiliated with anti-vaccine groups, and federal health agencies under his purview.

The CDC, for its part, has reportedly infused at least $100 million of extra public health funding to states for immunization programs and surveillance, and leading officials including Kennedy and new CDC Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., have described the MMR vaccine as safe and effective when asked directly. Still, the agency has not launched the type of broader vaccine messaging and awareness campaigns that it would have in years past, critics are quick to note.

Pennsylvania isn’t alone in raising alarms over rising measles cases. New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in early October, the first such declaration in recent years.

#5729. The surprisingly simple exercise that could lower your blood pressure

New research suggests that exercising just once or twice a week may be enough to maintain some of the blood pressure benefits gained from regular physical activity, at least over a short period. However, people who continue exercising three times weekly may experience larger and more sustained improvements.

The findings, published in BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine, suggest that even a single weekly session of isometric exercise could help people preserve improvements in blood pressure when they cannot commit to a more frequent workout schedule.

Isometric exercise involves tightening muscles while holding the body in a fixed position for several minutes. Common examples include wall squats, planks, and handgrip exercises.

Earlier research has found that isometric training can lower blood pressure more effectively than other types of exercise, sometimes producing reductions comparable to or greater than those achieved with certain medications. However, researchers have not fully understood how often these exercises need to be performed to maintain their cardiovascular benefits.

To investigate, researchers enrolled 100 adults whose average age was 37.4 years. Participants had systolic blood pressure ranging from normal to high-normal levels (120-140 mmHg) and did not regularly participate in structured exercise programs.

Under expert guidelines, systolic blood pressure between 130 and 139 mmHg falls into the "high-normal" category, which warrants specific lifestyle recommendations from healthcare professionals. None of the participants had been diagnosed with hypertension.

To qualify, volunteers had to be free of injuries and illnesses, have no current or previous use of blood pressure medication, and be nonsmokers. They also had to consume no more than 14 units of alcohol per week.

Participants were randomly assigned to five groups. One served as a control group, while the other four began the same four-week exercise program at home, focusing on isometric movements involving the lower body.

The training consisted of four wall squat holds per session, with two minutes of seated recovery between each hold. Participants completed this routine three times weekly during the first four weeks.

After this initial training period, the four exercise groups followed different schedules for another four weeks. One continued with three weekly sessions, another reduced its frequency to twice weekly, and a third performed the exercises only once a week. The fourth group stopped training altogether.

Researchers evaluated blood pressure, heart rate, and additional measures of cardiovascular function at the beginning of the experiment and again after four and eight weeks.

Even One Weekly Workout Helped Preserve Blood Pressure Benefits

After the first four weeks, all four exercise groups showed significant improvements compared with the control group. These included reductions in systolic blood pressure, which measures pressure when the heart contracts, and diastolic blood pressure, which measures pressure when the heart relaxes. Mean arterial pressure, a measure of average blood pressure throughout the cardiac cycle, also decreased significantly.

These initial results were consistent with earlier studies demonstrating the blood pressure benefits of isometric exercise. However, after participants switched to their assigned maintenance schedules, the groups no longer showed statistically significant differences in diastolic blood pressure.

By the end of the eight-week study, participants exercising just once or twice weekly had maintained significant reductions in systolic blood pressure and mean arterial pressure compared with the control group. Neither schedule maintained a statistically significant improvement in diastolic blood pressure.

The greatest benefits appeared among participants who continued performing wall squats three times per week. Their systolic blood pressure fell by an average of 13.73 mmHg (-13.73 mmHg) from the beginning of the study.

By comparison, the twice-weekly group experienced an average reduction of 6.95 mmHg, while participants exercising once a week recorded a decrease of 6.56 mmHg.

Those who maintained the three-session schedule also preserved improvements in other cardiovascular measurements, including total peripheral resistance (an indication that blood vessels have narrowed) and heart rate variability.

Stopping Exercise Caused Blood Pressure Benefits to Fade

The results also revealed what happened when participants stopped exercising completely.

Those who discontinued wall squats after the initial four weeks experienced a reversal of their earlier blood pressure improvements. By the end of the study, their readings were no longer statistically different from those of the control group.

This finding suggests that maintaining some level of regular isometric exercise may be important for preserving the cardiovascular improvements gained during training.

However, the researchers emphasized that the maintenance phase lasted only four weeks. Additional studies following participants for longer periods will be needed to determine whether less frequent training can preserve these benefits over months or years.

"The study demonstrates that while lower frequency isometric exercise training may be sufficient to maintain blood pressure reductions over the short term, higher frequencies are required to preserve these benefits and the associated vascular and cardiac autonomic adaptations," the researchers write.

"The study offers evidence that lower frequency isometric exercise training can help maintain short-term blood pressure reductions, providing a pragmatic option for individuals with limited time or adherence challenges."

#5728. Opinion: I moved to Europe for free health care. I miss my patient portal

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Breland is a co-founder of The Neuro Studio.

Tuesday, at exactly 7 a.m., I arrived at my general practitioner’s office, in the basement level of his house, two blocks from mine in Mellieħa, Malta. There are six chairs in the waiting area. Ikea, I think. People note who got there first and go in, in turn. On his desk, there’s an ancient laptop with a big monitor running a vaguely Y2K version of Windows. He wears a digital Casio watch I remember my dad having in the 1980s. My American doctor’s office had a water feature.

My Malta doctor does bloodwork by appointment only, Tuesdays at 7 a.m. You tell him in advance what you need, and he has the tubes ready, hand-labeled with your resident number. The tubes are tracking the two diseases I brought with me. The number is what gets you into a socialized system that spends a quarter of what America costs per person and still has an average life expectancy of five more years. It’s not the Mediterranean diet doing the work. Malta has the highest obesity rates in adults in all of the E.U.

While I sat there, gauze pressed on the vein that just held the needle, he filled out a form for the lab, correcting an error with white-out tape. You can buy that down the street at the store that sells water shoes and postcards.

I left the United States for a variety of reasons, including that you can swim in the Potomac but shouldn’t. You can bask in the Mediterranean and should. But mostly, it was a calculation about health care. American medicine saved me, literally, more than once. My care was extraordinary, and it was also about to become extraordinarily unaffordable. I pay 38 euros a week here — about $2,300 a year — and it covers me and my medications, including the one that costs $80,000 per year in the U.S.

My medical resume is diverse. I’ve had multiple sclerosis since 2002. I had breast cancer. I have half a liver. I once broke my leg in three places — while standing still. In my adult life I have hit the catastrophic out-of-pocket maximum nearly every year.

Like most insured Americans, I had coverage through my employer, and later through my husband Brian’s employer, the federal government. My doctors were department heads at Georgetown and Johns Hopkins. The surgeon who repaired my leg did his residency at the Hospital for Special Surgery, the top-ranked orthopedic hospital in the country. I got him because he was on call. My post-mastectomy plastic surgeon had once chaired the board that certifies plastic surgeons. All of them. For the whole country.

Every visit was a $40 copay. Self-referral. My maximum out-of-pocket was $6,000. The plan cost $26,888 a year — Brian paid $9,988 and his employer paid the rest. We never thought about it.

Then came DOGE, which was clearing out the federal workforce in the name of preventing waste, fraud, and abuse. Brian worked for an Inspector General’s office that investigated and prosecuted … waste, fraud, and abuse.

He never got fired. But we didn’t want to live in the risk. He wanted to move into consulting, which meant buying insurance on the exchange.

I am an insurance company’s nightmare. Federal law currently says they have to take me. To be extra safe, we planned to go to New York, where Brian’s family lives, because preexisting conditions are written into state law.

The cheapest mid-level plan, including copays and deductibles, ran about $30,000 for the year for both of us. That was the 2026 number. Open enrollment for 2027 coverage runs Nov. 1 to Dec. 15. That’s a shorter timeframe than previous years, and marketplace premiums are up an average of 26% for 2026. United Healthcare is requesting a 52% increase for New York for 2027. Millions of Americans are running the numbers now.

Two incomes down to one. Our health care costs tripling from what we paid with Brian’s job. After a lot of thought and a single Excel spreadsheet, we decided our best option wasn’t New York after all. My mother, long dead, ended up being the deciding factor.

My mother left me an E.U. passport. That is not a financial plan or a policy proposal or anything I earned — it is an inheritance like my green eyes and forehead veins, and it is the only reason any of what follows was available to me. Most Americans with a condition like mine don’t have an escape hatch to the European Union. I did. And I had been claiming socialized medicine was ideal — the way! — for decades without ever having participated in it.

My social security contribution — that 38 euros a week — gives the entitlement.

Hospital stay in Malta? Free. Emergency helicopter rescue? Free. There is no prior authorization. No requirement to fail a cheaper drug before getting a better one. Nobody has sent me the letter I used to get every year from my U.S. insurer, announcing they would not cover my medication because they believed I had a secondary insurance policy I have never had. Every. Single. Year.

At least twice a year, my doctor would be on the phone yelling at an insurance company for denying coverage. There are people whose entire job it is to file those appeals. According to a 2025 AMA survey, U.S. doctors average 40 prior authorizations per week, and their practices spend 13 hours a week on them. Forty percent of doctors employ staffers just to deal with insurance companies. And about three-quarters of physicians report that denials have increased over the past five years.

To be honest, in Malta, I pay for medical care all the time. I just pay differently.

There’s a two-tiered medical system. Public and private. The care is guaranteed. Speed and convenience live wholly in the private tier.

I can walk into almost any pharmacy in Malta and see a GP operating privately that same day for 15 to 20 euros. A specialist is 70 euros. Always cash. Sometimes you get a receipt. An ultrasound — if you want it fast — is 120 euros. Mine was performed by a doctor specializing in breast cancer imaging. No tech. No radiologist to read it later. I got the report at the appointment.

Most specialists here see patients both publicly and privately, and many private appointments happen inside pharmacies. There are tiny offices tucked in the back or upstairs. My neurologist works in a hospital one day a week. The other four days he works in four different pharmacies. You pick the one closest to where you live or work or shop. When I asked him why the system works that way, he said, literally, “to make it convenient for the patients.” There is no lease, no waiting room, no receptionist, and no billing department because there is nothing to bill. You pay at the counter where the eye drops are.

In Attard, where I see him because it’s closest to my house, he works Tuesday mornings alongside a gynecologist, a nephrologist, and an ophthalmologist. The next day will be a different group. Malta has more than 200 licensed community pharmacies, dispensing medical care alongside prescriptions, sunscreen, nail polish remover, a surprisingly robust collection of perfumes, and subpar dental floss. I ship that in from the U.K.

When I needed an oncology checkup, I found Dr. Brincat, who ran the oncology department at Mater Dei Hospital for 17 years. I called a private clinic where he works now. They checked his schedule, called me back the next day, and gave me an appointment just two weeks out.

He scanned (visually, not electronically) more than 100 pages of my records. Other than the paper on his desk, there was a stethoscope. No computer. No iPad. No phone. He ordered a hormone panel to see whether I should switch from tamoxifen to an aromatase inhibitor — something my American oncologist had said we’d get to at some point. They were in agreement on the protocol.

He ordered an ultrasound, handwriting a referral on letterhead and sealing it in an envelope from his top desk drawer.

It feels like time traveling back to the ’80s. But I’ve never had a doctor who needed to prove I needed anything. And a bill? Never seen one.

The private tier is easy. The public tier is where my medical fluency in the U.S. didn’t translate. I have to plan for things I never considered before. Like the speed of mail.

Before Dr. Brincat, I tried to do it the correct way, or rather, the free one. My GP requested a referral, and I was told to watch the mail for an appointment slip. The time you are given is not negotiable. The time is the time. The slip should arrive in roughly two weeks following the request.

I waited. When I called, they said they were still looking for a time for me.

The horror story Americans tell about socialized medicine is the wait. If you need a hip — good luck, check back in three years.

A friend of mine recently went from hip pain to a bad X-ray to a new hip in under 10 weeks in America. She also has excellent insurance, which is the entire sentence. America is the fastest system for some of its people. For the uninsured, the wait is not a year or three. It is indefinite.

I wasn’t prepared for the Maltese system paperwork, emphasis on the paper. To get my medication free, the Pharmacy of Your Choice program required proof that I had paid into social security — because there is no centralized system that simply shows that … I have. Buy a printer/scanner. You will need it.

I scanned and sent my receipts. They replied:

Thank you for contacting the POYC Schedule V office. This is to acknowledge receipt of your email. We will reply to your email in due course.

I have four similar messages in a folder named “Bureaucracy Stuff.”

After three weeks of due course, I called. My form had been mailed, they said, and must have been lost. They would mail it again. I could expect it in 10 business days. I asked whether I could just come get it. They said yes, they were open until 1 p.m. It took me 32 minutes, door to door, in heavy traffic.

In America, there is paperwork to prove you deserve a drug or surgery or treatment because the insurance company doesn’t want to give it to you. In Malta, there’s paperwork because there are forms and they are still on paper.

I have not received reminder texts here. No confirmation calls. I think I have a dermatologist appointment next week. Am I sure? No. I will show up and hope.

I worry that if my cancer comes back, I won’t have what I would have had in the U.S. The doctors are good here. But the bench isn’t as deep.

There are more MS drugs available in America than here — but not the one developed for my subtype. Tolebrutinib, sold as Cenrifki, is the drug American patients lobbied hard for. The Food and Drug Administration rejected it over risk of severe liver injury and questions of efficacy. The European regulator approved it in June. It’s the first drug shown to reduce disability in non-relapsing secondary progressive MS, and I’m in that group, and there is nothing else.

But it won’t come to Malta soon. Just because E.U. approved it doesn’t mean it gets to Malta because there aren’t enough patients to warrant it. There are more people with MS in the United States — nearly a million — than there are people in my entire country.

I did learn recently that there is a portal for the public system. For the private system, I keep a folder on my phone of photographs of my doctors’ notes. One of them is a lonely piece of paper under a stethoscope.

I have never received a bill here. I have no idea what a day in the hospital costs.

My neurologist and I are discussing a minor surgery — one overnight stay — to implant a device that delivers medication directly to my spinal cord. He told me we won’t get to choose the size, even though I would want the smaller one.

“It’s free,” he said, “so we don’t get as much say.”

Mariska Breland is a co-founder of The Neuro Studio, which provides movement education for people with neurological conditions and training for the professionals who work with them.

#5727. Mayo Clinic discovers new ways to fight the “zombie” cells that drive aging

Seven studies from Mayo Clinic are revealing new details about senescent cells, often called "zombie" cells because they stop dividing but remain active in the body. These aging cells release inflammatory substances that can contribute to diseases associated with growing older.

The research, published in Nature journals, was conducted by scientists at Mayo Clinic's Robert and Arlene Kogod Center on Aging. Rather than simply confirming that senescent cells play a role in aging, the studies investigate how to recognize different types of these cells, why they produce harmful inflammation and how their effects might be reduced.

The findings also contribute to a nationwide effort to create detailed maps of senescent cells throughout the human body. Known as the Cellular Senescence Network (SenNet) Consortium, the project brings together researchers across the United States and receives funding from the National Institutes of Health Common Fund. Its goal is to document where senescent cells occur in different tissues and how they change throughout a person's lifetime.

"This body of work is moving the aging field forward to precisely identify, understand and target the specific senescent cells that contribute to age-related dysfunction, which is the necessary groundwork to develop new therapies that support healthy aging," says Marissa Schafer, Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic scientist whose laboratory directed several of the investigations.

Scientists Discover That Zombie Cells Are Not All Alike

Identifying senescent cells reliably has long been a major obstacle for scientists studying aging. The new research shows that these cells are much more varied than previously understood. Their characteristics differ depending on where they are located in the body and which biological processes caused them to become senescent.

To help address this challenge, researchers developed a tool called the SenMayo gene set. It uses patterns of gene activity to identify senescent cells more consistently across tissues and experimental systems.

Scientists tested the approach using bone biopsies from older adults. They also found that the gene signature became less prominent after senescent cells were removed in preclinical experiments. Since its development, SenMayo has become a widely used resource for researchers investigating aging and related diseases.

Mayo Clinic endocrinologist Sundeep Khosla, M.D., served as senior author of the study, "A new gene set identifies senescent cells and predicts senescence-associated pathways across tissues." Other Mayo Clinic researchers who contributed to the paper include Nathan LeBrasseur, Ph.D., Diana Jurk, Ph.D., João Passos, Ph.D., and LaTonya Hickson, M.D..

A Hidden Connection Between Mitochondria and Chronic Inflammation

Other studies explored one of the most damaging features of zombie cells: their tendency to generate ongoing inflammation.

The researchers discovered additional biological processes that explain why senescent cells continue producing inflammatory signals. Several of these processes involve malfunctioning mitochondria, the tiny structures responsible for producing much of a cell's energy.

In one pathway, DNA and RNA originating from mitochondria activate immune responses that contribute to inflammation. Another involves changes in mitochondrial metabolism that influence inflammatory gene activity through epigenetic mechanisms. These mechanisms affect how genes are switched on or off without changing the underlying DNA sequence.

The discoveries suggest that researchers may eventually be able to interfere with the processes responsible for chronic inflammation while leaving the senescent cells themselves intact. This would offer another approach to treatment beyond attempting to destroy every harmful aging cell.

Dr. Passos served as senior author of three papers examining these mechanisms and the diversity of senescent cells:

Experimental Treatments Show Promise Against Aging Cells

The Mayo Clinic team also investigated possible ways to reduce the number of senescent cells or limit the damage they cause.

The approaches included senolytic medications, which are designed to eliminate senescent cells, a natural compound present in tomatoes, and genetic techniques intended to target particular populations of aging cells.

When tested in older mice, these interventions produced encouraging results. Depending on the approach, researchers observed reductions in inflammatory measures and improvements in several aging-related outcomes, including physical frailty, inflammation in the brain and performance on cognitive tasks.

Another investigation uncovered a possible way to measure aspects of biological aging through blood testing. Researchers identified IL-23R as a potential biomarker that might eventually help scientists evaluate aging-related changes and determine whether future treatments are working.

These results remain preliminary in terms of medical applications. More research will be necessary to establish whether the approaches are safe and effective in people. Nevertheless, the experiments provide valuable clues for developing treatments that more precisely address the cellular processes involved in age-related diseases.

Dr. Schafer was the lead author of two studies examining biomarkers and possible interventions:

A New Direction for Healthy Aging Research

Together, the seven studies represent an important shift in how researchers approach cellular aging. Scientists are moving beyond the broad observation that senescent cells contribute to age-related decline and toward identifying which populations cause the greatest problems, what makes them harmful and how those specific effects could be controlled.

The findings also challenge the idea that eliminating senescent cells must always be the primary treatment strategy. By understanding the molecular pathways that trigger persistent inflammation, researchers may be able to develop therapies that block damaging signals without removing the cells responsible for producing them.

Mayo Clinic researcher Darren Baker, Ph.D., served as senior author of the paper "Senotypes define the diverse landscape of senescent cells," which examines the varied characteristics of these aging cell populations.

The work also supports Mayo Clinic's broader Precure Research initiative. This program aims to equip physicians with better ways to identify and intervene in harmful biological changes before they develop into disease or advance into conditions that are difficult to treat.

By revealing how zombie cells differ, why they promote inflammation and which processes might be targeted, the research offers a more detailed roadmap for future treatments designed to support healthier aging.

#5726. Humana, athenahealth collaborate on expanded electronic prior authorizations nationwide

Humana, athenahealth collaborate on expanded electronic prior authorizations nationwide" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Humana and athenahealth are expanding electronic prior authorizations nationwide in a newly announced collaboration.

Through athenaPayer, Humana is able to connect with over 180,000 providers across the athenaOne network, which the partners said will create a more connected experience between the health plan and clinicians.

“Every phone call, fax and portal log-in adds work for a practice trying to get a patient the care they need,” said Paul Brient, athenahealth chief product and operations officer, in a statement. “Prior authorization shouldn’t require care teams to navigate a different process for every health plan. By connecting health plans and practices through one solution with a common workflow, we’re creating a more scalable way to exchange information, reducing work for both providers and payers while, most importantly, helping patients access care faster.”

Athenahealth internal data show more than 6,000 providers processed nearly 35,000 electronic prior authorizations with Humana in September, with over 70% completed without requiring additional information from staff.

The collaboration reflects Humana’s broader strategy to improve care access through requiring fewer prior authorizations and making the process simpler when needed, executives said.

“Our goal is straightforward: help people get the right care at the right time while reducing unnecessary burden on the physicians and care teams who serve them,” said Traci Granston, M.D., Humana vice president of clinical innovation and trend, in a statement. “… This collaboration with athenahealth is another step forward, ensuring that providers spend less time navigating administrative processes and more time focused on patient care.”

In June 2025, insurers nationwide—including Humana—agreed to take steps to reform prior authorization, including supporting electronic prior authorizations.

#5725. Scientists solve a 30-year mystery behind inflammatory bowel disease

Scientists from the University of Oxford, Newcastle University, and Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust have uncovered a previously unexplained cause of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The discovery could change how doctors understand, diagnose, and treat certain forms of the condition.

The findings indicate that IBD is not simply one disease. Instead, it appears to include several biologically distinct conditions that develop through different processes in the body. Identifying these differences could make it possible to provide treatments tailored to the specific cause of each patient's illness.

In a study published in the New England Journal of Medicine, researchers examined more than 4,900 people with IBD and identified two important findings. First, some patients produce antibodies that interfere with interleukin-10 (IL-10), an essential protein that helps prevent excessive inflammation. Second, this autoimmune reaction explains how one of the strongest known genetic risk factors for IBD contributes to the disease.

Under normal circumstances, IL-10 acts as a chemical messenger between cells, helping the immune system regulate inflammation. However, certain antibodies can block its activity, effectively disabling one of the body's built-in safeguards against excessive immune responses. Without this protection, inflammation can persist and become difficult to control.

Hidden Antibodies Reveal a Cause of Inflammatory Bowel Disease

Inflammatory bowel disease includes Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, two chronic conditions that affect approximately 500,000 people in the UK and millions more around the world.

Symptoms often first appear during adolescence or early adulthood, and patients may face lifelong medical challenges. Managing the disease can involve repeated hospital visits, medications that suppress immune activity, and sometimes surgery. Although treatments have improved, many people must try several different therapies without achieving lasting relief. This places a substantial burden on patients and creates significant costs for healthcare systems.

The researchers discovered that approximately 3.5% of patients with IBD had elevated levels of antibodies that neutralize IL-10. These antibodies were detected in people with both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, but not in healthy individuals.

Based on the prevalence of IBD in the UK, the researchers estimate that 15,000 to 20,000 patients nationwide could carry these harmful antibodies.

Scientists Solve a 30-Year Genetic Mystery

The investigation also revealed a strong association between the IL-10-blocking antibodies and a genetic variant called HLA-DRB1*01:03.

Scientists at Oxford first connected this genetic variant to a severe form of inflammatory bowel disease 30 years ago. However, the biological process linking the gene to the condition had remained unclear.

The new results help resolve that longstanding mystery. People who carry HLA-DRB1*01:03 are substantially more likely to develop antibodies that interfere with IL-10, providing an explanation for how this genetic risk factor can contribute to severe intestinal inflammation.

Professor Holm Uhlig, a pediatric gastroenterologist and Director of the Centre for Human Genetics at the University of Oxford's Nuffield Department of Medicine, was a senior author of the study.

"We've suspected an important role of interleukin 10 in patients with inflammatory bowel disease for decades. The study now provides clear evidence and contributes the missing link between a well-known genetic variant that had been linked to severe inflammatory bowel disease in the past and the very recently discovered autoimmunity to interleukin 10."

"Understanding what drives the inflammation, provides a clear explanation for disease in this group of people and opens the door to new treatments that target the autoantibodies themselves or cells that produce those autoantibodies."

How Earlier Discoveries Helped Explain Severe IBD

The findings build on more than a decade of research into rare inherited disorders that disrupt the body's ability to control inflammation.

Sophie Hambleton, Professor of Pediatrics and Immunology at Newcastle University, explained that studying these uncommon conditions provided important clues about the mechanisms involved in more widespread forms of IBD.

"This discovery shows how the study of rare, inherited disorders can shed new light on common conditions. The groundwork was laid over 10 years ago when genetic defects in IL-10 or its receptor were found in young children with severe IBD. Later, we realized that neutralizing autoantibodies against IL-10 were mimicking this effect in 2 little girls with colitis."

These earlier observations helped researchers recognize that antibodies blocking IL-10 could produce effects similar to inherited defects involving the same protein or its receptor. The latest study now establishes the importance of this mechanism in a larger group of patients with inflammatory bowel disease.

A Blood Test Could Lead to More Targeted IBD Treatments

Beyond explaining a previously mysterious cause of intestinal inflammation, the discovery could have important implications for patient care.

Researchers believe the results provide a foundation for developing a blood test that identifies people whose disease is associated with antibodies against IL-10. Such a test could help doctors recognize these patients earlier and select treatments that address the underlying immune malfunction.

Dr. Rainer Doffinger, a clinical immunologist at Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, highlighted the potential benefits for both patients and healthcare systems.

"By identifying patients early and giving them targeted treatment, we could reduce reliance on expensive ongoing therapy and prevent complications. Even modest reductions in biologic treatment, admissions and surgery could translate into savings of many millions of pounds annually for the NHS, alongside the major benefits for patients through fewer interventions, improved quality of life or even durable remission."

Targeting the antibodies themselves, or the immune cells responsible for producing them, could offer a new treatment strategy for this particular group of patients. The approach could potentially reduce the need for repeated therapies, hospital admissions, and surgery while improving the chances of sustained disease control.

Professor Simon Travis, Professor of Clinical Gastroenterology at the University of Oxford and the Kennedy Institute of Rheumatology, emphasized the significance of identifying a specific biological cause of IBD.

"This is the most exciting discovery in a lifetime specialising in IBD. It means that we can now identify a group where we know what is causing the disease and that creates a real opportunity to change how we manage this disease."

The research marks an important advance toward personalized treatment for inflammatory bowel disease. Rather than relying primarily on symptoms to guide medical decisions, doctors may eventually be able to use biological testing to determine what is driving inflammation in individual patients and choose more appropriate therapies.

The study involved researchers from the Nuffield Department of Medicine at the University of Oxford, Newcastle University's Translational and Clinical Research Institute, and the Department of Immunology at Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust.

Funding was provided through the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Biomedical Research Centres in Oxford, Cambridge, and Newcastle.

Materials provided by University of Oxford. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5724. Top health takeaways from the midterm elections

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

By Daniel Payne, Anil Oza, Sarah Todd, Bob Herman, Chelsea Cirruzzo, and John Wilkerson

Daniel covers the intersection of the health industry and the federal government. He reports on corporate influence in government, the health consequences of federal policies, and the politics of health care. Confidential tips can be sent on Signal at danielp.100.

Anil Oza is a general assignment reporter at STAT focused on the NIH and health equity. You can reach him on Signal at aniloza.16.

Sarah covers how industries like food and tobacco affect Americans’ bodies and minds. Her interests include ultra-processed foods; smoke-free tobacco; and wellness trends like perimenopause products and peptides. Confidential tips can be sent on Signal at sarahlizchar.47.

Bob covers the money in health care, focusing on health insurance and hospitals. His stories delve into Medicare Advantage, opaque prescription drug benefits, and how much executives actually make. He is also the author of the Health Care Inc. newsletter. You can reach Bob on Signal at bobjherman.09.

Chelsea covers the Department of Health and Human Services with a particular focus on power and influence at the top. Confidential tips can be sent via Signal at chelseacirruzzo.42.

John writes about the politics of health care, and he is the author of the twice-weekly D.C. Diagnosis newsletter. You can reach John on Signal at John_Wilkerson.07.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.

Good morning from a round-the-clock elections team at STAT, where we’ve been closely monitoring Election Day results nationwide. Below is a newsletter full of sharp analysis on how the results (so far) will affect American health care — read on!

WASHINGTON — Republicans — who pushed sweeping, unprecedented health reforms, from Medicaid cuts to MAHA’s upheaval — had a terrible, no good, very bad election night on Tuesday.

Democrats gained control of both chambers of Congress, with shocking victories in deep red states like Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina: a sweeping, decisive result after many candidates ran on health-focused agendas.

The strong political signal is likely to be interpreted as, among other things, a rebuke of the GOP’s health reform agenda. That frustration and anger could be seen even among relatively new allies like the Make America Healthy Again movement, which attached itself to the Trump administration through health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Jeffrey Tucker, president and founder of the MAHA-aligned Brownstone Institute, told STAT that the GOP’s “failure to take its mandate seriously — to give people back their lives and liberties — has led to what looks like yet another populist revolt in a different form.”

“This loss tonight was well-deserved,” he said, echoing other MAHA leaders online.

Though non-health issues — gas prices, the cost of groceries, and the war in Iran — loomed large, broad voter support for congressional Democrats could be taken as a mandate for the party to take bigger swings on health care.

Democratic candidates who ran on trust in science and on their health credentials saw strong results, with the group 314 Action, which supports such candidates, calling the night a “STEM Wave.”

And some key MAHA-aligned candidates lost on Tuesday. Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas), who was among the founding members of the MAHA Caucus, lost his race, as did MAHA champion Zach Lahn, who ran to be governor of Iowa.

The election, of course, will also have lasting impacts on America’s health policy. Democrats will now have powerful new tools to investigate the administration’s actions and push back on its agenda.

Late Tuesday night, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), a health policy leader in Congress, posted one word on X: “Subpoenas.”

In several closely watched races, candidates made health care affordability a key campaign plank, promising to restore Affordable Care Act subsidies and fight the Medicaid cuts passed by Republicans as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill act in 2025.

In Ohio, physician Amy Acton won the state’s governorship after pledging to make health care a major focus in office. Acton, who led Ohio’s Covid-19 response, prioritized protecting the accessibility of Medicaid, forgiving medical debt, tackling surprise billing, and creating a new prescription drug plan to lower costs. Her opponent, billionaire biotech entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy, frequently sought to turn the race into a referendum on the lockdowns and school closures that occurred during Acton’s pandemic-era tenure in state government.

In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governorship, becoming the first Black woman to occupy that position in any state. Bottoms also pushed for more aggressive health coverage for the state’s lowest earners. Georgia’s controversial Medicaid program, which partially expanded coverage to low-income adults if they proved they were working, expires at the end of the year. Bottoms promised to switch to full Medicaid expansion provided under the Affordable Care Act. She defeated Republican Rick Jackson, the wealthy founder of Jackson Healthcare, a large physician and nurse staffing company. — Sarah Todd and Bob Herman

A microbiologist. A doctor. A nuclear engineer. These are some of the Democrats who won seats in Congress last night.

Perhaps the most surprising was pediatrician Annie Andrews. Andrews won South Carolina’s open Senate seat, which had been held by Republican Lindsey Graham for 23 years before his death. She, along with Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed (more below on El-Sayed, who completed medical school but not residency), will be the the first Democrats with medical degrees in the Senate since 1969.

In her campaign ads, Andrews frequently wore her scrubs, and made walking back Trump’s health policies central to her campaign.

“My two decades as a physician have shown me in a thousand heartbreaking ways just how broken our health care system is,” her platform for reducing health care costs reads. Her platform included health care being a “right” and not a “privilege.” To that end, she said she will work to maintain access to vaccines and ensure rural hospitals do not close.

For a sense of how far Andrews has come, when our colleague Margaret Manto wrote about her last year, for NOTUS (now the Washington Sun), her race was considered a longshot. “This is not a path I ever envisioned for myself. I was perfectly happy in my role as a pediatrician,” she told Margaret at the time.

While not a doctor, Xavier Becerra, who served as health secretary in the Biden administration, cruised in his race to become California governor. From that perch, he could continue his focus on drug pricing, which has also been a priority for the state’s leaders.

On the other side, longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, a prominent booster of federal support for academic research who criticized the Trump administration’s moves to reshape that system, lost her reelection campaign to Democrat Troy Jackson. — Anil Oza

He ran as a model MAHA candidate — an enemy of Big Agriculture, a friend of Kennedy.

And yet Republican Zach Lahn lost his race for the Iowa governorship, a crushing blow to the Make America Healthy Again movement. The MAHA PAC poured a million dollars into Lahn’s campaign and Kennedy enthusiastically backed him.

The loss may reflect the waning power of the MAHA movement, which has been on shaky ground over the last several months amid frustration by some members that the Trump administration was too slow on achieving real progress, including on pesticides. Lahn had promised to take down Big Agriculture, ban Covid-19 vaccines from the market, and tackle Iowa’s high cancer rate.

Sen. Roger Marshall (R) lost his reelection bid in Kansas. Marshall, a doctor, started the congressional MAHA Caucus. Although high prices for diesel and fertilizer were the initial drivers of discontent in the state, Marshall has spent the final two months of his campaign fending off reports of aggressive medical debt collection as an OB-GYN.

Marshall also faced an unusually well-suited Democratic contender, Adam Hamilton. Hamilton leads one of Kansas’ largest megachurches and has gained crossover appeal, including endorsements from two former Republican governors. – Chelsea Ciruzzo and John Wilkerson

Abdul El-Sayed’s win in a Michigan Senate race sets him up to be Democrats’ principal challenger to Kennedy. When I talked to him last week, he said he wants to lay the groundwork for a 2028 administration to rebuild the Department of Health and Human Services, but in the meantime he aims to hold Kennedy and Trump “accountable for all of the failures.”

While his race was one of the most closely watched of the cycle, largely because of Democrats’ angst about the direction of their party, many in academia and public health had hoped he could be a fighter for them. El-Sayed trained as a physician-scientist, doing research on health disparities and maternal health before becoming the head of Detroit’s public health department.

Through the race, he also amassed a huge platform that he will leverage to advocate for Medicare for All, as well as his vision for public health. We’ll have more to say later today, when my colleague Sarah Todd, who wrote about Acton’s gubernatorial campaign in Ohio, and I will have a breakdown of how doctors and scientists on the ballot fared. — Anil Oza

A new kind of medical clinic is surprising some patients with thousands in ER bills, STAT

#5723. Medicare Part D premiums projected to rise 50% in 2027 without plan switching: KFF

Medicare Part D premiums projected to rise 50% in 2027 without plan switching: KFF" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Medicare beneficiaries who remain in their current stand-alone Part D drug plans could face sharply higher premiums in 2027 if they don’t switch to lower-cost plans during open enrollment, according to a KFF analysis.

The average monthly premium for stand-alone prescription drug plans, or PDPs, is projected to rise 50%, from $34 in 2026 to $51 in 2027, if current enrollees remain in the same plans, according to the analysis from KFF, an independent source for health policy research, polling and news.

The increase would widen the gap between stand-alone drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans that include prescription drug coverage. KFF projects that drug coverage through Medicare Advantage plans that offer Part D coverage, or MA-PDs, will average $9 a month in 2027, compared with $51 for PDPs. The average PDP premium would rise by $17, compared with an increase of less than $2 for MA-PDs.

For Medicare Part D prescription drug coverage, the average beneficiary has 28 Medicare Advantage prescription drug plans (MA-PDs) and 9 stand-alone prescription drug plans (PDPs) to choose from, with varying costs associated with these different options. KFF analysts examined premiums and cost-sharing requirements for Part D coverage in 2027 and how these costs have changed over time, based on Medicare plan landscape and benefits data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS).

The $51 figure assumes current PDP enrollees remain in their existing plans. The actual average premium could be lower as beneficiaries switch to less expensive plans during open enrollment and new beneficiaries select coverage.

CMS projected a much smaller increase in the national average Part D premium, from $35 to $36. KFF noted that CMS, which based its estimate on September 2026 enrollment, did not explain its calculation methodology.

Among PDP enrollees who do not receive low-income subsidies, 76%, or 10.4 million people, would pay higher premiums if they keep their current plans. About 2.4 million would see their monthly premiums increase by more than $50.

That's a sharp increase from 2026, when only 38,000 enrollees faced monthly premium increases exceeding $50, according to KFF. The Trump administration’s decision to discontinue the Part D Premium Stabilization Demonstration after 2026 ended the additional premium subsidies that were provided to PDP sponsors and the cap on the maximum allowable monthly PDP premium increase, which was set at $50 for 2026, according to KFF analysts.

Another 4.1 million beneficiaries without low-income subsidies are enrolled in zero-premium PDPs this year, but no zero-premium PDPs will be available in 2027.

“With some plans increasing premiums substantially, the stakes are higher this year for people with Medicare stand-alone drug coverage if they sit on the sidelines during open enrollment,” Juliette Cubanski, a vice president and director of the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, said in a statement. “There are relatively low-premium PDP options, but people facing large premium increases need to take action if they want to avoid paying significantly more.”

According to KFF's analysis, if PDP enrollees who are not receiving Part D Low-Income Subsidies (LIS) keep their current plan in 2027, more than half (55%), or 7.5 million people, will pay premiums of less than $20 per month, but nearly 30%, or 3.9 million people, will pay at least $100 per month.

Average monthly premiums for the eight national PDPs are projected to range from around $6 to $204 in 2027. Among national PDPs, the two lowest-premium plans are Centene’s Wellcare Value Script Rx, an enhanced PDP with an average premium of $6.50 for 2027, up from $5.80 in 2026,  and Wellcare Classic, a basic PDP with an average premium of $10.90 for 2027, up from $8.60 in 2026, according to the analysis. The national PDPs with the highest average monthly premiums are United’s AARP Medicare Rx Preferred at $204.50, up from $126.00 in 2026, and Humana Premier Rx Plan at $137.40, up from $119.60 in 2026.

The analysis also finds that most Part D enrollees will face a deductible of several hundred dollars for drug coverage in 2027, including 85% of MA-PD enrollees, up from 80% in 2026, and virtually all PDP enrollees, 99.8%, up from 96% in 2026, based on current enrollment. The average Part D deductible in 2027 will be $643 for PDP enrollees, up from $540 in 2026,  and $489 for MA-PD enrollees, rising from $360 in 2026. The standard Part D deductible in 2027 is $700, up from $615 in 2026.

Most Part D enrollees will also face coinsurance rather than fixed copayments for preferred-brand and non-preferred drugs, potentially making their out-of-pocket costs less predictable. Virtually all PDP enrollees will face median coinsurance of 25% for preferred brands and 35% for non-preferred drugs, according to KFF.

#5722. Wall Street’s AI Sell-Off Exposes a Weak Spot in the Bank of Mom and Dad

As more adult children count on the Bank of Mom and Dad to help them buy homes, Mom and Dad, in turn, may be counting on Wall Street.

That arrangement looked a little less secure on Friday, when fears about the cost of the artificial intelligence boom sent stocks tumbling.

The Nasdaq lost 2.9% on Oct. 30, its worst day since June, as investors grew worried about the billions of dollars companies are spending on AI. Intel shares plunged 28.6%, while chipmakers AMD and Nvidia fell 10.9% and 4.2%, respectively, according to Reuters.

The consequences could reach well beyond Wall Street and Silicon Valley. Baby boomers held approximately $35.2 trillion in stocks and mutual funds as of the second quarter of 2026, or roughly 55% of the household total, according to Federal Reserve data analyzed by Yardeni Research.

And some of that money is already making its way into their children's down payments. Half of parents who had helped or planned to help their children purchase a home reported drawing on investment accounts, according to an April survey by Veterans United Home Loans.

Of course, one bad day won't drain the Bank of Mom and Dad. But if the losses keep piling up, the damage could spill out of parents' portfolios. Research shows that after substantial financial setbacks, parents tend to scale back the money they give their adult children—or stop giving it altogether.

The AI boom has played an enormous role in the stock market's recent run. Since ChatGPT's launch in November 2022, AI-related stocks accounted for roughly 75% of S&P 500 returns, according to a JPMorgan analysis.

And that rally has helped swell the fortunes of a generation already poised to pass down an extraordinary amount of wealth.

Approximately $105 trillion will pass to heirs through 2048, according to estimates from the weath management firm Cerulli Associates—with baby boomers and older generations accounting for the vast majority of the projected transfer.

But some of that money is changing hands much sooner, as parents and grandparents help adult children overcome the financial barriers to homeownership.

Nearly one-quarter of parents surveyed by Veterans United expected to contribute between $50,000 and $99,999 toward their children's home purchases, while 12% anticipated providing between $100,000 and $199,999.

They're shocking sums, and years of rising stock prices may have made those commitments easier to make.

"When their stock portfolios go up, they feel more able to help with a down payment," says Michelle Riehn, a certified financial planner and founder of Money Momma. "People feel richer."

The trouble is that those feelings—and the financial resources behind them—can change when markets fall.

In a 2025 study published in The Review of Economics and Statistics, economists Jessamyn Schaller and Chase Eck examined how financial transfers between parents and adult children changed following setbacks such as wealth losses, job exits, and health problems.

They found that parents sharply reduced financial assistance following losses of wealth and earned income, particularly in households with fewer accumulated assets.

An earlier working-paper version estimated that among lower-wealth households, a major loss of net worth reduced the likelihood of parents making a financial transfer by 6.1 percentage points, or 18.7% relative to the group's baseline rate.

The research examined financial assistance broadly, not just down payments, and didn't isolate stock market losses. Still, the findings have important implications for housing, where financial help from parents can make the difference between buying a home and remaining a renter.

Already, parental transfers account for 13 percentage points, or 27%, of young households' homeownership, according to a 2025 Federal Reserve working paper.

Naturally, the next question for a generation waiting on those transfers is what happens if AI stocks continue to fall.

Friday's slide was far from the end of the AI boom. Despite losing more than $1 trillion in market value that day, technology stocks were still worth trillions, with Nvidia alone valued at roughly $4.9 trillion.

But researchers have examined what a much larger reversal could mean for U.S. households.

In September, Allianz Research modeled the consequences of disappointing AI investments triggering a broader market downturn.

Under its more severe scenario, a 25% decline in the S&P 500 would erase approximately $27 trillion in U.S. household wealth—nearly 14% of total household net worth—and help push the economy into recession.

That's a hypothetical scenario, not a forecast. And even losses of that magnitude wouldn't affect every family's ability to help their children equally.

Financial advisers say much depends on whether parents have already set aside the money they intend to give—or are counting on their investments to cover the gift when the time comes.

"There's a difference between help that was planned and requests that come unplanned," Riehn says.

Parents who have committed to helping their children buy homes often move that money into conservative investments well before the purchase, she explains. Doing so can shield a planned gift from a sudden drop in stock prices.

But when parents haven't prepared, a downturn can force tougher decisions.

"A lot of times they're selling stock to do it, and that's where it gets tricky in a downturn," says Greg Black, a certified financial planner and president of Tencap Wealth Coaching in Utah.

A parent who expected to sell appreciated investments to cover a $100,000 down payment might have to liquidate more shares after a substantial market decline. Rather than lock in those losses, the parent could decide to reduce the gift or postpone it.

"So if the down payment money is sitting in AI stocks and they drop, that gift might have to wait," Black says.

Even parents who could still afford to help may think twice. Riehn says watching a portfolio lose value can make affluent households more reluctant to part with money, particularly when their children make unexpected requests.

David Talley, a certified financial planner with Talley Wealth in Johnson City, TN, offers a counterpoint: Families with sufficient cash reserves and diversified investments should generally be able to maintain gifts that fit within their long-term financial plans.

"With the cash layer in place, the gift doesn't have to wait for a recovery," he says.

But younger homebuyers might not have that flexibility.

Allianz estimated that a 15% market correction could take six to nine months to reverse under one scenario. In its more severe scenario, recovering from a 25% decline could take as long as two years.

That extended timeline points to another potential consequence of an AI bust: Any prolonged downturn could also change what parents expect to leave their children.

In an earlier working-paper version of their research, Schaller and Eck found that a major household wealth loss was associated with roughly a 5-percentage-point decline in parents' reported probability of leaving an inheritance worth at least $100,000.

That finding measures parents' expectations, not the inheritances their children ultimately received. And the consequences of a market correction would depend partly on how much of a family's wealth is tied to the stocks losing value.

"The real exception is a family with a concentrated position in one company whose net worth has doubled in a few years," Talley says. "That genuinely changes what they can give."

And if those gains reverse, so can the amount available to pass down.

Still, Riehn cautions that inheritances operate on a different timeline from down payment gifts. Children expecting to inherit investments decades from now may have time to ride out a market downturn. Those counting on that wealth for a home purchase in the nearer future may not.

The recent AI sell-off is far from a market crash, and there's no evidence it has already disrupted parental gifts or inheritances. Instead, it highlights an uncertainty at the heart of the Great Wealth Transfer: The fortunes younger Americans expect to receive aren't necessarily the fortunes their parents will ultimately leave behind.

And until that money changes hands, the next generation has little control over how much will be there—or when it will arrive.

#5721. A simple liquid can stop cavities without drilling, major study confirms

A cavity doesn't always have to mean drilling, injections, or an uncomfortable visit to the dentist. A major clinical trial has confirmed that a simple, inexpensive liquid can stop tooth decay in young children, potentially preventing painful infections and the need for dental surgery.

The treatment, called silver diamine fluoride (SDF), takes only seconds to apply to each affected tooth. Rather than removing damaged tooth material and placing a filling, a dentist uses a tiny sponge tipped applicator to paint the liquid directly onto the cavity. The process requires no drilling, injections, or sedation.

The findings could have enormous implications for childhood dental care. Every year, thousands of young children in the United States visit emergency departments because of untreated cavities. Emergency physicians generally cannot provide the dental procedures needed to address the underlying problem, leaving some children with ongoing pain and infections. Others ultimately need dental surgery under general anesthesia, which makes them completely unconscious during the procedure.

Now, researchers led by the University of Michigan have produced compelling evidence that a much simpler approach can stop many cavities from getting worse.

Major Clinical Trial Confirms Silver Diamine Fluoride Works

Published in JAMA Pediatrics, the Phase III clinical trial included 830 children younger than 6. Participants were recruited through dental clinics, pediatric medical practices, and Head Start and Early Head Start programs in Michigan, New York, and Iowa.

Head Start and Early Head Start are federally supported programs that provide early childhood education and related services to eligible families.

The results showed that a solution containing 38% silver diamine fluoride successfully stopped decay in more than half of the affected baby teeth when treatment was provided at six month intervals.

Dentists refer to this as arresting tooth decay, meaning the damaged area stops deteriorating. Unlike a traditional filling, the treatment does not replace lost tooth structure. Instead, it helps prevent existing decay from progressing.

SDF works through the combined effects of silver and fluoride. Silver helps combat bacteria associated with tooth decay, while fluoride helps strengthen the mineral structure of teeth and resist further damage.

"This is a very effective and safe treatment -- even in children as young as 1," said Margherita Fontana, professor of dentistry at the University of Michigan School of Dentistry and the study's lead investigator.

A Simple Treatment Could Help Millions Avoid Dental Pain

Tooth decay is the most common chronic disease among children, affecting more than 40% of American children. Although cavities may initially cause few noticeable symptoms, untreated decay can eventually lead to severe toothaches, infections, problems eating and sleeping, missed school days, and repeated medical appointments.

For young children, conventional dental treatment can also be particularly challenging. Some are too young to remain still throughout a procedure, while others experience significant fear or anxiety.

SDF offers an alternative for many of these patients because it can be applied quickly without the equipment and procedures required for a traditional filling.

Fontana said the benefits could extend well beyond young children. Older adults, people with developmental or physical disabilities, individuals with severe dental anxiety, and patients who have difficulty obtaining conventional dental care could also benefit.

There is, however, one important tradeoff. SDF permanently turns the decayed portion of a treated tooth dark, which can be especially noticeable on front teeth. The discoloration is primarily cosmetic, but it may influence whether patients and families choose the treatment.

For many people, avoiding pain, drilling, or more invasive procedures may outweigh that drawback.

Why This Decades-Old Treatment Could Soon Reach More Patients

Silver diamine fluoride is not a newly invented substance. Dentists have successfully used it to manage cavities in numerous countries for decades.

In the United States, the FDA approved SDF as a medical device for treating tooth sensitivity in 2014. Dentists have also used it off-label to stop cavities, meaning they apply an authorized product for a purpose beyond its original approved indication.

What has been missing is large-scale clinical evidence from U.S. populations establishing its safety and effectiveness for treating tooth decay, a key step toward obtaining FDA approval for that specific use.

The University of Michigan trial was designed to help fill that gap.

"If we want more children and families to benefit from this treatment, we need rigorous evidence showing both that it works and that it's safe. From a public health perspective, if we want broader implementation across the United States, including in medical settings, we need carefully collected data in U.S. populations, and we now have that," Fontana said.

The investigation began in 2018 and continued despite the major disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

The researchers believe stronger clinical evidence could make SDF more widely available, including in pediatric medical settings where children often receive care long before their first dental appointment.

"In medicine, clinicians want high-quality evidence before changing practice," Fontana said. "It is important to have data they can refer to because young children often see pediatricians years before they ever visit a dentist, broader acceptance could allow many more cavities to be treated while a referral to a dental home is successful, and before they become painful, infected or require surgery."

A dental home refers to an ongoing relationship with a dental care provider who can deliver preventive care, treatment, and follow-up services.

Expanding access to SDF could allow more children to receive early intervention before relatively manageable cavities develop into serious dental problems.

FDA Approval Could Expand Access to Cavity Treatment

The trial brought together researchers from the University of Michigan, New York University, the University of Iowa, and Indiana University. The National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research, part of the National Institutes of Health, provided more than $12 million in funding.

The product tested was Advantage Arrest 38% SDF, supplied by Elevate Oral Care.

The findings provide clinical trial evidence that the manufacturer can use in an application seeking FDA approval of SDF as a drug for arresting dental caries, the medical term for tooth decay.

Amr Moursi, a professor of pediatric dentistry at New York University College of Dentistry and a co-principal investigator, emphasized the potential importance of that regulatory change.

"Our results support FDA approval of SDF for managing arrest of tooth decay in young children. Removing SDF from off-label status would be an important innovation which could lead to increased utilization by providers, enhanced payments by insurers and more consistent product quality," said Moursi, a co-principal investigator on the study.

For some children, receiving another application of SDF every few months could be sufficient to keep a cavity under control until the affected baby tooth naturally falls out.

Adults could also benefit, either by using SDF to manage decay over a longer period or as a temporary solution until a filling or another restorative procedure becomes affordable or practical.

The treatment is not suitable for every cavity, and stopping decay does not necessarily eliminate the need for future dental work. Nevertheless, the findings suggest that a procedure requiring only seconds to perform could help many patients avoid more complicated treatment.

"For almost anyone, this can arrest the decay and stop the infection and the pain it causes," Fontana said. "This could benefit many people."
