#5703. EXCLUSIVE: Jim Carrey Lands a Buyer for His $35 Million Hawaii Home—One Month After Putting It on the Market

Jim Carrey has found a buyer for his sprawling Hawaii waterfront retreat, less than one month after listing the tropical property for $35 million and after tying the knot with his longtime partner, Min Ah.

The 64-year-old "Ace Ventura" star married Ah in an intimate ceremony in Los Angeles, with a representative for the actor confirming the nuptials to People.

Fresh off their wedding, Carrey made another major life change by putting his lavish Maui estate on the market.

Now, Realtor.com® can exclusively reveal that the home is in the "pending" stage, meaning Carrey has found a buyer.

The actor purchased the waterfront property for $16.5 million in 2016, according to records. Its $35 million asking price means Carrey is hoping to more than double his investment after a decade of ownership.

Built in 2002, the three-bedroom, 4.5-bathroom residence spans 4,717 square feet and sits on nearly an acre along Keawakapu Beach.

Listed by Blake Hill of Hawaii Life, the property is being offered fully furnished and is described in the listing as a "bohemian luxury unicorn."

"Close to an acre on Keawakapu Beach, where South Kihei Road ends and Wailea begins. Roughly 170 feet along the water lets the homes stand far back behind a wide green lawn and a grove of tall coconut palms," the listing states.

Surrounded by lush tropical greenery, the estate was designed to embrace seamless indoor-outdoor living while taking full advantage of its oceanfront setting.

Inside, soaring ceilings and an expansive floor plan create an airy atmosphere, while coastal-inspired furnishings complement the home's enviable location.

"The great room rises into the trusses and opens fully to a covered stone lanai," the listing adds

The chef's kitchen features two large islands, white cabinetry, and high-end appliances, while the primary suite takes the home's relaxed aesthetic one step further with a swinging bed and floor-to-ceiling windows.

Its accompanying bathroom is equally luxurious, complete with a statement soaking tub and dual vanities.

The dining area continues the breezy beach aesthetic, with a large wooden table and multiple seating areas providing plenty of space for entertaining.

Outside, the amenities become even more resortlike.

"Between the homes, a freeform pool curves through natural rock, hiding a grotto and a slide, with a shallow ledge for lounging and an elevated spa," according to the listing.

The property was designed by architecture firm Ike Kligerman Barkley, with the listing emphasizing the rarity of its expansive oceanfront setting.

"This bohemian luxury property is truly a unicorn. Oceanfront land like this is uncommon in Maui. Designed by Ike Kligerman Barkley. Offered fully furnished and in excellent condition," the description states.

Carrey's decision to sell comes just after he and Ah marked a major milestone in their famously private relationship.

Their marriage followed a rare public appearance together at the César Awards in Paris in February, when Carrey accepted an honorary award and offered a sweet tribute to his partner from the stage.

While accepting the honor, the comedian thanked his daughter, Jane, and grandson, Jackson, before referring to Ah as his "sublime companion" and declaring his love for her.

The couple has otherwise kept their romance largely out of the spotlight, despite reportedly having been together for several years.

The "Truman Show" star has spent significant time in Hawaii, where his waterfront Maui residence provided a dramatically different backdrop from the Los Angeles lifestyle he maintained for decades.

Reports have painted a picture of a decidedly low-key existence for the actor on the island, with Carrey spending his time reading, writing, walking, painting, and sketching.

That makes his decision to part with the property particularly notable. It remains unclear whether Carrey plans to maintain a home in Hawaii after the sale or if he will return to his California roots.

In 2022, Carrey revealed that he was "fairly serious" about stepping away from acting, explaining that he had become content with the life he had created outside the relentless pace of Hollywood.

"I really like my quiet life," he said at the time while discussing his passion for painting and his spiritual life.

Carrey had spoken about his affinity for solitude even earlier. In 2018, he described his Maui lifestyle as "an isolated life" while explaining that he enjoyed spending time alone.

His move toward a more private existence also coincided with the end of another major chapter in his real estate portfolio: his decadeslong ownership of an impressive Brentwood estate.

Carrey purchased the Los Angeles property for $3.8 million in 1994—the same year his career skyrocketed with the release of "Ace Ventura: Pet Detective," "The Mask," and "Dumb and Dumber."

Over nearly three decades of ownership, the 2-acre property became an amenity-packed private retreat.

Built in 1951, the ranch-style residence spans more than 10,000 square feet and features five bedrooms, six fireplaces, an art deco-style movie theater, and a circular sunroom.

After owning the property for nearly 30 years, Carrey decided it was time to move on. He initially listed the Brentwood estate for $28.9 million in February 2023, revealing at the time that he was no longer spending much time there.

Finding a buyer proved to be a lengthy process. The asking price was subsequently reduced to $26.5 million and then $23.95 million. In May 2024, Carrey lowered the price again to $21.9 million before trimming it to $19.75 million that September. The home ultimately sold for $17 million.

#5702. Scientists discover that cranberry juice may help fight tooth decay

Cranberry juice may offer an unexpected benefit for your teeth. New research suggests that pure, unsweetened cranberry juice can slow the growth of dental plaque and reduce the production of acids that contribute to tooth decay.

Cranberries are a familiar part of holiday celebrations. They appear in sauces, salads, and cocktails, and even serve as colorful seasonal decorations. But beyond their tart flavor and festive appeal, these small red berries contain natural compounds that may support oral health.

Christine Wu, a researcher at the University of Illinois Chicago College of Dentistry, has been investigating whether cranberry juice could help protect teeth from harmful bacteria. Her findings suggest that the popular beverage may have benefits that go beyond its traditional association with urinary tract health.

How Cranberry Juice Affects Harmful Bacteria

Cranberry juice has long been used to help prevent urinary tract infections. One reason is that cranberries contain compounds called proanthocyanidins, which have anti-inflammatory properties and can interfere with the ability of certain bacteria, including E. coli, to attach to cells.

Wu wanted to determine whether these same compounds might also affect bacteria found in dental plaque. These microorganisms feed on sugars from food and drinks, producing acids that gradually weaken tooth enamel and contribute to cavities.

Rather than testing isolated cranberry compounds, Wu chose to investigate pure cranberry juice, a product people can readily purchase and consume.

"Just like sugar damage is linked to diet, I'm interested in how the food and beverages we consume can help combat the harmful bacteria and benefit our oral health," Wu said.

To investigate the potential effects, researchers conducted a small human study involving 22 participants, including 14 children and eight adults.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of three beverages: pure, unsweetened 100% cranberry juice, a cranberry juice cocktail containing 27% juice and added sugar, or plain water.

"It was important to us to conduct these tests with human participants and use products available on the market. Most cranberry juice studies have been conducted using laboratory-prepared cranberry juice extract. Moreover, limited studies have been performed in children," said Wu, who is a professor of pediatric dentistry.

On the morning of the experiment, participants arrived with dental plaque that had accumulated overnight. Researchers first collected plaque samples using cotton swabs on one side of each participant's mouth.

After rinsing with water, participants consumed three small amounts of their assigned beverage. They swished each drink around their mouths several times before swallowing.

Thirty minutes later, researchers collected another set of plaque samples, this time from teeth that had not been swabbed earlier. Comparing the samples allowed the team to examine how each beverage affected plaque activity over the short testing period.

A Surprising Effect on Plaque and Tooth Decay

The results revealed a promising effect of pure cranberry juice. Dental plaque exposed to the unsweetened beverage showed slower regrowth than unexposed plaque samples.

Researchers also found that swishing with pure cranberry juice reduced acid production in dental plaque from both children and adults. This is particularly important because acids produced by oral bacteria can gradually erode tooth enamel, increasing the risk of cavities.

The findings suggest that cranberry juice may interfere with two important processes involved in tooth decay: the buildup of bacterial plaque and the production of damaging acids.

Wu believes these results could eventually support the development of cranberry juice as a "functional beverage" that offers benefits for oral health. The findings are especially interesting because other commonly consumed fruit juices, including orange and apple juice, have not shown the same promise in this research context.

"Most people think of cranberry juice as very sour, very acidic and sugary, and therefore may not contribute positively to oral health. This study found the opposite: that cranberry juice affected dental plaque regrowth and acid production, which may counteract some of the damage done by sugar," she said.

Could Cranberry Juice Become Part of Oral Care?

Although the findings are encouraging, the researchers emphasize that further investigation is necessary. With only 22 participants and a testing period lasting just 30 minutes after consumption, the study cannot establish whether drinking cranberry juice regularly prevents cavities or produces lasting improvements in dental health.

Larger studies conducted over longer periods will be needed to determine whether the observed changes in dental plaque translate into meaningful protection against tooth decay.

Still, Wu sees potential in occasionally using pure cranberry juice as a mouth rinse. One challenge is its intensely tart flavor, which some people may find unpleasant without added sweetness.

"But maybe by adding an appropriate sugar substitute," she said, "to make it a bit more palatable."

The research was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

#5701. Why some “lower-risk” childhood cancers turn deadly

Some childhood cancers may be far more dangerous than their initial risk classification suggests. Scientists have discovered that certain tumors considered less threatening can contain hidden populations of highly aggressive cancer cells, potentially explaining why some children experience devastating outcomes despite lacking the usual genetic warning signs.

The discovery could change how doctors identify children at risk of life-threatening cancer, allowing treatment to be better matched to the true aggressiveness of their disease.

The findings, published in Cancer Research, come from scientists at the Wellcome Sanger Institute, the University of Cambridge, Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH), University College London, and collaborating institutions. Their research focused on rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS), an aggressive cancer that develops from muscle tissue and is among the most common soft tissue cancers affecting children younger than 15. Approximately 55 children are diagnosed with the disease in the United Kingdom each year.[1]

Unlike many adult cancers, which can develop after years of aging or exposure to environmental factors, childhood cancers often result from genetic changes that occur during early development.

Why Some Childhood Cancers Defy Risk Predictions

Doctors generally divide rhabdomyosarcoma into two main categories based on whether a tumor carries a particular genetic warning sign. This marker occurs when two genes that are normally separate become fused together, creating an abnormal genetic combination associated with especially aggressive disease.[2]

Children whose tumors contain this fusion have substantially lower survival rates than those without it, even when they receive intensive treatment.

But this classification has a troubling limitation. Some children whose tumors lack the high-risk genetic marker still develop aggressive cancers that can prove fatal. Until now, scientists have struggled to explain why these supposedly less dangerous tumors sometimes behave so aggressively.

To investigate this mystery, the research team compared tumors from children with different forms of rhabdomyosarcoma, looking beyond the genetic markers traditionally used to estimate risk.

The researchers examined tumor samples from 16 children, including four whose cancers lacked the fusion marker but proved fatal, four with fusion-positive tumors, and eight children with fusion-negative disease who remained alive.

Using advanced genetic analysis, scientists studied the tumors at a level of detail that conventional techniques cannot easily achieve.

One of their main tools was single-cell RNA sequencing, a technology that measures gene activity in individual cells. Rather than examining a tumor as a single mass, this approach allows researchers to investigate the behavior of its different cell populations and identify potentially dangerous cells that might otherwise go unnoticed.

The scientists also used spatial transcriptomics, a technique that maps gene activity to specific locations within a tumor. This provided a clearer picture of where aggressive cancer cells were concentrated and how they were distributed throughout the tissue.

The results revealed a striking similarity between tumors that had previously been placed in different risk categories. Some cancers classified as non-high-risk contained cells with gene activity patterns closely resembling those found in high-risk tumors.

Even more surprisingly, these aggressive tumors did not need the same genetic mutations to produce similar behavior. Researchers identified rare genetic changes that affected many of the same cellular pathways involved in the most dangerous forms of the disease.

This suggests that different genetic abnormalities can ultimately push cancer cells toward a shared aggressive state. In other words, tumors can reach a similarly dangerous biological condition through multiple genetic routes, even when they lack the warning sign typically used to identify high-risk disease.

Dr. Karin Straathof, co-senior author at UCL Cancer Institute and GOSH, said:

"By studying tumors one cell at a time, we uncovered hidden populations of aggressive cancer cells that conventional methods miss. Although these tumors carry different genetic changes, many converge on the same aggressive pathways. This helps explain why some children who appear to have lower-risk disease can still have a devastating outcome."

A New Path Toward More Precise Cancer Treatment

The findings could have important implications for how childhood cancer is diagnosed and treated.

If doctors can identify the distinctive biological signatures of aggressive cancer cells at diagnosis, they may be able to recognize children who face a greater risk of relapse or death, even when standard genetic tests suggest otherwise.

Such an approach could also help prevent unnecessary treatment. Children with genuinely lower-risk tumors might avoid some of the harmful side effects associated with intensive chemotherapy, while those with hidden aggressive disease could receive stronger or more targeted treatment earlier.

The researchers are particularly interested in identifying markers that could be used to develop therapies aimed specifically at the most dangerous cancer cells.

One possible direction involves immunotherapy, including CAR-T cell therapy. This treatment uses specially modified immune cells to recognize and attack cancer cells. Although such treatments would require further development and testing for rhabdomyosarcoma, they could eventually offer a more precise alternative to conventional chemotherapy, potentially reducing damage to healthy tissues.

Scientists are now expanding their research to include hundreds of additional tumor samples. By studying a much larger group of patients, they hope to uncover more of the rare genetic changes capable of producing aggressive cancer and accelerate the development of personalized treatments.

Sara Wakeling, Chief Executive Officer and co-founder of Alice's Arc, said:

"Every child with cancer deserves the best possible chance of survival. We're proud to support research into rhabdomyosarcoma, showing how cutting-edge technologies can uncover the biology driving aggressive childhood cancers. These discoveries bring us closer to more personalized treatments and better outcomes for children."

Dr. Laura Danielson, Children's and Young Person's Lead at Cancer Research UK, said:

"Discovery research like this is essential to understand the unique biology of these cancers. This important study demonstrates that aggressive tumors may share similar features, even if they carry different genetic changes. By helping researchers understand what these high-risk cancers have in common, this work adds a vital piece to the puzzle and could help guide future efforts to improve treatment for children and young people with rhabdomyosarcoma."

Rethinking How Doctors Identify Dangerous Childhood Cancers

Beyond its potential treatment applications, the discovery challenges a fundamental assumption about how rhabdomyosarcoma should be classified.

Instead of viewing aggressive disease primarily through the presence or absence of one genetic abnormality, the researchers suggest that doctors may need to consider the broader biological state of the cancer cells themselves.

This distinction is important because tumors with different mutations can behave in remarkably similar ways. Identifying the shared features of aggressive disease could provide a more reliable way to recognize children who need intensive treatment, regardless of the particular genetic changes driving their tumors.

Professor Sam Behjati, co-senior author formerly at the Wellcome Sanger Institute and Head of the Department of Paediatrics at the University of Cambridge, said:

"This work changes how we think about rhabdomyosarcoma. Rather than a single, abnormal gene, we've shown that there is an overarching cell state of aggressive disease that defies conventional classification systems. Understanding this shared biology could help identify children who need more intense treatment to improve their survival."

Although further research is needed before these findings can change routine clinical care, they provide a promising foundation for more accurate risk assessments and treatments tailored to each child's cancer.

By revealing aggressive behavior hidden beneath seemingly reassuring genetic classifications, scientists hope to improve survival for children with the most dangerous tumors while sparing others from treatment they may not need.

The research received support through a Cancer Research UK -- Children with Cancer UK Innovation Award, with additional co-funding from Alice's Arc and funding from Wellcome.

Even in its third season, HGTV’s “Scariest House in America” is able to continue unearthing the most unsettling homes in the country—and transform them into gorgeous abodes the owners are proud to call home.

After touring a whopping 20 terrifying properties across the country, interior designer Alison Victoria and comedian Retta have finally decided which home takes the cake for spookiest: a spine-chilling former nursing home in Harrisburg, PA, where the homeowners have reported a series of suspicious experiences.

Upon moving into the home from their previous dwelling in Vermont, Donovan claimed that “strange things started happening almost immediately,” and told Penn Live that the family witnessed unexplained noises, water pouring from the kitchen cabinets, and even their dryer setting ablaze.

In one particularly unusual moment, the owners told camera crews that “there were wet footprints leading from the side of the tub, and the tub was dry.”

When speaking to “Good Day PA,” Donovan said the family “immediately loved” the property when they first toured it, and even noted “the spooky stuff never really bothered” them.

“There was no aggression. It was just weird stuff,” said Herzig.

Still, there was room for improvement. The family was awarded a $150,000 home makeover, where the “Sin City Rehab” host stepped in to switch up the home’s dated layout, give it a fresh color palette, and renovate the bathrooms.

The renovation also included a refashioning of what the family agrees is the “most haunted room of all”—their daughter, Aoife Herzing's, bedroom, which was brightened up with playful floral wallpaper.

Herzig and Donovan recalled having just 48 hours to relocate to a temporary rental after learning their home had won the title of “Scariest House in America,” and spent the summer away from home so Victoria could step in and flex her design skills.

Although Herzig noted that they were not active participants in the renovation, they were asked to share their “design preferences” with HGTV, and to flag what to avoid and which items they “really want to keep” at the home.

The home's exterior was painted sage green—a vibrant upgrade from the dreary white siding it showcased previously.

“This is truly the scariest part of ‘Scariest House in America’ for me: painting someone’s entire house,” Victoria said.

While the decision was difficult for her to make, the TV personality ultimately landed on the hue she chose for a very good reason.

“Green is a very statement color that gives classic Victorian vibes,” she said.

The previously dark and dismal kitchen was brightened up with a calm, neutral color palette and fresh furnishings. It also received an upgrade to its functionality with a new range and hood, plus plenty of storage.

Victoria and Retta found some antique corbels to bring character to the large parlor space that the owners said had been underutilized. The room also received a custom mantel and a pair of vintage chandeliers.

The primary suite may still be the site of “footsteps and giggling” that the owners can’t quite pinpoint, but it also now boasts a recently added walk-in closet and a rich forest green color palette.

The en suite bathroom takes a modern approach to Victorian style, with vintage-inspired sconces framing a moody freestanding tub.

To make better use of the room’s space, Victoria also relocated the sauna—which was previously housed indoors—to a spot out back, where the landscaping also got some love.

The process also included restoration of the home’s original hardwood floors—an element Herzig was thrilled to see renewed.

#5698. 42AI launches with $62.5M to predict how traders act when markets turn volatile

Israeli artificial intelligence startup 42AI launched today with $62.5 million in funding to build what it calls a behavioral world model.

Its first customers are brokerages that want to know how individual traders will act when markets turn volatile. 42AI offers software that estimates the odds of each choice a person might make in a given situation. “Behavior is not deterministic; it’s constantly probabilistic,” co-founder and Chief Executive Amit Gal-Or told TechCrunch.

The company turns what it knows about a person into mathematical representations of personality traits, and a transformer-based world model works out the probabilities from there. A separate language model writes up which traits and context drove each prediction.

42AI says a brokerage can see what each client is likely to trade over the next 24 hours, including the instrument, the direction and the volume. If clients look set to pile into the same trade, a risk desk can hedge before the exposure lands on its book. Know-your-customer checks done at onboarding are one source of input, and the model also weighs how often a client calls and the sentiment in their voice.

Ten large brokerages are working with 42AI, which charges either a flat fee or a percentage of the value it helps generate. Revenue has reached seven figures, Gal-Or said, without giving a precise number.

By the company’s account, one brokerage gained about $30 million in additional value through dynamic hedging. The company also claims 98% accuracy on trades. That figure tracks whether trading flows land inside a predicted range, according to Gal-Or, and does not measure whether every individual trade was predicted correctly.

Three years of research went into the model. Thousands of people took psychological assessments in the first study, and by the time the team moved on to government and biobank datasets, the sample had passed 2 million. Customer data now spans about 30 million people.

Chief Technology Officer Ehud Ezra and three co-authors described one piece of the work in a paper posted in February. Their Large Behavioral Model adapts an 8 billion-parameter version of Meta Platforms Inc.’s Llama 3.1 to predict a person’s strategic choices from a detailed psychometric profile.

Asked whether a brokerage could turn those predictions against its own clients, Ezra called it “a valid concern.” The founders pointed to regulation, monitoring and an internal ethics committee as checks on that kind of use.

Gaming, fraud prevention and cybersecurity are the next markets 42AI is exploring, with helping robots and AI agents understand people as a longer-term goal. Wherever it runs, the model loses accuracy when it misses outside influences, such as a trader acting on a colleague’s advice. “There’s a natural ceiling because you really don’t have access to everything that a person experiences,” Gal-Or said.

The $62.5 million, which 42AI describes as seed funding, came from the founders and Infinity Group over three years. Amir Gal-Or, the startup’s co-founder and chairman, founded Infinity Group. Dan Shechtman, who won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, is among the advisers to the research team. 42AI plans to raise more money.

#5697. ‘Homestead’ Actor Bailey Chase Reveals the ‘Final Straw’ That Inspired a Move to a North Carolina Home That Wouldn’t Have Been ‘Affordable’ in L.A.

“Homestead” actor Bailey Chase is one of the many celebrities who have quit Los Angeles in pursuit of a slower pace, and he has recently opened up about his family’s decision-making process.

The “Buffy the Vampire Slayer” alum, 54, moved to North Carolina five years ago with his wife, Amy, 50, daughter Waverly, 12, and twins Maggie and Gauge, 10.

In a Nov. 2 interview with Fox News Digital, Chase explained that the cross-country move came in “the throes of COVID.”

“My wife and I picked up sticks with our three young children when they were mandating vaccines out there,” he said. “They couldn’t go back to school without it, and that was the final straw. And we’ve been in the mountains of North Carolina ever since, living our best life.”

Although Chase’s work schedule keeps him busy—and he films “Homestead” on an estate in North Salt Lake, UT—the father of three said keeping up with his children is his priority.

“I love my job, and when I’m off filming, I’m 100% focused on that. But when I’m home, I’m home. There’s no greater job than being a dad,” he said.

Chase’s kids are enrolled in a slate of activities that he was excited to discuss.

“I’m like soccer dad right now. It’s soccer season, so we’re going here and there,” he shared. “My oldest is really into ballet, and I couldn’t be more proud of her and getting ready for ‘The Nutcracker’ in December, and basketball season’s around the corner.”

The family currently resides in Amy’s hometown of Hendersonville, NC—a move they always knew was in the cards. The town is in the Blue Ridge Mountains, located 25 miles south of Asheville.

Chase admitted that it was a “hard decision” to leave California behind and “give up” on the “dream” of living in Los Angeles.

“But we haven’t looked back,” he explained.

In an Aug. 12 Instagram post celebrating his daughter’s first day of seventh grade, Chase shared some reflections on his family’s daily life, noting that he had “taken some time away from social media” and “even passed on some work” to “focus on his family.”

“The great news is we created lifelong memories going on vacations and just being present,” he wrote. “Our oldest started school today and the twins have been back for a few weeks. We also had dear friends and family in town but now shift into our routines of school, practice, home and repeat.”

Alongside a photo of himself posed with his daughter on a sports field, he added, “I’m loving this chapter of life and know it will fly by, so doing my best to enjoy every moment before work calls again.”

#5696. Anthropic’s quarterly revenue jumps to $17B, losses grow ahead of IPO

Anthropic PBC today published an updated version of the S-1 filing for its upcoming public offering.

The original document, which the company released last Monday, didn’t contain its third-quarter financial results. The new version reveals that Anthropic generated $17 billion in revenue during the three months ended Sept. 30. That’s more than 11 times more than what it made a year earlier, but represents a deacceleration in quarter-over-quarter growth. Anthropic’s top line grew 47% on a quarterly basis, down from 144% three months earlier.

The artificial intelligence provider faces multipronged competition from open-source models, OpenAI Group PBC and tech giants such as Google LLC. The Alphabet Inc.’s newest model, Gemini 4 Carbon, outperforms Claude Opus 5.5 across multiple benchmarks.

Anthropic is investing heavily in training infrastructure to stay ahead of the competition. The company took a $5 billion charge in the third quarter because demand for computing hardware was higher than expected, which required it to purchase hardware at a premium. Hardware bought on short notice is more expensive than Anthropic’s usual capacity commitments, which it books 12 to 18 months before they’re needed.

The AI provider also took a $2 billion charge in connection with its non-cash employee donation matching program. That left Anthropic with a $536 million operating loss at the end of the third quarter. Three months earlier, it posted $974 million in operating income. Anthropic’s adjusted operating income, which excludes stock-based compensation and charitable contributions, jumped by $300 million on a quarterly basis to $2.5 billion.

The company had $895.4 billion in outstanding infrastructure commitments as of Sept 30. Leases signed with Google LLC and Broadcom Inc. accounted for nearly a third of that sum. In April, the two companies agreed to supply Anthropic with several gigawatts of computing power powered by the search giant’s TPU chips, which Broadcom helped design. The AI provider also has computing deals with Amazon.com Inc., Oracle Corp. and SpaceX Technologies Corp. that are each worth more than $100 billion.

Anthropic plans to not only rent more computing capacity but also build its own data centers. The company’s purchase commitments jumped from $55 billion at the end of 2025 to about $314 billion in the third quarter.

Alongside the new financial figures, Anthropic’s revised S-1 filing provides an update about its efforts to mitigate AI risks. According to the document, the company is considering “to require human review and approval of certain” research tasks that are currently performed automatically by its models. It believes that its models will soon be capable of “dramatically” accelerating AI development.

Anthropic hasn’t yet disclosed how much it plans to raise through its public offering. According to Bloomberg, the company hopes to at least match the $86.2 billion that SpaceX pulled in when it listed its shares earlier this year. Reuters reported that Anthropic is seeking a valuation of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion.

#5695. Rebecca Gayheart Reveals Shock of Eric Dane’s Death—and How They Made His Hospital Room Feel Like Home in His Final Moments

Eric Dane's estranged wife, Rebecca Gayheart, has lifted the lid on the shock that came with the actor's death, revealing that she had "no idea that was it."

While speaking to NBC's Maria Shriver on Nov. 3—the same day the late Hollywood star's memoir, "My Book of Days," hit shelves—Gayheart, 55, reflected on the final moments of Dane's life.

The actor, was diagnosed with the degenerative neurological disease in April 2025 and died on the afternoon of Feb. 19, 2026. Gayheart confessed that she and their two daughters, Billie and Georgia, "never, ever anticipated" that he would pass away when he did.

“He had gone to the hospital so many times before, and they would patch him up, so to speak, and he would come home,” Gayheart explained. “And he’d be OK. And we’d go back to the normal routine, which did change week by week.”

She then recalled her estranged husband's first day in the hospital during his first trip there.

“I said, ‘Listen, I’ll be back. I have a dinner. I’m going to this event.’ I had no idea that that was it, that that week was going to be our last week,” Gayheart revealed. “And nor did my daughters. It really took a few days for us to understand the gravity of what that last trip to the hospital meant.”

She noted that she and their daughters began to realize how bad things had become a few days into the hospital visit.

“I think it was like day three in the hospital where it shifted. Everything shifted. Just the tone of when the doctors were talking to us, and some of the information we were given," Gayheart said.

At the same time, Dane was also beginning to come to terms with his last days.

“He was fully aware it was shifting, and he was still communicating with us. Not well verbally, but I could understand him most of the time. The kids could most of the time, his closest friends," she revealed.

Meanwhile, friends of Dane and Gayheart helped her through the emotional turmoil as she struggled with "decision fatigue."

“It was figuring it out as we went, but I remember the moment Eric decided to make some choices, and he did. ... He was in control of the way he was going to leave," she said.

Because they couldn't set up their usual family sleepover at home, they brought everything they needed to the hospital to ensure they could spend Dane's final moments with him.

“The girls and I just camped out there with him, and we had our family sleepovers, and we brought in those little candles that aren’t real candles. They have batteries. And we played his favorite music, and we tried to make it as nice as you can be in the hospital room," she revealed.

Although they cherished their final moments with Dane, Gayheart revealed she wasn't prepared for how quickly the time to say goodbye came.

“A lot of people will say, ‘Well, at least you knew, and you could have those last conversations.' But we didn’t know, because there is no road map. No one can tell you what the journey looks like because it’s so different for every patient. He was becoming more alive mentally, but losing all of his physical abilities. And for the girls, that was really hard to watch as well. But overall, it’s a blur, because it was just so overwhelming," she said.

Dane was meant to meet with Shriver shortly before his death; however, they had to reschedule their plans because the actor wasn't feeling well and mere days later, Dane died.

In Dane's memoir, which was released Nov. 3, he revealed he was initially diagnosed with multifocal motor neuropathy, a treatable autoimmune condition, just months before he received his ALS diagnosis.

Speaking about the book, Gayheart previously told People, she was “grateful he did, because it gives my girls the opportunity to know their dad as a human being.”

In the days leading up to his death, the family found comfort in familiar routines, eating sushi, watching movies, and gathering for game nights.

“We tried to be present through all of our fear and frustration and uncertainty. It was truly an exhausting and heartbreaking experience, but it also showed us his extraordinary strength every day, and that was really wonderful for the girls and myself to witness,” she told People.

In an excerpt previously published by the outlet, Dane recalled the devastating phone call in which he told Gayheart about his diagnosis.

“I say to Rebecca on the phone, ‘It’s what we feared.’ I don’t remember a single word I said after that,” he wrote.

Despite their separation, Dane made clear that he and Gayheart remained a family.

The “Grey’s Anatomy” actor described the news as a “violent impact,” comparing the feeling to “getting the wind knocked out of me.”

As he struggled to process the diagnosis, he recalled hearing Gayheart “wailing on the other end of the phone.”

“My sobs make my body shudder, and I hear her words pouring out amid her tears, ‘I’m here, we’ll fight this together, I’m not going anywhere,’” he wrote.

Throughout the memoir, Dane described how his daughters gave him a sense of purpose as he faced the disease.

“I’m going to show my girls how to walk through this life with grace and dignity, no matter what. I am going to FIGHT. This has become my purpose. My reason. This is now my job,” he wrote.

Dane's death was revealed in a statement by his representatives.

“He spent his final days surrounded by dear friends, his devoted wife, and his two beautiful daughters, Billie and Georgia, who were the center of his world.

Following his death, many of his celebrity friends have come forward to lay bare the actor's final moments.

Dane and and Gayheart, 54, tied the knot in 2004, and share daughters Billie Beatrice, 15, and Georgia Geraldine, 13.

Gayheart filed for divorce from Dane in 2018. However, in March 2025, just one month before the "Grey's Anatomy" alum announced his diagnosis, she dismissed the filing.

While speaking on the podcast "Broad Ideas," Gayheart had opened up about the state of their relationship, insisting that she will always be there to support Dane, even though their marriage had ended.

“We’ve been separated for eight years. The kids live with me 100% of the time. There’s been lots of just stuff, other stuff,” she told hosts Rachel Bilson and Olivia Allen.

She added that it is important for her to be a "role model" for her daughters, particularly in how she treats her former spouse.

“I am definitely trying to show them that we show up for people, no matter what. He is our family. He is your father. We show up, and we try to do it with some dignity and some grace and just get through it and that we will get through it the best we can," she said.

Gayheart noted that she was staying afloat and helping her loved ones by trying to "stay optimistic."

ALS, also known as Lou Gehrig's disease, is a disorder that affects nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord, according to the ALS Association.

For around 90% of cases of ALS, there is no known family history or a genetic mutation linked to ALS.

For 5% to 10% of cases, there is a family history of the disease. This is often referred to as familial ALS.

There is currently no known cure for ALS. However, there are FDA-approved medications that may help slow down the progression of the disease.

After sharing his diagnosis, Dane closely guarded many of the details of his medical battle.

According to his IMDB page, the actor had three projects that were due to be released: "Euphoria" Season 3, which premiered April 12, 2026; a 13-episode thriller called "Countdown"; and a movie called "Family Secrets."

Dane rose to stardom after appearing in ABC's hit medical drama "Grey's Anatomy," where he played the role of Dr. Mark Sloan, who was often referred to as "McSteamy."

At the time of his death, Dane was believed to be residing in a three-bedroom, three-bathroom pad that spans 2,265 square feet, which he snapped up with Gayheart in 2000 for $949,000.

Kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. She previously wrote for Daily Mail, True Urban Culture, and JMedia Corporation, where she specialized in covering celebrities, relationships, psychology, and gender issues. She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. When she isn’t updating readers on A-listers' moves, she is spending time with her cat, Mary, and cheering on the Albanian soccer team.

#5694. Rack-scale AI: How Dell and AMD are building infrastructure

Dell Technologies Inc. and its partner Advanced Micro Devices Inc. face similar competitive pressures. Both tech powerhouses operate in a business climate where success is now measured across central processing units, graphics processing units, rack-scale systems, memory capacity, network bandwidth and tokens per dollar.

The pressure to compete across those measures underscores what theCUBE Research has termed “Engineering Velocity.” Since the Dell Technologies World event in May, AMD and Dell have not slowed their pace of collaborations and announcements.

AMD and Dell are working to build enterprise AI infrastructure that can keep pace with changing workloads and customer requirements.

“In AI infrastructure, the winner may not be the company with the best benchmark on keynote day,” said theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante. “It will more likely be the company whose engineering system learns, validates and improves the entire platform faster than anyone else.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of the architectural shifts powering continuous, production-grade AI. Be sure to check out theCUBE’s “Dell AI Data Platform Event: From Ambition to AI at Scale” and its past coverage of this year’s Dell Technologies World. (* Disclosure below.)

A cornerstone of the Dell and AMD relationship is the server giant’s PowerEdge portfolio. Dell expanded its PowerEdge server line in May and has followed that up with additional details surrounding the integration of AMD processors.

The two companies have pursued a strategy designed to facilitate server consolidation as agentic AI drives a surge in demand for general-purpose compute. Agents rely heavily on CPUs, yet data centers don’t have a lot of extra room to add servers in rooms already stacked with GPUs.

Systems powered by AMD processors will deliver 70% gen-over-gen performance gains and can fold 13 servers from Dell’s 14th PowerEdge generation into one, according to Pradyumna Narendra, product planner and senior consultant at Dell.

“For every 10 to 13 servers you replace, you get so much of that productivity gain back because now you can do that with one server,” he told theCUBE. “When you expand that across data centers, that’s like an accelerating effect that you get to capitalize from.”

Dell and AMD must also accommodate a wealth of AI use cases and the accompanying demand for compute. Dell’s three-rack-unit server requires less power for cooling than a two-unit equivalent, allowing customers to pack more computing power into each rack, according to Narendra.

“By deploying servers that are slightly larger in package, you deliver more density at a rack level, which seems sometimes counterintuitive,” he explained. “As AI accelerates, inferencing and agentic AI around it will accelerate and grow faster. As these use cases scale out, you get exponential growth in the need for compute.”

Beyond server consolidation, Dell and AMD have been steadily enhancing a modular solution to simplify AI deployment and scaling: the Dell AI Platform with AMD.

The on-premises enterprise AI solution integrates AMD Instinct accelerators and EPYC processors with Dell PowerEdge servers, PowerSwitch networking and PowerScale storage for model training, fine-tuning and high-throughput inference. The platform is designed to let customers begin with configurations that meet current workloads and expand compute and GPU density over time, without rearchitecting.

“What we’re finding is customers want modular solutions. They want to think about [solutions] across the whole platform,” said Varun Chhabra, senior vice president of product marketing and infrastructure solutions group at Dell, in a discussion with theCUBE. “Compute, storage, networking [and] GPU. The software framework on top of it, the models: Have they all been tested? Have they all been validated?”

Dell has integrated the AMD ROCm software stack into the platform to support training, fine-tuning and serving large language models on-premises. The modular platform lets customers begin with smaller deployments and expand on the same infrastructure, according to Chhabra.

“You can start small with these composable units of storage, compute, networking, pre-integrated with AMD Instinct and EPYC CPUs with the ROCm software as well as the open ecosystem that sits on top of it,” he said. “We test it, we validate it, and the customers can use it and once they start seeing value in it, they know they can scale in a modular way with the same frameworks.”

Dell announced support for AMD Instinct MI350P PCI Express GPUs in its PowerEdge XE7745 and R7725 servers beginning in July, giving enterprises another option for scaling agentic and generative AI deployments. It also represents an important boost in memory bandwidth which matters in time-to-first-token latency.

The MI350P offers 144 gigabytes of HBM3E memory, which can be a key differentiator for inference performance, according to Mike Darby, senior manager of business development, Instinct Data Center GPUs, at AMD, during an appearance on theCUBE.

“It’s a lot of memory, but it’s also HBM3E, so [it has] an amazing amount of bandwidth,” he said. “The main use case being inference: It’s all about that latency, time to first token [and] the user experience, so that your attention span doesn’t move somewhere else while you’re waiting for your response.”

AMD and Dell’s collaboration on PCIe integration has another angle worth watching. AMD’s PCIe-based GPU supports air-cooled deployments, providing users with a path to deploy AI within existing data center infrastructure.

As the tech industry has encountered resistance in recent months to the buildout of large data centers across the U.S., concerns have centered on the environmental impact and use of water-based cooling systems. Separately, Dell found that, as it deployed its next-generation PowerEdge servers, some enterprise customers were still not prepared to adopt liquid cooling within data centers.

“Working with Dell, we added a PCI card to our air-coolable roadmap for GPU Instinct so that it fit in more Dell PowerEdge servers that go to the broader enterprise,” said Robert Hormuth, corporate vice president of architecture and strategy for the Data Center Solutions Group at AMD, during a conversation with theCUBE. “Not everybody is adopting direct liquid cooling.”

Dell’s work with AMD this year has extended beyond joint product announcements. In June, the two companies announced a partnership with the University of Cambridge to establish a Sovereign AI Innovation Lab (SAIL) in the United Kingdom.

The collaboration is designed to help advance the next generation of AI infrastructure and AI-powered scientific breakthroughs. It builds on Cambridge’s expanded AI research infrastructure, including the Zenith AI supercomputer, powered by fifth-generation AMD EPYC processors and AMD Instinct MI355X GPU accelerators integrated into Dell infrastructure.

Dell and AMD have also collaborated in recent months on a telecom initiative with AT&T Inc. Telecom data is a heavy lift when it comes to AI, with AT&T having processed over one trillion tokens to train models. AMD has provided the high-performance hardware foundation for both training and inference workloads involving the OTel 2.0 models developed through the Open Telco AI initiative.

Dell integrated this technology with AI-optimized servers for telecom environments to create a production-grade foundation for operators across data-intensive, real-world network environments. OTel 2.0’s training infrastructure uses Dell’s PowerEdge XE9785 server configured with eight MI355X GPUs.

The alliance between Dell and AMD highlights a key development in the growing AI infrastructure market: There are plenty of opportunities for competition. Both Dell and AMD appear committed to building portfolios that offer enterprise choices in AI processing solutions.

“AMD didn’t present its new products … as ‘respectable alternatives,’” Vellante said. “It claimed outright leadership across CPUs, GPUs, rack-scale performance, memory capacity, network bandwidth and tokens per dollar. It extended the argument across enterprise AI, robotics, ultra-low-latency inference and a rapidly expanding partner ecosystem.”

(* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the Dell AI Data Platform Event. Neither Dell, the sponsor of theCUBE’s event coverage, nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)

#5693. Confused by Home Price Headlines? Here’s Why.

Whether you own a house already or you’re looking to buy one, you probably care about home prices. But it’s not always easy to figure out what’s really happening right now, especially if you look at the headlines.

One says home prices are falling. The next says they’re still climbing.

So, which one’s right? It comes down to where you live.

Part of the confusion out there may be based on what’s happening to asking prices and how the media is talking about it. They’re calling attention to how asking prices are falling, but don’t give the full context or say that seasonality is at play. So here it is.

Right now, there are more homes on the market than at any other time since November 2019. And with mortgage rates rising since the spring, those homes are taking a little longer to sell. One way to help a home sell quickly in that environment is to have a lower asking price.

According to HousingWire Data, the median asking price is down from $449k in early August to $435k just 2 months later (see graph below):

That’s a dip of about 3%, and a lot of it is normal for this time of year.

Asking prices cool off every fall once the busy summer season wraps up. With fewer buyers this time of year, sellers price a bit more competitively. Today’s rates play a role too, since sellers are pricing to match what buyers can afford right now. And that’s a good thing. Smart pricing helps homes sell.

Just keep in mind, that’s a national list price. It doesn’t show what homes near you are actually selling for. So before you react to a headline, ask a local agent what’s really happening in your area.

“While national headlines might suggest a buyer’s market is taking hold, the reality on the ground depends heavily on where and what you’re trying to buy. Local trends can diverge sharply from national averages, especially when you factor in price range, property type, and post-pandemic market dynamics.”

The latest numbers from S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Index show how true that is. Over the past year, sales prices in Chicago rose almost 7%. In Seattle, they dipped about 1.6%. That’s a gap of nearly 9 percentage points between two major cities (see graph below):

That gap changes your game plan. Selling in New York, where prices are up almost 6%? You may not need to cut your price. Buying in Denver or Las Vegas? You may have more room to negotiate.

Just in case you’re seeing those slight declines in some markets and worried it means a bigger crash is coming, here’s what you need to remember. Even in the major metros where prices are down, the declines are 2% or less. That’s a long way from a crash like 2008. And if you look back at the graph above, there are more cities in the green than in the red.

And over time, home values have a strong track record. The Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) says national prices have grown year-over-year every quarter since 2012. Go back further, and a $100k home bought in 1991 would be worth about $436k today, even with the 2008 crash factored in (see graph below):

So, this short-term dip probably won’t stick around. The small declines we’re seeing now are in markets that overheated during the pandemic. As a whole, the market is headed back to normal – and normal means prices should rise over time.

National headlines can’t tell you what your home is worth or how much room you have to negotiate. Local data can. If you’re thinking about buying or selling, connect with a local real estate agent to look at how prices are moving in your area, so you can set your price or make your offer with confidence.

#5692. Trump Remains ‘Laser-Focused’ on Housing Affordability Despite Final Midterm Speech on DC Reflecting Pool, White House Says

In his final message to voters ahead to the pivotal midterm elections, President Donald Trump touted renovations to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool without uttering a word about housing affordability. Still, the White House says he remains squarely focused on the issue.

"President Trump has been laser-focused on making housing more affordable," White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Realtor.com® in a statement.

Ingle noted that Trump in his second term had signed an executive order prohibiting large Wall Street firms from purchasing single-family homes, directed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to purchase $200 billion in mortgage bonds that helped drive rates to four-year lows, and "cut unnecessary red tape at a historic pace to boost supply, speed construction, and lower costs."

"The President will not stop fighting until the American Dream of homeownership is within reach for every American, which is why he continues to sign bold new executive orders and calls on Congress to pass further legislation," he said.

During his speech on Monday evening by the reflecting pool in the heart of Washington, DC, Trump spoke at length and in exhaustive detail about the extensive repairs to leaky pipes, surface coating, and cracked granite.

"This is a massive piece of pool," Trump told an audience of several dozen people gathered for the unveiling of the refurbished monument, which has been one of his signature projects since the opening months of his second term.

Trump reiterated claims that the pool had been vandalized by "sick" saboteurs. However, federal prosecutors and the U.S. Attorney's Office for DC previously acknowledged in court filings that the damage to the pool lining that accompanied massive algae blooms was the product of shoddy installation by contractors rushing to complete the job before the 250th Independence Day festivities.

Beyond his breakdown of the pool makeover, which is projected to cost taxpayers about $16 million, Trump touted his record in his second White House term, claiming that his administration had reduced crime in DC by "close to 90%," carried out sweeping beautification projects, and cleared out homeless encampments.

It was not until 23 minutes into his address that Trump finally mentioned the looming midterm election, which will determine control of Congress and could shape the final two years of his time in the White House.

"This is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm, I believe in our lifetime," said the president.

The stakes could hardly be higher: control of the U.S. Senate and House, dozens of governorships, crucial ballot measures on housing, and the legislative direction of the second half of Trump's term.

Final preelection polling showed Democrats holding a meaningful advantage in the generic congressional ballot and leading in several key Senate battlegrounds, including Michigan, Texas, and Maine, driven by widespread voter frustration with the surging costs of fuel, groceries, and housing.

While Trump did not bring up affordability in his remarks, Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum, who joined him at the event in DC, briefly touched upon the subject, arguing that Trump's policies have paved the way to "food security, more grazing for our country, more timber production for affordable homes, and more oil and gas to drive the price and affordability of energy down in our country."

This fall, average 30-year mortgage rates surged back past the 7% mark, propelled by surging oil prices linked to the president's ongoing war in Iran, severely eroding homebuyers' purchasing power.

The broader cost-of-living squeeze has not gone unnoticed by the electorate across the political spectrum, prompting Trump to hit the campaign trail in traditional Republican strongholds like Texas and South Carolina to shore up support for vulnerable GOP candidates.

Yet in his concluding remarks on the eve of the election, the president struck an uncharacteristically fatalistic tone and appeared resigned to a potential "blue wave."

"Usually whoever the sitting president is—Republican or Democrat, good or bad, good president, great president, bad—for some reason, the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms," he said. "But we gave this a very strong shot."

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5691. To Sell or Rent? How To Choose the Best Path for Your House.

Selling your house is a big step, and you want it to go smoothly. And with houses taking a little longer to sell these days, renting it out might start to sound like a nice backup plan.

But the reality is, while renting can work well for some people, it’s also a big commitment. So before you decide, it helps to see the whole picture first.

Lately, some sellers are choosing to hang on to their houses and rent them out instead. According to Parcl, around 9% of homes for rent right now were previously up for sale.

Some homeowners put their houses on the market expecting a faster process than they got or a certain price buyers didn’t respond to. And when things didn’t go exactly as planned, they decided to rent instead. As Kara Ng, Senior Economist at Zillow, explains:

“Bargaining power is tilting toward buyers and homes are taking longer to sell, making renting out a property one way to buy time rather than compete aggressively on price.”

But here’s the important distinction. Just because some sellers are choosing to rent doesn’t mean selling isn’t working. In many cases, the difference comes down to how well a house is priced, prepared, and marketed for today’s buyers.

Parcl data shows where these “accidental landlords” – owners who planned to sell but decided to rent instead – are most common (see graph below):

They make up around 17% of homes for rent in places like Sherman and Houston, TX, but less than 4% in markets like Des Moines, IA and Bloomington, IN.

That’s a pretty big difference. And it shows why you have to know what’s happening in your neighborhood. Your market, your asking price, and your strategy all play a role in how your sale goes.

A local agent can show you how houses like yours are selling, what strategies work best, and help you weigh your options – not to push you to sell, but so you at least have the full picture based on today’s market. And part of making an informed decision is understanding what renting your house would actually take.

While renting might sound like easy passive income on paper, in practice, it’s a hands-on job with rules to follow. As Invest West Management puts it:

“Even if you never intended to become a landlord, the law still sees you as one — and you must meet all legal obligations that come with that role. This often includes registering the tenancy, providing tenants with certain disclosures, and ensuring the property meets safety standards.”

You’d also be the one chasing missed rent payments, fixing damage between tenants, and covering unexpected repairs. Not to mention fielding weekend calls about leaky dishwashers or broken AC units.

There are expenses beyond regular maintenance and repairs, too. According to Bankrate, these are a few of the biggest:

Insurance premiums (landlord insurance typically costs about 25% more than a standard homeowners policy)

Management fees (if you hire a property manager, they usually charge around 10% of the rent)

Gaps between tenants, when you pay the mortgage without rental income

If you want to be a landlord and you’re prepared for the responsibility, renting may be a great fit. But if you’d really rather sell, don’t let today’s market convince you that you can’t.

A great agent can make it happen. The key is having an open conversation up front with your agent about pricing and how to market your house. Nailing those details from day 1 helps your house make a great first impression, so renting doesn’t have to be your fallback.

Renting can be a good fit for the right person with the right house, but it isn’t the only option. A smart sales strategy can help your house stand out to buyers from day one.So, if you’re on the fence, a local real estate agent can help you compare what selling and renting would each look like for you.

#5690. Apple’s stock drops as new CEO John Ternus delivers his first earnings call

Apple Inc. just delivered its first earnings call since new Chief Executive John Ternus took over the company from Tim Cook on Sept. 1, and the results beat expectations on the top and bottom lines. But the company missed expectations on iPhone sales and offered disappointing guidance going forward, and the stock fell in late trading.

The company reported fourth-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $2.10 per share, comfortably ahead of Wall Street’s target of $1.99 per share. Revenue for the period rose 12%, to $114.48 billion, easing past the $113.39 billion analyst forecast. All told, its net income came to $30.71 billion at the end of the quarter, up from just $27.46 billion one year earlier.

When Ternus (pictured) stepped up to relieve Cook in the CEO’s chair a couple of months ago, he realized he was stepping into a job with sky-high expectations, following in the footsteps of two of the most successful company leaders in American history. Steve Jobs was credited with revolutionizing consumer devices, while Cook took the company to spectacular new heights thanks to his operational expertise, establishing it as one of the world’s most iconic brands.

The weight of expectations is reflected by Apple’s enormous valuation. According to Oppenheimer analyst Martin Yang, the iPhone maker is trading at about 36 times next year’s expected earnings. That represents a premium compared with the rest of the technology market, even though its earnings are only expected to grow 1% this year, slower than many of its peers.

Nonetheless, investors have piled into Apple because it’s something of an outlier in the artificial intelligence boom. While its rivals are all spending hundreds of billions of dollars on building data centers, Apple has remained extremely capital-efficient, pouring cash into share buybacks and dividends for shareholders. That has given the company a strong margin for safety, but its position could still be threatened if Ternus can’t find a way to speed up Apple’s innovation engine.

The company has already been criticized for its lackluster performance in AI. Its long-awaited Siri AI chatbot finally arrived during the past quarter, but it came across as stale the moment it arrived. By the time it had launched, it had already been surpassed by autonomous AI agents such as Dots and Muse that can perform multistep tasks on behalf of users, while Siri is still fumbling around with answering questions.

Analysts wanted to know if Apple is planning to offer more AI features through subscriptions or services, but Ternus declined to reveal what the company’s future plans are. But he insisted that Apple has “lots of opportunities” for monetization in future. “One example is the hardware side, right?” he said. “It offers a compelling reason for upgrading or switching.”

Jacob Bourne of Emarketer told SiliconANGLE that Apple’s stock premium is likely linked to the growing concerns some investors have over the enormous cost and uncertain returns of the AI boom, which is being driven by all of Apple’s big tech peers. “Its tepid approach to AI infrastructure spending has helped to preserve its cash flow, and through strategic partnerships Apple may be able to strengthen its AI capabilities without taking on the same financial risks as its peers,” Bourne said. “But Apple faces its own challenges as AI-enabled devices such as smart glasses could eventually challenge the iPhone’s central role in iOS. Apple’s long-term advantage will hinge on combining its hardware strengths with compelling AI capabilities in a way that preserves its reputation.”

In the meantime, the pressure is on for Apple to give consumers more reasons to buy its expensive devices, especially as the costs of those products have been getting higher. Today’s report was the first full quarter of higher-priced Apple products following a price hike in June that stemmed from the rising cost of memory supplies and other components.

The price of most iPhone handsets was hiked by around $100, but consumers didn’t appear to punish Apple. On the contrary, iPhone revenue was a bright spot, reaching $57.58 billion in the quarter, up 17% from a year earlier and above the $56.54 billion consensus estimate. That’s despite the quarter including only eight days of new iPhone 18 Pro sales and none of the new flagship device, the iPhone Duo.

Apple needed a good quarter from the iPhone because its main growth engine, the services business, is slowing. Revenue there came to $31.57 billion, just below the Street’s forecast of $31.58 billion, growing less than 10% during the quarter, its slowest rate of growth since September 2022. The business includes revenue from a wide range of products and services, such as iCloud storage, AppleCare warranties, App Store fees and licensing revenue from Google LLC for putting its search engine as the default option in the Safari browser.

“We saw strong performance in many service categories, with all-time records in video, cloud services, payment services and advertising, and a September quarter record in music,” Tetanus told analysts.

Apple saw a better performance in its Mac computer division, with sales of $10.79 billion comfortably topping the Street’s forecast of $9.61 billion. The unit’s revenue grew almost 24% on an annual basis, following the launch of new Mac Studio and Mac Mini laptops in August.

The iPad division was a disaster, however, as sales declined more than 10% from the previous year to $6.3 billion, trailing the Street’s forecast of $6.7 billion. Last month saw the launch of a new iPad Mini model, following the debut of the updated iPad Air back in March, but despite those releases, there has been no flagship model launching this year, and that appears to have hurt the business’ performance. When asked about the miss, Ternus blamed supply constraints and a difficult comparison with last year as the main reasons for its disappointing performance.

Holger Mueller of Constellation Research said today’s earnings call was close to a baptism of fire for Ternus, who had to field analyst’s questions for the first time in his capacity as the company’s new CEO. While Apple’s overall growth was okay, it did not translate those revenue gains to its bottom line. “There is one good explanation that still encourages investors to bet on Apple’s future, namely that there was a substantial increase in R&D spending compared to the previous year, up more than $10 billion in fact,” the analyst said. “The iPhone remains the star of Apple’s portfolio and the company depends on its success more than ever. If iPhone sales don’t grow, that means lower services growth. The introduction of a touchscreen Mac will perhaps finally show if Steve Jobs was right about one thing — that touch on a PC will cannibalize iPad sales.”

The disappointing performance of Apple’s services and iPad units was compounded by what was seen as weak guidance for the current quarter, which includes the peak Christmas sales period. Apple Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh didn’t offer concrete numbers, but said the company expects its revenue to grow by between 7% and 10% in the quarter. Wall Street analysts are looking for higher growth of 11.4%, however. Parekh also revealed that Apple is forecasting its gross margin to fall between 45% and 46%, declining from the fourth quarter.

Apple’s stock fell almost 3% on today’s report, but it’s still up more than 24% in the year to date compared with a gain of just over 10% for the broader S&P 500 index.

#5689. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle Find a New Home Base in the Cotswolds

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have reportedly moved into a new Cotswolds home on their friend's estate.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex, who moved to the U.K. in August with their two children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, have been settling into their new lives across the pond.

After making the move, the couple was living "in the main house" of their pal's sprawling property.

However, now, their living situation has reportedly changed, with the Daily Mail reporting that they have moved onto another property "on the estate."

According to the outlet, the friend is a wealthy businessman who Harry, 42, befriended through their mutual support for various charities.

Harry and Markle were rumored to have been house hunting, with several reports noting that the former actress was even looking to replicate the luxury they had in their Montecito mansion.

The duchess reportedly wants the U.K. residence to boast nine bedrooms—the same number as their California estate—as well as plenty of luxurious amenities.

The news of their move came mere weeks after Harry opened up about their decision to leave California behind  and relocate their family to the U.K., revealing that their children's education and his desire to reconnect with his roots played a major role in the decision.

In an interview with GQ that was filmed in September but released only recently, Harry explained that the opportunity to enroll his children in British schools was particularly meaningful to him.

“Opportunities for the family, being able to put the kids in a British school has meant a lot to me. I didn’t know how important it was to me,” he said.

“I always thought it was going to be something that I would try to do or that we would try to do, but now they’ve been in school for two weeks. They’re loving it, and it’s just giving them a whole different experience.”

Harry emphasized that his decision was not a criticism of the U.S. education system, but rather an opportunity for Archie and Lilibet to experience life in two different countries.

“I’m not criticizing American schools, but I think for kids at 7 and 5 to be able to have that comparison and to have two completely different cultural experiences is so important today,” he explained.

Beyond their education, Harry said returning to Britain has allowed his children to spend more time with relatives and develop closer relationships with family friends.

Another motivation for the move, he explained, was to “be back closer to my family and to be back on U.K. soil for longer than a few days or a week here or there.

“It’s been nice to be close to friends, family, friends and friends and their children as well, to be able to have endless playdates to really, like, help our kids settle in," he said.

Despite the significance of the relocation, Harry admitted that he and Meghan, 45, had not necessarily mapped out the move years in advance.

“For us, when certain stars align, and it’s clear that this should or probably will end up being the case, then we lean into that,” he said.

After spending six years living in California, he said he increasingly wanted his children to become familiar with the country where he spent his own childhood.

“Having been here for six years now and only being able to go back to the U.K. for short periods of time, to actually have my whole family there with me, the place that I grew up, wanting to be able to show my kids where I grew up and have them have the experiences to some extent that I had—the good rather than necessarily the bad—provided real, proper, serious thinking as to, ‘This is an opportunity, let’s do it now,’” he said.

Harry also addressed his complicated history with the British press, expressing hope that his family's return could mark the beginning of a more positive chapter.

“Once you’ve been through it, once you’ve been able to talk about it and raise awareness to it, then people see it for what it is, which makes the environment slightly easier,” he said.

“And it’s not going to necessarily stop the behavior, but then that’s the second part, which is the behavior: My hope is that it will change.”

The duke acknowledged that tensions have persisted in the years since he and Meghan stepped back from their roles as senior working royals, but suggested he would welcome an opportunity to move forward.

“What happened back then was then, what’s happened over the last six years has been a continuation of that. There are some battles that have been fought, necessarily so. But hopefully we can all draw a line under that,” he said.

He added that he hopes both his family and the British media can put certain disputes behind them.

“I am optimistic. I’m hopeful,” Harry said. “I’m not naive. I have been naive in the past. But I think it’s important to remain optimistic.”

The interview surfaced just days after Harry and Meghan made their first official joint appearance in the U.K. since their relocation.

On Oct. 15, the couple traveled to Nottingham, England, where they greeted approximately 100 people during a public engagement.

The pair also spent time interacting with local schoolchildren, crouching down to speak with them. Meghan was presented with flowers and a balloon during the visit.

"It's great to be back," she told one person.

The warm welcome was filled with several special moments, including one that saw the crowd shouting, "I love you Duchess Meghan."

The appearance marked their return to a city that played an important role in their early relationship, having served as the location of their first official joint engagement following their November 2017 engagement announcement.

Their outing came days after it was reported that they were turning their attention to their professional and charitable commitments after spending their first several weeks in Britain adjusting to their new surroundings.

Their latest chapter comes more than six years after the couple stepped away from their roles as working members of the royal family and established a new life in North America.

The visit came as an insider close to the couple told People that Harry and Meghan are eager to devote more attention to their philanthropic endeavors, having initially concentrated on helping their children adapt to living in a new country.

Their transition has not been without complications.

According to the outlet, Archie and Lilibet were forced to change schools just two days into the academic year due to security and logistical concerns surrounding their commute.

However, the children have reportedly adapted to their new environment, allowing their parents to devote additional time to commitments outside the family home.

A source told People that Harry and Meghan have established a schedule centered around their children's school hours, while continuing to prioritize spending time together as a family.
