#5663. Where Health Care Employment Has the Biggest Footprint

Health care is more than a service for residents. It is also an important piece of the employment landscape. Preliminary August data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics shows significant differences in both the number of health care and social assistance jobs across states and the industry’s share of total employment.

In absolute terms, the country’s largest states naturally account for some of the biggest health care workforces. Unsurprisingly, California leads with over 3.18 million health care and social assistance jobs, followed by New York at 1.91 million and Texas at 1.76 million.

However, the health care industry’s share of a state’s total employment base may tell a different and potentially more useful story.

West Virginia stands at the top of the list, with health care and social assistance representing approximately 19.6% of total employment. New York follows at 19.1%, with Pennsylvania at 18.9%. Connecticut, Minnesota, and Massachusetts are also among the states where the industry accounts for a comparatively large share of employment, at roughly 18.1%, 17.9%, and 17.8%, respectively.

At the other end of the spectrum, health care represents just 8.8% of employment in Wyoming, 10.6% in the District of Columbia and Nevada, 10.8% in Alabama, and 11% in South Carolina.

That variation matters because a sizable health care sector can serve as an important economic anchor, providing a meaningful source of jobs that support the broader housing market.

Access to health care might become an increasingly relevant consideration in retirement location decisions. Affordability matters, but so do physician availability, provider access, and the distance residents need to travel for care.

Demographic trends reinforce that dynamic. Per the U.S. Census Bureau, the old-age dependency ratio, which measures the number of adults age 65+ relative to the working-age population, rose from 20.8 in 2010 to 29.7 in 2024, pointing to future pressure on health care systems, retirement programs, and elder care resources.

As the population ages, health care will matter to housing markets from both an economic and demographic perspective. The sector supports local employment, while access to care can influence where older households choose to live.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s National Outlook subscription.

Maria Barr is a research analyst within Zonda's economics department, where she supports housing market analysis at both the national and market level. She earned a B.A. in economics and English from Middlebury College.

#5662. Trend of the Month: 6 Ways Floor Plans Are Changing

Current floor plan trends don’t necessarily bring anything brand new to home design, but rather represent subtle shifts to better support how people want to live in their homes today.

Functionality and flow are driving many of the current trends, including these six:

As a result, floor plans are balancing the benefits of open-plan living with spaces that permit partial or total separation from the main living areas. Ideally, a floor plan lets a homeowner choose.

While the kitchen and adjacent living areas remain open, “what is changing is everything around that center. Homeowners still want visual generosity and togetherness, but they also need places for focused work, calls, study, rest, hobbies, or simply a quiet moment,” says Darian Wagner, managing principal and senior architect, DAHLIN Architecture.

The key, says Justin Julian, senior principal and senior architect, DAHLIN Architecture, is not to treat open and closed spaces as opposites.

The most desirable plans “create layers between fully shared and fully enclosed space, so homeowners can adjust the degree of connection throughout the day,” says Julian.

Meanwhile, “Smaller cozy corners can remain open to the main space while using placement, furniture, partial screens, or an offset opening to create a sense of retreat,” says Wagner.

Away rooms are trending, which are simply secondary living spaces set off the main living area, with a closing door, and often increased soundproofing, devoted to peace and quiet.

Back kitchens and sculleries physically separate food prep, appliances and cleanup from the main kitchen, where much of daily living and entertaining takes place.

Upstairs retreats, homework rooms, and secondary living spaces create further separation, giving household members somewhere to do their own thing without sacrificing the openness of the kitchen and great room.

Wet rooms are not a new feature but are gaining more attention and are influencing bathroom layouts and design, no longer reserved just for higher-end homes.

“One reason is that you can use every inch of that space, which can mean a larger shower and a more spa-like feel,” says Debra Purvis with Design House.

A wet room typically is an open-concept bathroom, where a bathtub and a shower share an enclosure, sometimes separated by a glass partition from the rest of the bathroom.

Wet rooms offer great decorative potential too, with soaker tubs, steam showers, and statement fixtures. They also lend themselves naturally to other trends like tile drenching, which provides a dramatic, upscale look.

They are family friendly too. “Kids splash water out of the tub; it’s not a problem. Between the tile and floor drains, you are covered,” says Purvis.

Flex rooms offer opportunity in a floor plan without adding square footage, one reason they remain among the most sought-after features in new homes. But today’s buyers are looking for flex rooms with purpose, rather than just a blank-slate bonus room.

Practical considerations, such as outlets, storage, layered lighting, and easy access without crossing through other spaces, offer flexible futureproofing. The flex room needs to be appropriately sized and configured for the potential use too.

Location in the home indicates flex room potential too.

While two-story floor plans remain in-demand, one-story floor plans are showing modest growth.

“A one-story plan is going to be more accessible, generally speaking, which opens it up to buyers in many different life phases,” says Aurora Zeledon, director of digital content and marketing for Zonda House Plans, including Houseplans.com.

While land availability and cost might be driving the uptick in one-story floor plans, the versatility of living on one level has design upside and broad-based appeal, including 55+, multigen households, and younger families who appreciate having everyone on the same level.

One-story plans offer easier circulation, without stairs and landings occupying transitional spaces. Typically, one-story homes benefit from a stronger indoor/outdoor connection, often an anchor of the design, an in-demand feature as well.

According to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), two-story plans still accounted for over half of single-family home starts in 2025 nationwide, although that number had dropped slightly, while the number of single-story homes inched up. Notably, there were significant differences across regions.

Meanwhile, Zeledon reports that the majority of floor plans they have sold, dating back to 2019, are for one-story homes, including their current bestseller. However, she notes that year-to-date there has been a modest increase in one-story house plan sales, compared to last year, pointing out that much of the activity is concentrated in the South and Southeast.

As homes generally scale down in size, storage becomes essential for homeowners to retain the functionality of a larger home in a smaller footprint.

“The overarching idea is to utilize every square foot. When storage is thoughtfully integrated into the architecture, we can maximize the home for multiple purposes—and, importantly, multiple storage solutions—without making the spaces feel overly utilitarian,” says Hannah Sloan, creative marketing specialist with Unscripted Interior Design.

She reports that drop zones are gaining attention, as are Costco closets, laundry/mudroom and owner’s entrances.

Sloan says that some rooms are benefiting from space-specific storage that improves functionality, like in the primary bathroom with more thoughtfully designed vanities and built-ins. Meanwhile, fitness closets are appearing in home gyms to free up floor space for exercise.

“Then there are the found spaces—under-stair book nooks, hidden speakeasy-inspired bars, and other whimsical design opportunities. These spaces can become highly functional while also adding personality and surprise to a home,” says Sloan.

This article was originally published on NewHomeSource.com.

#5661. Startup Athena raises $2.5M in pre-seed funding to revamp the revenue model for legal AI

Athena Circle Corp., an artificial intelligence-native legal technology startup that’s automating the nitty gritty of commercial real estate deals, said today it has raised $2.5 million in pre-seed funding.

The round was led by Andreessen Horowitz’s accelerator program, a16z Speedrun. No other investors were named.

Legal AI technology is nothing new, but its adoption in the industry has been somewhat haphazard, for the technology has exposed an awkward problem: Most law firms are still billing their clients by the hour, and that makes automation less lucrative. If a law firm can use AI agents to get a 10-hour contract review done in just a couple of minutes, then it’s going to let an awful lot of billable revenue slip through its fingers, killing any incentive there might be to adopt them.

Athena’s co-founders Cem Ucan (pictured, left) and Kieran John Keenan (right) and founding engineer José Braz all cut their teeth at the pioneering legal AI tech startup Legora AB, where they quickly realized how AI conflicts with the industry’s standard business model. They came up with an entirely different business model to convince legal firms of the benefits of automation. Instead of selling software tools directly, it provides a legal service through its affiliated law firm, charging a fixed fee per transaction that’s typically 30% to 50% lower than standard rates. In this way, it ensures that revenue is better aligned with efficiency.

“Most legal AI companies sell tools to traditional law firms, but we took a different approach,” Ucan said. “Our AI works hand-in-hand with a law firm designed around it from day one, with experienced attorneys focused on the judgment and negotiation that actually move deals forward.”

The startup is focused on automating the intricacies of commercial real estate acquisitions, sales and financing. Its AI agents are designed to automate the creation and review of purchase agreements and loan documents, and will handle all of the due diligence and administrative closing hurdles needed to get deals done, while ensuring human lawyers remain fully in the loop to make all of the final legal determinations.

In this way, Athena basically takes care of the grunt work, giving commercial real estate firms much more agility. That’s a real advantage, because commercial real estate is an industry where speed is of the essence: The faster a law firm gets things done, the more likely it is to actually secure the deal, which is the end result that everyone wants. With investors often submitting dozens of bids for each property listing, the ability to get the paperwork done in a matter of hours rather than weeks or days means buyers can lock in a deal before their rivals know what’s happened.

Keenan, who serves as the startup’s chief technology officer, explained that each new workflow begins with an incoming agreement that’s ingested by its AI agents. They cross-reference the terms of the deal against their standard deal sheets in order to flag inconsistencies, prepare redlines and draft client communications.

This work is informed by historical transactions, which allow its agents to adapt to each client’s negotiating style, Keenan said. Human attorneys then review this work, make strategic judgment calls when required, and approve all deliverables before they’re sent to clients.

“I measure our progress by how quickly an attorney can review an AI agent’s work and confidently stand behind it,” Keenan explained. “A draft produced in minutes can still leave a lawyer with hours of work. Making that review more efficient is how our platform helps us deliver faster legal services with the quality clients expect.”

Athena’s agents are already proving their worth, with the startup having signed up 22 legal firms as clients so far, just two months after launching its service. By learning continuously from attorney’s edits and client’s preferences, its agents have reduced review times by an average of 70%.

L. Miguel Arce, chief executive of the Texas-based multifamily real estate and property management firm Mox Living, said Athena was able to deliver a complete purchase agreement in less than 48 hours, the fastest turnaround he has ever seen. “A lot of firms in our industry have an AI task force in name only,” he said. “What stood out about Athena is that the system learns from every deal, from what the attorneys change to what we prefer. Speed only matters if it’s quality work, and Athena gets us both.”

Keenan said Athena is primed to strike while the iron is hot. He said the industry is bracing itself for a wave of new commercial deals as properties financed through short-term loans in 2021 and 2022 hit their refinancing deadlines, and he’s hoping that the startup can win a significant amount of that business. In any case, growth is on the horizon, for Athena also plans to expand into new markets and property classes and even new legal domains.

A16z Speedrun’s Troy Kirwin said AI automation is all well and good, but clients still demand to speak to a human who can take responsibility for the work that gets done. “Athena is building around that need with a system that can improve through real legal work and a team that’s obsessed with scaling fast,” he said.

#5660. Chad Lowe Lists $3.2 Million Los Angeles Mansion—1 Month After Losing His 13-Year-Old Daughter to Suicide

Actor Chad Lowe and his producer wife, Kim Painter, have put their sprawling Los Angeles home on the market for $3.2 million—just over a month after their 13-year-old daughter, Fiona, died.

Lowe, 58, and Painter, 52, listed the four-bedroom dwelling on Oct. 16, just weeks after announcing the devastating news of their daughter's passing, as first reported by the TMZ.

Now, not only have they put the pad on the selling block, they have also accepted an offer of $3.24 million.

However, the offer is contingent on certain conditions being met.

The home comes complete with three bathrooms and sprawls across 3,239 square feet.

Lowe and Painter purchased the Spanish-inspired abode in March 2025 for $3.15 million.

Fiona's death was announced via a statement from the family shared to People on Sept. 29 that read, “We are deeply heartbroken by the loss of our beloved Fiona. She was adored by her sisters and she was deeply loved by her parents,” the family said, adding, “In fact, she was the light of our lives.”

Fiona was the second of their three daughters. They also share daughters Mabel Painter, 17, and Nixie Barbara, 10.

Mabel honored her sister in a heartbreaking social media post following her death, penning, “I love you so much, Fiona. I wish your short time here was easier and I hope your mind is at ease now. I will honor you forever and keep your memory alive. I love you, I hope you knew just how much.”

On Oct. 2, Fiona's cause of death was determined to be a suicide.

After her death, a family friend told the Daily Mail that Fiona had been devastated by the loss of their California home due to the Palisades fire last year.

Mykesha Robinson told the outlet, "Something happened when the fires happened," adding, that the family “lost everything.”

#5659. Why Waiting for Rates to Fall Can Create Other Affordability Problems

Mortgage rates are giving homebuyers another reason to hesitate.

The average rate for a 30-year fixed mortgage reached well over 7% in October, its highest level in 13 months, according to Freddie Mac. That followed a climb from 5.98% in late February to 6.65% by Aug. 20, figures cited in a recent U.S. Bank housing-market analysis.

For a buyer, even a small rate change can alter the monthly payment considerably. Waiting for lower borrowing costs can therefore be a reasonable decision, particularly when today’s payment would leave little room for maintenance, insurance or other expenses.

However, a lower future rate does not guarantee a cheaper home purchase.

“If rates fall enough to bring more buyers back, the benefit can be partly absorbed by stronger competition,” says Jeremy Olsher, a real estate professional and Principal at Mizner Residential Group. “A buyer might secure a better rate but pay more for the property, face multiple offers or have less negotiating room.”

Additionally, lowering rates can be a sign of economic instability, including perhaps a significant response to mass unemployment and rampant inflation. While that might make homeownership more alluring, families could feel the strain in other ways, from job loss to rising grocery bills to big losses in their retirement portfolios.

Olsher recommends considering three factors before making lower rates the sole condition for buying.

Can the payment work today? Buyers should calculate the full monthly cost under current conditions, including principal, interest, property taxes, insurance, association fees and a realistic maintenance allowance. If that total is uncomfortable, the buyer may need to wait, reduce the price range or reconsider the type of property. The calculation should work without assuming that refinancing will become available later.

“Refinancing can be an option if rates eventually fall, but it should not be the reason someone accepts an unaffordable payment today,” Olsher says. “The purchase needs to stand on its own using the numbers the buyer can actually secure.”

How long does the buyer expect to stay? Transaction costs matter more when a buyer may move again within a few years. Closing costs, maintenance and future selling expenses can make a short ownership period difficult to justify, even if the mortgage payment appears manageable.

A buyer expecting to remain for several years has more time to spread those costs and absorb short-term changes in value. Someone with uncertain employment, family or relocation plans may benefit from the flexibility of renting.

Olsher says the right question is not simply whether ownership costs more than rent this month. Buyers should consider how long they expect to remain, what flexibility they need and how much cash the purchase would leave available afterward.

What does waiting cost? Delaying a purchase is not automatically costly. In some markets, renting may remain the more practical and affordable choice. Realtor.com®’s 2026 midyear forecast projected rents would decline 1.2% during the year, potentially benefiting renters in many areas.

Still, waiting can carry personal and financial costs. A household may need to renew a lease, pay moving or storage expenses, remain in an unsuitable space or postpone a relocation. The selection of available homes can also change before rates do.

“The cost of waiting is different for every buyer,” Olsher says. “For one person, another year of renting is perfectly sensible. For another, it means paying for a home that no longer fits their family while hoping the market delivers a better combination of rate, price and inventory.”

Trying to identify the perfect week to purchase gives one unpredictable number too much control over a long-term decision. Buyers can make a more grounded choice by comparing today’s full payment, the expected ownership period, available homes and the real cost of remaining where they are.

Buyers should commit when they are financially ready. If they find a home that fits their budget today, buying lets them lock in the house before prices climb further. If mortgage rates drop significantly in the future, they can refinance their loan to a lower rate without having to compete against a massive wave of new buyers.

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5658. Exclusive: Cogent Security’s VR-1.1 model outscores Claude Code and Codex on vulnerability repair

Vulnerability management startup Cogent Security Inc. today released VR-1.1, a new version of its frontier reasoning model that writes fixes for newly disclosed software vulnerabilities.

On a public repair benchmark, the model outscored Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code and OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex.

The release goes after the part of vulnerability management that has not sped up. In July, research group Epoch Artificial Intelligence Inc. counted about 2,500 high- and critical-severity disclosures from major organizations, roughly five times the monthly record set before Anthropic announced Claude Mythos Preview in April.

Each repair still needs an engineer who understands the flaw well enough to change the code without breaking something else. Co-founder and Chief Executive Vineet Edupuganti called that stage “where security teams are stuck.”

To test the model on that repair work, Cogent turned to LiveCVEBench. Researchers at Harbin Institute of Technology and Kuaishou Technology built the benchmark from vulnerabilities disclosed in recent months and add new ones regularly. VR-1.1 produced a working repair for 57.9% of the benchmark’s 190 tasks. Claude Code and Codex tied at 45.3%.

Each task drops an agent into a real development environment with a vulnerability report and the affected codebase, in one of 14 programming languages. To pass, a patch has to close the vulnerability without breaking the software, which the benchmark checks with separate security and functionality tests.

Cogent blocked outbound network access during repairs and hid the grading tests until each agent was done. Inference budgets differed across the three systems, according to the full methodology Cogent Research has published.

Where the environment allows, VR-1.1 starts by writing its own proof of concept that triggers the reported flaw. From there the model follows the vulnerability through the affected code, including related paths that share the same weakness. The fix itself stays small, for example checking an index before use.

Every patch goes to a separate review that starts from a fresh context and hunts for a way around the fix. New bugs introduced by the change are part of that check. The model also leaves behind regression tests, which fail if a later code change reopens the flaw. When an attempt fails, the diagnosis and failure details carry into the next try.

“A patch might block the exact payload from a bug report, but leave the same vulnerability open via a different endpoint or break core functionality for users,” said Geng Sng, co-founder and chief technology officer of Cogent. “We designed VR-1.1 to check its own work for both problems before it finishes.”

Cogent introduced VR-1 in July to find and prove the attack paths an adversary could reach inside an enterprise. The new release extends the remediation capabilities that model introduced.

Founded in 2025, the company sells artificial intelligence agents that detect and fix vulnerabilities, with customers choosing whether a human signs off on each change. According to Cogent, Fortune 500 users have cut the exposure window for critical vulnerabilities by 97%.

Greylock Partners backed its $11 million launch round in July 2025, and Bain Capital Ventures led the $42 million Series A in February that took total funding to $53 million.

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Is Microsoft bearish on Ripple? Its AI bot, Copilot AI, predicts that something potentially severe could be approaching for XRP by January 1, 2027. When prompted, it called for a hypothetical, unlikely black swan event in Q4 that would cause the token to crash to unprecedented levels.

The idea centers on a coordinated multi-jurisdictional regulatory and banking decision in which major economies and international financial bodies simultaneously classify XRP as a high-risk or non-compliant asset for institutional cross-border settlement use.

In this framework, banks, payment providers, and financial institutions would face significant new restrictions or disincentives to use the XRP Ledger and hold XRP, triggering reduced utility demand, forced de-risking, and a prolonged period of structural selling pressure.

On the higher timeframes, XRP has been consolidating in the $1.20–$1.30 region after recent volatility. Price continues to defend intermediate supports while facing overhead resistance around the $1.35–$1.45 zone.

In a standard corrective phase, a sustained break below $1.15–$1.10 would confirm intermediate weakness and open the path toward deeper retracement targets.

Under the extreme coordinated institutional restriction scenario outlined above, losing key multi-month support levels would likely trigger powerful measured-move downside extensions and multi-cycle Fibonacci retracements from the prior advance.

Momentum indicators currently sit in neutral-to-weak territory with room to deteriorate into the deeply oversold readings typical of sharp risk-off moves.

Key nearer-term supports sit near $1.18–$1.22 and $1.05–$1.10; failure to hold those zones would keep the broader structure vulnerable.

Several external factors could exacerbate the bearish outlook. Globally, an escalation or prolonged intensification of major geopolitical conflicts could prompt investors to seek refuge in traditional safe-haven assets, moving away from higher-risk assets.

Economically, a steeper-than-expected slowdown or renewed inflationary pressures may compel major central banks to maintain restrictive policies longer, tightening financial conditions and reducing interest in speculative assets.

Within the cryptocurrency space, a series of large-scale security incidents involving exchanges or protocols, ongoing regulatory uncertainty in key markets, especially regarding digital asset classifications, a decline in institutional interest in alternative payment systems, or a broader trend of shifting investments from altcoins into Bitcoin and traditional assets could create a challenging liquidity environment that significantly impacts XRP.

#5656. 10-Acre Florida Ranch With NBA-Level Facility Is Listed for $38.9 Million in Celebrity Enclave Where Gisele Bündchen Lives

An enormous 9.69-acre Florida compound with a brand-new 10,500-square-foot entertainment facility "that can be transformed into anything you can imagine" and resort-inspired grounds has just hit the market in Southwest Ranches for an astonishing $38.9 million.

If it reels in anywhere near its asking price, the 23,442-square-foot estate could become one of the top sales in the ultrahigh net worth neighborhood that celebrities, professional athletes, and supermodel Gisele Bündchen call home.

"I have never seen a property done to this scale before," says Tommy Crivello of the Tommy Crivello Real Estate Group, who is co-listing the property with Angeline Earnest of Coldwell Banker Realty.

Once the home of Mexican singer Juan Gabriel, the luxury residence last traded hands for $9,000,000 in 2022. Its asking price of $1,659 per square foot is currently the highest-priced listing in the exclusive Sunshine Ranches enclave of Southwest Ranches.

"Everything has been completely redone with extensive remodeling," Earnest notes. "The landscaping, garage, pools, and the 10,000-square-foot recreational facility are all new. Every structure also has a new roof."

The sprawling property boasts a five-bedroom primary residence, a three-bedroom guesthouse with a catering-grade kitchen, a members-style clubhouse with a full bar and private theater, and a gym and spa wellness retreat with a massage room and cold plunge.

Private lakes, immersive art, koi ponds, "producing orchards," a Tiki pavilion, and two pools, including one with a custom 10-foot rock-jumping wall, can also be found on the enormous lot. An outdoor basketball court and hockey rink round out the property.

"There are 10 acres of walkable space," she adds. "It feels like the whole property is livable and is not overwhelming."

"We are seeing a lot of high-end celebrities coming here," Crivello says. "I see an entrepreneur, hedge fund person, athlete, or real big car collector buying this property. It could also be someone who is looking for a place for the entire family, as it is designed for multigenerational living."

A custom-engineered lighting system transforms the pathways into nocturnal works of art. For equestrians, the sale also includes plans for a seven-stall barn with oversized paddocks.

"The property is large enough that there is room for another outdoor facility, and it has direct access to miles of riding trails," he says. "Everything in Southwest Ranches has rural zoning, so you can have a garden and any kind of animal on property. It just flows effortlessly."

Created as a "fully integrated private campus," the serene property also features art installations and curated gathering spaces for entertaining.

“You can get to the beach in 30 minutes, Amerant Bank Arena in 15 minutes, Las Olas Boulevard for the nightlife, and Pembroke Gardens is just 10 minutes away,” Crivello says. “You can retreat to the country, or you can be in the limelight as much as you want to be.”

Built in 1964, the Chicago brick-clad main estate boasts a renovated interior with two guest suites, each with a private entrance and that “function as private apartments within the residence.”

A lavish upstairs primary wing has a breakfast bar, a refrigerator, a seating area, dual bathrooms, separate closets, and a private terrace.

Other highlights include an executive office, a chef’s kitchen, a built-in wine preservation system, a custom bar, and a wraparound covered balcony on the main level.

A detached garage pavilion spanning nearly 2,000 square feet is fully air-conditioned. The four-vehicle structure has lift capability to accommodate up to eight vehicles. It also has floor drains, integrated compressor and vacuum systems, EV-ready outlets, workstation walls, and extra storage space.

One of the most impressive features of the property is its enormous entertainment facility, “currently home to a nonprofit basketball program.”

The “NBA-level” structure features professional athletic flooring, locker rooms, conference spaces, a viewing balcony, and a smoothie bar.

Its flexible design could also be reimagined into a 50- to 100-vehicle auto showroom, a private museum, a production studio, or an event venue.

“The nice thing about the facility is that it has a second mezzanine where you can have spectators watch,” Crivello notes.

“You could also transform it into an indoor equestrian facility. It offers the peace of mind that upscale riders want. There has been a big shift for people who are car collectors, so the facility could also be transformed into an auto showroom. The building is huge and would be a focal point for an equestrian, athlete, or car collector.”

In A Nutshell: Rates have mellowed a bit coming into a big week with a Fed meeting and the first read of Q3 GDP data.

Last Week’s Highlights: Oil prices continued to increase last week, but rates came down, as doubts about the AI narrative battered stocks, sending money into the bond market. On the housing front, the increase in mortgage rates has sent builder confidence down to its lowest level in 14 years. Permits for single-family homes also fell to a multiyear low.

Upcoming Attractions: The biggest event of the week is the Fed decision and press conference Wednesday afternoon. The committee is not scheduled to update its forecast (the “dot plot”) this time. Markets believe the Fed will hold and then hike on December 9th for an every-other-meeting hike cadence, so the attention will be on clues for the next meeting rather than the outcome of this one. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will hold a press conference but is likely to stick to his usual practice of not foreshadowing upcoming decisions. Fed watchers may get more color out of SF Fed President Daly and St. Louis Fed President Musalem’s remarks on Friday.

Apart from the Fed, there are also a couple of important data releases this week. The first look at Q3 GDP is coming on Thursday morning. Part of the thesis for rates increasing so much these last few months is a belief that the economy is growing faster. At one point, estimates had Q3 GDP growing as fast as a 5% annual rate. Forecasters are expecting this advance estimate to land around 3.2%, which would be a meaningful pick-up from 2.2% in Q2. And finally, the September durable goods report will be released on Tuesday with forecasters expecting a solid reading of 2.0% month-over-month growth. This report tracks new orders, shipments, and inventories of long-lasting manufactured products, which is a signal of how confident businesses and consumers are about the future.

#5654. Novee’s External Surface Testing checks which exposed assets attackers can actually exploit

Artificial intelligence penetration testing startup Novee Cyber Security Ltd. today added External Surface Testing to its platform so its AI-driven attacks can reach a customer’s entire internet-facing footprint.

External Surface Testing is aimed at the scramble after a critical vulnerability is disclosed, when security teams have to work out which exposed assets are affected and whether any can actually be exploited. Novee argues that attackers see a target as a single environment with many ways in, including forgotten subdomains and staging servers someone left exposed.

Conventional external attack surface management products catalog a company’s exposed assets and score them by severity. Netta Rager Dan, vice president of product at Novee, said those products “show you what’s exposed, but don’t give you the full picture of real risk.” In the company’s telling, security staff are left to validate long lists of exposures on their own.

Novee’s version needs nothing more than a domain name to get started. From there the software works outward the way an outside attacker would, and it keeps track of what it learns about each asset and service as it goes. A newly disclosed vulnerability gets run against a customer’s live systems to see whether anyone could actually exploit it.

Findings exported from other vendors’ attack surface tools go through the same check. Novee says the testing also catches flaws nobody had logged, chained attack paths among them, and the customer ends up with a short, prioritized list of validated issues backed by evidence.

Until now Novee’s testing has stopped at the application layer. External Surface Testing runs on the same platform as the company’s Application Pentesting product, so a host found during external discovery can be promoted straight into a full gray-box or white-box pentest. Whatever the discovery phase learned carries over. Novee claims no other fully autonomous AI pentesting platform covers the external attack surface as well as web, mobile and AI applications.

Limits are built in to keep the testing safe. Customers approve the scope before anything runs, and the probes come from outside the perimeter without agents or customer-supplied credentials. Exploit attempts don’t use destructive payloads. Traffic is held under configured caps so testing doesn’t cause load spikes or bury the security operations center in noise.

Former national-level offensive security operators Ido Geffen, Gon Chalamish and Omer Ninburg founded Novee in May 2025. YL Ventures LP, Canaan Partners and Zeev Ventures LP backed the company when it launched in January with $51.5 million in funding.

External Surface Testing is available now as part of the Novee platform.

#5653. Open Real Estate Claims Early Broker, MLS Support as Initiative Touts ‘Significant Interest’

Open Real Estate, the national initiative launched by big brokerage leaders last week that has promised to create a shared “infrastructure” for property listing data, today announced it has received 826 letters of support from real estate brokerage leaders.

Behind the strength—and size—of its four founding brokerages (HomeServices of America, AGNT, Keller Williams and Real REMAX Group), the announcement made waves as it promised to maintain an “open and transparent” real estate market while allowing brokers to control their listings.

Open Real Estate is claiming that pledge and those principles have quickly found support among the broader brokerage community.

“We have already received significant interest from across the real estate industry since our announcement, and we look forward to continuing to engage with brokerages of all sizes, MLS organizations, and technology providers as we develop a platform that expands consumer choice and transparency for home buyers and sellers,” said the founding members of Open Real Estate.

Of the support letters received, 493 (59%) came from independent brokerages, according to Open Real Estate—from single-office independents to some of the largest independent brokerages in the country, including Atlanta Communities, Iron Valley Real Estate, LoKation Real Estate and Realty of America.

Open Real Estate is also claiming support from prominent MLS leaders. Designed to complement existing MLS organizations, the initiative aims to work alongside them to expand access to listing information for brokerages, agents and the consumers they serve, Open Real Estate said.

RISMedia spoke to a handful of MLS leaders about Open Real Estate, who largely said they were “cautiously optimistic” for the initiative. Council of Multiple Listing Services (CMLS) CEO Jessie Edgerton specifically said she had “deep, deep hope” around its principles and founders, while adding there were many unanswered questions around governance and execution.

In a release from Open Real Estate, four prominent MLS leaders also offered statements of support.

“We welcome the initiative of Open Real Estate and look forward to actively participating and partnering with industry leaders to build on the capabilities already in place at Bright and advance a more connected, efficient, broker-driven marketplace,” said Brian Donnellan, president and CEO, Bright MLS.

“Strategically, California Regional MLS and Open Real Estate are in alignment with the concept of allowing brokers to bring listing data in from outside the CRMLS MLS Input Platform,” said Art Carter, CEO, CRMLS. “We look forward to working with Open Real Estate to see how that possibility comes to fruition within their platform.”

“NTREIS remains dedicated to fostering a transparent, cooperative, and neutral marketplace that serves all Broker Participants equally by delivering consistent listing access and empowering exceptional consumer service. In alignment with this mission, we welcome constructive dialogue with Open Real Estate,” said Chris Carrillo, CEO, North Texas Real Estate Information Systems (NTREIS).

“Broker-led innovation shouldn’t be viewed as a threat to the MLS. It’s an opportunity to strengthen the cooperation that has served our industry for decades,” said Tim Dain, president and CEO, NorthstarMLS. “I hope this initiative brings even more brokers and MLSs to the table.”

MARIS MLS previously wrote a letter offering similar support of “the concept of (Open Real Estate),” while saying it hoped for more details as well. One MLS leader, who requested anonymity in order to speak candidly about the initiative, previously told RISMedia they saw the initiative as similar to a private listing service, adding they believed it would push MLSs to go “back to basics.”

#5652. The Holiday Season Is the Best Time For Homebuyers to Score a Deal in These 7 U.S. Metros

Early November is the best time for homebuyers to score a bargain in three U.S. metro areas: Milwaukee, Riverside, CA and Tampa, FL.

In Detroit and three Florida metros–Fort Lauderdale, Miami and West Palm Beach–house hunters may benefit from holding out a little longer. Mid-December is typically the best time of year to get a deal in those places.

This is according to a Home Economics and Redfin analysis of housing market data; the analysis was originally completed in April. The analysis identifies the time of year when discounts off a home’s original asking price–through price drops and/or negotiations between buyer and seller–typically approach their seasonal peak.

Nationwide, discounts tend to peak in early fall before plateauing or shrinking as winter approaches. But housing is local, and in these seven metros, peak discounts typically arrive later. Homebuying slows as the holidays approach, leaving sellers with fewer potential buyers–giving the buyers who remain more room to negotiate. And some late-year listings have been sitting for months, making sellers more motivated to strike a deal before the end of the year.

“There’s a tradeoff to shopping for a home late in the year: Buyers may have fewer fresh listings to choose from, but they also face less competition, and many sellers are ready to make a deal,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “A seller who has been waiting months for an offer may be more willing to negotiate on price or other costs than they were in the spring. Buyers shouldn’t purchase a home just because the calendar says it’s a good time for deals, but those who find the right home may have room to negotiate.”

In Florida, the best deals for buyers typically arrive in November or December, partly due to weather. South Florida’s biggest wave of buyers–retirees and seasonal residents–often show up after the new year, when the weather is sunny and comfortable in Florida but cold in the Northeast.

“Local buyers have a good shot at getting a deal in November, mainly because it’s just before the snowbirds arrive,” said Todd Edwards, a Redfin Premier agent in Tampa. “House hunters have a window of opportunity to negotiate on listings that have been lingering on the market since summer: Sellers want to close a deal before the new year, and there’s often not much competition from out-of-towners yet.”

Hurricane season, which runs through early fall, also keeps some house hunters away and leaves lingering listings ripe for discounts once it passes. Additionally, Florida’s high concentration of luxury homes tend to sell below asking price, especially late in the year when sellers are eager to get those properties off their books.

The story is a bit different in Milwaukee and Detroit. Those northern metros have a fairly short selling season: Cold-weather markets compress the window for touring and closing on homes; sellers keep at it later into fall, trying to close a deal before the depth of winter hits and buyers hibernate.

That delays the usual seasonal slowdown until November in Milwaukee and December in Detroit, later than in most of the country.

The November and December discount windows in Milwaukee, Riverside, Detroit and much of Florida aren’t a one-time event; they show up as a recurring pattern each year, regardless of whether the broader market favors buyers or sellers.

But the seasonal advantage could be particularly useful to buyers this year. The U.S. housing market is already firmly tilted toward buyers, with 63% more sellers than buyers—the biggest imbalance in Redfin records dating back to 2013. A jump in listings coupled with sluggish homebuying demand has given house hunters in many parts of the country more options and more negotiating power. Miami is one of the strongest buyer’s markets in the nation, with more than twice as many sellers as buyers. Tampa, West Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale, Riverside and Detroit are also buyer’s markets.

Milwaukee is one of just five seller’s markets in the country. With more buyers than sellers in Milwaukee, deals aren’t commonplace–so buyers there may want to pay extra attention to seasonal patterns.

The best time to buy a home is more complex than the week when buyers are most likely to score a discount.

There’s typically a tradeoff between selection and savings. New listings generally peak months before the best deals arrive. For instance, Milwaukee typically has the most new listings in mid-May and the most fresh inventory in mid-July,then its best deals arrive in early November. Detroit’s new listings typically peak in early August and fresh inventory in early September, months before its mid-December dealmaking sweet spot.

That means buyers who wait until November or December may have fewer homes to choose from. But those who prioritize price—and are flexible about their timing—may find sellers more receptive to negotiations. Ultimately, buyers should balance price, selection and their own circumstances.

Please note that this table includes 3 key moments for buyers; it’s important for buyers to balance what’s most important for them–choice or price

To identify the best time to buy, this Home Economics and Redfin analysis focuses on the seasonal indexes for three metrics: new listings, fresh inventory, and the average discount.

#5651. Groundcover turns its Wand acquisition into a Kubernetes rightsizing beta

Observability company groundcover Inc. today added Autonomous Infrastructure to its platform in beta to rightsize the processor and memory requests automatically on customers’ Kubernetes workloads based on how each workload behaves in production.

The technology comes from Kubernetes resource optimization startup Wand Cloud Ltd., which groundcover acquired in September.

The release is aimed at the processor and memory requests Kubernetes has engineers set for each workload up front, usually before it has handled any real traffic, and groundcover said most teams seldom return to those numbers. When one is set too low, the first sign is often a service throwing out-of-memory errors. Padding that goes unused ends up on the monthly cloud bill.

Because the groundcover sensor has been collecting production history all along, a customer on a supported version can open Autonomous Infrastructure for the first time without installing anything and find the data the feature needs already in place. Requested processor and memory for each workload appear next to actual usage. Estimated monthly savings sit beside a count of under-provisioned workloads, and a chart tracks over time how much of the potential saving has been realized.

Dollar figures in the beta are based on a price per processor and memory unit that customers enter themselves. Public cloud pricing is the next step, according to groundcover, and billing data such as the Cost and Usage Report from Amazon Web Services Inc. will come after that.

Most resource optimization tools size each workload in isolation, groundcover argues, so a request that looks right for one service can still starve its neighbors on a crowded node. Stability is the first constraint in groundcover’s own software. Before Autonomous Infrastructure raises a request, it checks how tightly the node is already packed so one workload’s increase does not leave the rest short of resources.

Shahar Azulay, groundcover’s co-founder and chief executive, said customers can check what their clusters stand to save, from data already held in their own cloud accounts, before they let Autonomous Infrastructure “change anything.” The feature stays off until an engineer turns it on and picks the deployments, namespaces or clusters it manages.

During the beta the software touches requests only and leaves limits where they are. Each policy carries minimum and maximum bounds for processor and memory, and an audit log records who assigned each workload to a policy and when. Groundcover suggests starting with lower-risk workloads such as development namespaces and leaving alone something like a production database that needs room to grow.

The beta is available now at no additional cost to every groundcover customer running its sensor on Kubernetes, and the company is also recruiting design partners to work with its product team while it runs. Demonstrations are scheduled for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City Nov. 9-12.

Groundcover is a venture capital-backed startup that has raised $160 million to date, including a $100 million Series C round led by One Peak in July.

#5650. Fed Holds Rates Steady, But Sets Up a December Hike

Takeaway: The Fed skipped hiking rates at today’s meeting, as expected. But they set up a hike at the December 9th meeting.

The Fed’s main message: Future hikes may be necessary because the economy is strong and inflation is too high. But they’re also patient, willing to skip hiking at some meetings in the interest of waiting for more data.

Chairman Warsh also announced a big change for Fed meetings starting next year, setting aside one meeting for big picture deliberation.

#5649. Tribeca Dominates Manhattan Luxury Sales This Week With Top 2 Penthouses on Same Street

Tribeca took the crown for the hottest neighborhood in Manhattan luxury sales last week, nabbing the top two priciest sales in the borough.

The lower West Side neighborhood, which John F. Kennedy Jr. and his bride, Carolyn Bessette, did much to make famous, has continued to push toward the Hudson River with new luxury residential skyscapers.

Last week's top two sales were coincidentally on the same street, with contracts signed at 111 Murray St. and 71 Murray St. Both were penthouse condos.

"I like to call it 'Tribeca lite,'" says Brown Harris Stevens agent Lisa K. Lippman, who not only represents real estate in the neighborhood, but also lives in it. "It's not prime Tribeca."

The broker says "prime" Tribeca would be around the the area of Duane and North Moore Street. (JFK Jr. and Carolyn lived in 20 North Moore St.)

But as prime Tribeca filled up, development spread east and west—with the western edge closer to sweeping river views, as well as the Hudson River Greenway bike path and all of the riverfront parks and piers.

"The area feels less residential," she tells Realtor.com of Murray Street and the surrounding streets, which are packed with glass skyscrapers. "There's always people who want to be on a higher floor, have a lot of amenities, but pay a little less."

The top sale for the week ending Nov. 1 was Penthouse One at 111 Murray St., with an asking price of $33.95 million. The penthouse, inside a 64-story tower built in 2018 and designed by architect David Mann, was a sponsor sale.

The sprawling, extra-large unit—at 7,675 square feet with five bedrooms and 6.5 bedrooms—was snapped up by Richard Saghian, the founder and chief executive of Fashion Nova, for $31 million, according to multiple reports.

According to Forbes, the 45-year-old fashion mogul is worth $2.1 billion and is the No. 1,900–ranked richest person in the world.

The penthouse will be added to his growing property portfolio, which includes a $141 million Bel-Air mansion and two Miami Beach properties: a $30 million double lot and a $32 million estate.

His latest acquisition offers 360-degree views of New York Harbor, as well as 233 square feet of private terraces with which to enjoy them.

The sweeping river views really helped move the property, says listing agent Emily Sertic of Douglas Elliman, who has headed up sales in the building since its launch.

"You'll capture a glimpse of Central Park, the Empire State Building, all the historic bridges, the rivers, and the harbor," she says. "From its view line only, it really encompasses an incredible experience of New York. Everywhere you turn, there are these astonishing view lines that just go on and on."

"The view line and the grandeur of the space for entertaining was really important," she says of what helped attract the billionaire buyer, who was represented by Ryan and Emilia Serhant of Serhant.

The great room alone is over 2,000 square feet, says the broker, and boasts an eat-in kitchen, butler's pantry, and private terrace.

"Whether it's for work, entertainment, guests, or family, the bedrooms were a huge draw to the space," she says.

Saghian, the college dropout son of Iranian immigrants, is reportedly single with no children.

The fast-fashion mogul appears to appreciate a real estate deal—creditors of his Bel-Air mansion originally wanted $295 million at auction and a judge had to approve the sale because of the relatively low price it ended up fetching. And the Tribeca penthouse originally asked for $50 million back in September 2025.

"It has all the features that any trophy buyer is looking for," says Sertic.

Some of those features fit for a billionaire include a chef's kitchen with Wolf, Miele, and Sub-Zero appliances, dual fridges and dishwashers, a 60-inch custom gas cooktop, multiple ovens, and a full-height wine refrigerator.

The full-service luxury building contains the usual array of amenities one would expect at this price point.

There is a 24/7 door attendant, concierge service, and valet team; a full-service wellness center and spa complete with hammam, treatment rooms, and a 75-foot lap pool with private cabanas; a fitness center; a children's playroom with splash pad, and a teen arcade room. There's also a private dining room, screening room, and landscaped garden.

The penthouse comes with a $36,000 monthly fee, including HOA dues and taxes.

The second top sale of last week was also on Murray Street. The glass-walled triplex penthouse at 71 Murray St. is a four-bedroom, 4.5-bath unit with a price tag of $18.5 million.

Listed by Jeremy V. Stein of Sotheby's International Realty, the sprawling 6,700-square-foot condo included an astonishing 3,148-square feet of terraces, including two roof terraces decked out for entertaining with a full Viking kitchen, fire pit, and dining area. There is also a floating glass staircase and 36-foot climbing wall.

Topping a boutique building with only 12 residences, the penthouse has monthly common charges and taxes totaling $17,232.

The two downtown top sales aren't that unusual—the former warehouse district has been trendy since the late Kennedy scion took up residence there in the early 1990s. (Actor Robert DeNiro—who moved there in 1981—can truly claim pioneer status.)

Sertic says the typical neighborhood buyers tend to be "youngish buyers and their families" who work in the surrounding neighborhoods, especially the Financial District.

"A lot of our buyers walk to work," she says. "They are high-performing and fast-moving, so convenience is huge."

Despite Tribeca nabbing the top two sales, it was the Upper East Side that pulled the most luxury (over $4 million) contracts again this week. Of the 34 contracts signed, the UES dominated with the highest amount of sales for the 10th time this year.

As is usual, condos outsold co-ops, 17 to 12. However, with only five sales between them, co-ops are holding their own.

The upward sales trajectory of co-ops—where buyers tend to be subject to a rigorous board approval process—is likely the effect of luxury inventory being so slim, say experts.

It also probably helps that co-ops often trade lower than condos, with an average ask of $6.48 million versus $10.44 million for condos, according to Olshan Realty.

The most expensive co-op of the week was a new build, constructed in 2023. The Lenox Hill penthouse at 200 East 75th St. had an asking price of $16.85 million.

#5647. Justin Baldoni Discreetly Sells Former Los Angeles Home for $2.1 Million After Making a ‘Fresh Start’ in Nashville

Actor Justin Baldoni discreetly offloaded his former Los Angeles home months after relocating to Nashville, TN, for a “fresh start.”

The three-bedroom, three-bathroom Culver City abode went for $2.1 million in an off-market transaction in August, according to Page Six. The 1,992-square-foot house was built in 1952 and sits on a 5,736-square-foot lot.

“He hasn’t lived there in years,” a People magazine source said. “The family has been living in Nashville for a bit now, but they moved to Ojai before that.”

The “It Ends With Us” director and his wife, Emily Baldoni, reportedly bought the home in 2017.

In an October 2020 People magazine interview, the couple opened up about life in the “urban farmhouse.”

The Baldonis said they invited loved ones to visit the home to write prayers and affirmations on its exposed wooden beams after completing a nine-month renovation.

“In the beams of the house is literally love,” Justin said.

The home had a host of interesting features, including a climbing wall in the garage for their children, Maiya and Maxwell.

There was also a built-in Wolf coffee machine and a top-of-the line Kohler toilet the actor compared to a “Transformer.”

While Emily shared that the plumbing feature “takes care of everything,” Justin noted that the family “didn’t panic as much as some others when all the toilet paper disappeared.”

The sale of the Los Angeles property isn’t the only quiet real estate move Justin, 42, has made this year.

Property records indicate that he listed his sprawling Ojai, CA, compound for $8.88 million on Feb. 5. The listing came just days after a rental listing for the same property—which was asking $40,000 a month—was taken down.

The estate, which the couple purchased for $2.2 million in 2020, has since been taken off the market.

The five-bedroom, 4.5-bathroom dwelling on a 10-acre lot in the picturesque neighborhood of Santa Paula was described by Emily as a “magical place” in a 2023 Architectural Digest interview.

Inspired by their trips abroad, the couple went to lengths to design “the whole house with feng shui in mind,” a practice inspired by his mother, “who’s done it for 30 years.”

“When we went to Tulum and parts of Mexico, we would take pictures of lamps or couches—just as inspiration—and then we started to put together a Pinterest board of things that we liked,” he said.

The couple made a series of upgrades to the home to create a “sanctuary.” According to the since-removed listing, the home was outfitted with “a state-of-the-art medical-grade air filtration system,” electromagnetic frequency shielding around the primary bedroom, a saltwater pool, and a “regenerative orchard.”

It also included a hot tub, sport court, custom-designed gym, LED-lit in-ground trampoline, koi pond with waterfall, fire pit, and walking paths.

Additional technological amenities included EV charging stations, a state-of-the-art security system, and fire mitigation systems.

The family packed their bags for Tennessee in December 2025, amid the highly publicized legal drama Justin was involved in after actress Blake Lively sued in 2024, claiming he had sexually harassed her during the filming of “It Ends with Us.”

“It’s obviously been an incredibly difficult time for the whole family, but Nashville has given them a fresh start,” a People magazine source previously shared.

After denying the allegations, Justin filed a $400 million countersuit against Lively and her husband, Ryan Reynolds, her publicist Leslie Sloane, and Sloane’s PR firm, citing defamation and breach of contract.

The suit was later dismissed by a judge, as were Lively’s sexual harassment claims. The actress later pursued allegations of retaliation against Justin, as well as his production company and publicity team.

Justin and Lively reached a private settlement days before the case was due to go to trial in May 2026.

However, the dispute continued when Lively sought $8 million in legal fees from Justin. She was awarded a total of $407,451.75 in an Aug. 26 order.

In July, when the dispute was still ongoing, the Baldonis posted an Instagram Reel to address the situation for the first time.

“We have not spoken publicly for the better part of the last two years, and it’s not because we haven’t had anything to say,” Justin said. “It just felt like every time we went to make a video like this, we wanted to speak, something was telling us not to. It just didn’t feel like the right time, and we were talking about it and feeling into it and praying about it.”

While Justin kept his statement fairly vague and never named Lively, the couple did share that they had experienced a lot of “trauma.”

"What I will say is that there have been so many painful things that have been spoken into existence over the last couple of years,” he said. “That created so much noise, and we didn’t want to add to the noise. So we just wanted to let the justice system run its course."

The couple noted that they had “so much more to say,” but that they were “going to focus on continuing the healing” and “hanging out” with their “kiddos and enjoying life.”

According to the New York Post, the family’s new Nashville home is a $3.4 million newly built abode. The six-bedroom, six-bathroom property spans 7,000 square feet and is situated on an acre lot.

#5646. Snowflake expands agentic AI platform with business context and governance tools

Snowflake Inc. today announced a sweeping collection of artificial intelligence capabilities designed to bring business context, governance and autonomous development into the same environment, as enterprises increasingly hand over software engineering and everyday operations to AI agents.

The announcements, during the company’s Expedition 2026 virtual conference, include a new Business Ontology framework, expanded agent governance through Cortex AI Gateway, and autonomous data engineering capabilities that allow AI agents to build, monitor and troubleshoot data pipelines with less human intervention.

The company is betting that more coders and engineers will use AI throughout the software development lifecycle as creation moves even faster, while other back-end departments begin to adopt agents in their day-to-day work. For example, sales operations are creating agents that can analyze sales risks and prepare customer outreach without writing code.

“AI is industrializing software creation. Actually, it’s industrializing intelligence,” Chief Executive Sridhar Ramaswamy said. “What once took months can now take hours, days, or even minutes.”

Ramaswamy noted that while AI is changing the economics of software development, as agents take over tasks usually relegated to specialized developers, business users become developers. This is changing the competitive landscape, meaning that the advantage no longer goes to specialists, but to proprietary knowledge.

Snowflake is taking the field by helping ordinary AI models understand and contextualize that business knowledge. It does this with Business Ontology, an extension of its existing semantic views that lets organizations establish approved definitions used across the organization. Without a standard definition, two agents could respond to the same business-related question with incompatible answers, even when both agents have accurate underlying data.

Using information from Business Ontology, Snowflake CoCo, the coding agent for data teams, and Snowflake CoWork, the personal work agent for knowledge workers, use these approved business concepts to ground their responses.

This new feature is currently in private preview, but is headed to public preview soon.

Cortex AI Gateway arrives to become a single front door for agents within an organization. It is not entirely new; Snowflake introduced it in July 2026 as a centralized way to govern and monitor agents.

Today’s announcement expands its capabilities rather than introducing the gateway for the first time. The new updates include agent abuse detection, observability and tracing, Cortex sandboxes, AI cost governance, dynamic model routing and tools integration using technology from Snowflake’s Natoma acquisition.

“An agent that acts on your business has to be trusted, and it has to know three important things: what the data means, which data to trust, and what it’s allowed to do,” said Ramaswamy.

The platform most importantly applies existing security mechanisms, including data masking and access restrictions, to agent-driven operations while adding capabilities to monitor activity, detect potential abuse and maintain records of what agents do. The information technology and security teams can also apply cost controls, select models based on efficiency or accuracy and restrict which external tools agents can access granularly.

The underlying role of this governance, control and transparency is aligned with giving agents the same sort of role observation granted to employees. Treating them similarly in terms of autonomy.

Snowflake’s push comes amid a broader industry race to establish the control layer for enterprise AI agents. SAP has been expanding its Autonomous Enterprise architecture and governed Joule agents, while Salesforce has introduced its Enterprise AI Harness and AI Control Plane to secure autonomous workflows. Snowflake is approaching the same problem from the data platform side, seeking to become the foundation through which agents access trusted business information and operate under enterprise policies.

Snowflake also announced the public preview of Cortex Training, which will allow customers to tailor open-weight AI models with their own proprietary information.

The service is designed to make it simpler to create specialized models using post-training without needing vast arrays of graphics processing units. Snowflake lets them train models without managing the underlying infrastructure.

“Specialized, smaller models that come with more efficient responses, faster responses, and frequently cost benefits in terms of tokens,” Executive Vice President of Product Christian Kleinerman said.

Many enterprise companies will require sovereign control of their own AI models as increasing restrictions on foreign open-weight AI or regulations on handling sensitive information. It’s easier to audit what passes through an AI model on your own hardware than in a third-party vendor’s cloud.

Separately, Snowflake announced an expanded partnership with Oracle Corp. to make its platform available as a first-party service on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The integration will give customers easier access to Snowflake’s analytics and AI capabilities while allowing them to work directly through Oracle databases and applications.

#5645. California Voters Could Approve ‘Secondary Mortgages.’ Can the Golden State Solve the Housing Crisis?

Lawmakers and advocates have made many attempts recently to address the affordability crisis that pervades the housing market—some more impactful than others. Legislative bodies have enacted laws addressing private listings, while President Donald Trump recently signed an executive order aimed at cutting costs for title and mortgage insurance and manufactured housing.

In tomorrow’s general election, California voters will vote on a meaningful and unique new measure that essentially allows first-time buyers to borrow the bulk of their down payment, theoretically removing a big barrier to homeownership (with several caveats).

California Proposition 37—or the Second Mortgage Homebuyer Program and Revenue Bond Initiative—would create an assistance program for first-time homebuyers, offering them loans that could cover up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, meaning a buyer only needs to put 3% down to reach the 20% threshold needed to avoid mortgage insurance.

One of the primary sponsors of the initiative, former California Senate Majority Leader and Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg spoke with RISMedia and desired for more California residents to achieve homeownership.

“We’re really underhoused in California, so much of the focus has been on subsidized tax supported rental housing. I don’t take that away for a second, but we haven’t done a really good job at making sure that middle-class folks—the missing middle—are able to buy a house,” he says.

The initiative would authorize the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to issue up to $25 billion in bonds to offer secondary mortgage loans for down payments, to eligible buyers.

To qualify for the program, applicants must have been residents of California for at least one year, agree to occupy the home as a primary residence within 60 days of closing, fall under the middle-income buyer threshold and provide a down payment of no less than 3% of the purchase price of the qualified homes.

The proposition is aimed at “middle-income buyers,” or buyers who have an income at or below 200% of the area median income.

A qualified home includes any “newly constructed homes, townhouses, row houses, condominiums, or manufactured homes, or a condominium or other residence in a nonresidential building repurposed for residential use, where the borrower is the first purchaser,” according to the proposition.

Within these limitations, the program theoretically allows buyers to put down much less while still getting the keys (the 3% down payment still comes out to around $17,000 for a median-priced new home in the state).

As for the $25 billion in bonds, Hertzberg emphasizes that funding does not rely on taxpayer wallets, but rather investors. What’s more, the bonds will be recycled continuously.

“The bottom line is, it’s evergreen. Evergreen means that it’s not over. When you pay off the loan, it’s evergreen and the money goes back out to somebody else,” Hertzberg notes. “Thirty years from now when all these initial loans are paid off, there’ll be brand new loans. We hired a professor from UCLA who analyzed it and said that it’ll raise $150 billion in new construction and 190,000 new homes.”

Michael Lane—state policy director at the San Francisco Bay Area Planning and Urban Research Association (SPUR)—approves the initiative because it focuses on new homes.

“There are some programs the state has implemented which are just down payment assistance programs without creating new housing,” he asserts. “You’re actually just creating—with those programs—more demand for the existing housing stock, which means more competition which will also boost prices. We think it’s important for this to focus on new construction as well as the down payment assistance.”

Within the proposition, a “secondary mortgage” is a somewhat unique concept. In this case, a secondary mortgage refers to the loan offered to qualified homebuyers, of which goes toward a home’s down payment.

“This is different from a second mortgage,” David Garcia, deputy director of Policy at the Terner Center for Housing Innovation UC Berkeley, stated.

A website made by supporters of the proposition contains a tool that allows voters to view median home price by each county in California, and uses data provided by the California Association of Realtors®.

As with many coastal states, California has a divided housing market. According to the latest data, California metros were not immune to the effects of elevated mortgage rates, as pending home sales fell even in high activity cities such as San Francisco and San Jose.

Construction has fared no better, as the latest report from The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and the Census Bureau shows that housing starts in the West are down over 23% monthly, and down 25% from the previous year.

In that context, Proposition 37 is particularly relevant as the state seeks to sustainably increase housing that is affordable in a market that is both land constrained and highly regulated.

“We’re also focused on construction defect liability reform and liquidated damages for condominiums in California,” Lane notes. “We’re at a disadvantage compared to other states; it makes it more risky to build condominiums here. That’s why we don’t produce very many—about 3,000 developments of five units or more—compared to other states and nations which do 10 times that amount with lesser populations.”

Homebuilders cite global tensions and labor shortages for faltering construction rates. Although the conclusion of each year typically ushers in a slowdown in housing activity, the latest data for new-home sales showcases further deceleration, likely caused by high mortgage rates and economic unease.

The Terner Center for Housing Innovation at UC Berkeley does not take positions on bills or legislation. But Garcia does note that the initiative may encourage more than buyers.

“By limiting the use of funds to newly built housing, it also may act as an incentive for builders to build more homes that are for sale,” he says.

Although his focus is on housing in Sacramento, Lane points out that California’s homeownership rates leave much to be desired.

“We have one of the lowest homeownership rates in the nation here in California because of our high housing costs and the median home price of over $800,000; it makes it very difficult for working families to scrape together the 20% down payment,” he notes.

Notably, California is one of only a few states where new homes are cheaper than existing homes, making Proposition 37 potentially more powerful at addressing affordability.

Lane also believes that more changes to California’s housing market will come, specifically by drawing investors and builders to the state.

“We’ve been working on this issue for decades and will continue to do so; there’s always more to do,” Lane says. “In California, the cost of construction and the rules for project approvals can make it very difficult and time-consuming. That’s why investors oftentimes look for other opportunities rather than investing in housing in California. We’ll continue to make it more business-friendly and friendly for housing construction.”

With five years’ worth of work nearing its climax, Hertzberg states that his goal with Prop 37 is to encourage the supply of affordable homes, in the hopes of addressing California’s low homeownership rates.

“It’s the simplest rule in economics, supply and demand,” he adds. “You get more supply, it works better. People can say all the arguments they want to make, but we don’t have enough middle-class housing.”

Despite his retirement, Hertzberg noted that he’s met with a handful of opposing groups, but states that many arguments against the initiative have not “done their homework.”

The League of Women Voters in California (LWV) declined to speak with RISMedia on the proposition, but they are opposed to it. The group’s argument is that the proposition essentially adds a second mortgage for buyers to repay, alongside their primary mortgage, each month.

“The program could reinforce racial and economic gaps instead of targeting families facing the greatest barriers,” the LWV’s voting recommendations state. “Generations of housing discrimination have left many Black and Latino families with less wealth to draw on, but Prop 37 gives no priority to first-time or first-generation buyers and does not exclude current or former homeowners. Households earning up to twice the area median income could qualify, including some earning more than $300,000 a year, while buyers would still have to provide at least 3% of the home price.”

The LWV also stated that voters would not know the interest rate, loan term or monthly payment amount prior to the program’s approval. Essentially, the LWV argues that the program would put homeowners in more debt.

Hertzberg rejected these notions, responding that the group’s arguments are “ridiculous” and that with purchase money security interest (PMSI), the only players to take a loss should there be a significant downturn in home prices are the banks and bondholders.

“PMSI means that there is no liability,” Hertzberg claims. “Assume we had a downturn, where a home’s value drops significantly. The bank and the bondholders take the loss. The only thing that the buyer loses if they buy a house for $900,000, is $30,000. There’s no downside risk beyond losing your down payment.”

He also emphasizes the safeguards the initiative includes, in reference to the 2008 financial crisis that rocked the world.

“People in 2008 had variable-rate mortgages. Their mortgage went from $1,200 to $2,400, and they couldn’t afford it. These down payment loans are fixed-rate mortgages. For renters, I promise you this much: In 10 years your rent’s going up. That doesn’t happen in a fixed-rate mortgage,” Hertzberg stresses.

While it may not be the optimal option for all first-time homebuyers, Garcia does acknowledge that some buyers in California may find use out of the program.

“I think it’s useful in a circumstance where a homebuyer or family has the income to cover the payments for both a first and second mortgage, but don’t have the liquidity,” he says. “It’s just an alternative pathway for individuals who just don’t have a lot of cash on hand to afford homeownership.”

Desirae Sin is an assistant editor for RISMedia. She graduated from the University of Connecticut in 2025 with a double major in Journalism and Political Science. Prior to joining RISMedia, Desirae wrote stories geared toward policy issues for the Connecticut Mirror. She also worked as a staff writer for The Daily Campus, UConn's student-run newspaper.
